Explore → Hypnosis Experience, Training & Approach As the former owner and primary hypnotist at Baltimore Hypnosis
      Center, I bring years of experience working with hypnosis,
      mindfulness, visualization, and other approaches to personal
      transformation. I became a Board Certified Hypnotist through the
      National Guild of Hypnotists (NGH) in 2007 and have continued to
      build on that foundation through experience, study, and exploration
      of different approaches to behavior and change. My training includes the structured 5-PATH approach to hypnosis,
      which provides a systematic framework for conducting a hypnotic
      session and working with the patterns that may be involved in a
      person's particular concern. I also draw from mindfulness,
      visualization, NLP, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), Dialectical
      Behavior Therapy (DBT), and other behavioral and contemplative
      approaches. These approaches give me a broader toolkit rather than a single
      formula that has to work for everyone. Whether someone is working
      on a habit, stress, confidence, behavior change, personal
      development, or another challenge, the approach can be adapted to
      the individual and the goal. My work with hypnosis has included concerns such as weight
      management, smoking cessation, stress, fears, habits, and other
      areas where changing established patterns may be useful. I also
      have a particular interest in the relationship between hypnosis,
      mindfulness, behavior, and addiction and recovery. Hypnosis isn't a replacement for appropriate medical or mental
      health care, nor is it a magic solution to every problem. I see it
      as one practical tool that can be incorporated into a larger
      approach to understanding ourselves and creating meaningful change. If you'd like to learn more about my professional experience,
      training, and work at Baltimore Hypnosis Center, you can read my Hypnosis Professional Experience page. Hypnosis is Often Misrepresented by Hollywood Hypnosis: Not as Mysterious as It Seems The word "hypnosis" can make the subject sound far more mysterious
      than it really is. Movies and television often portray hypnosis as something
      mysterious: a hypnotist waves a pocket watch, says a few carefully
      chosen words, and somehow takes control of another person's mind. That's a great premise for a movie. It isn't a very good description
      of hypnosis. Much like computers, medicine, psychology, and many other subjects,
      hypnosis has been represented in popular culture in ways that don't
      necessarily correspond to how it works in real life. My view of hypnosis is considerably less mysterious. I see hypnosis
      as a useful term for a collection of ordinary human processes,
      including focused attention, absorption, imagination, expectation,
      suggestion, emotion, perception, and the way we respond to
      information and context, that can be deliberately harnessed for
      personal change. These processes aren't unique to hypnosis. We experience them
      throughout everyday life. What makes hypnotic work interesting is
      that we can deliberately structure and direct these natural
      capacities toward a particular purpose. Hypnosis Is Something You Experience, Not Something Done to You A hypnotist doesn't magically create hypnosis inside another
      person's mind. I think of the hypnotist more as a guide or coach. The practitioner
      provides structure, language, suggestions, imagery, and direction
      that can help a person deliberately focus their attention and
      become more deeply absorbed in an experience. The person experiencing hypnosis remains an active participant.
      Their expectations, interpretation of the experience, willingness
      to participate, attention, imagination, and response to suggestion
      all matter. This is one reason the relationship between the hypnotist and
      client is important. A hypnotist can have tremendous technical
      skill, but if a client doesn't trust the practitioner, doesn't
      understand the process, or believes that hypnosis cannot work for
      them, simply performing a technically perfect induction isn't
      likely to accomplish very much. Hypnosis isn't a magic trick that works independently of the person
      experiencing it. It is an interaction between the practitioner,
      the participant, the context, and a collection of psychological
      processes that are already part of being human. Focused Attention and Selective Thinking One of the central ideas in my approach is that hypnosis involves
      more than simply "going into a trance." It involves changes in how
      attention is directed and how information is processed and
      interpreted. When attention becomes highly focused, some information becomes
      more prominent while other information fades into the background.
      Our thinking can also become more selective. We may temporarily
      give greater attention and significance to certain ideas,
      sensations, memories, images, or possibilities while paying less
      attention to others. This happens all the time without anyone calling it hypnosis. You can become completely absorbed in a movie and temporarily stop
      analyzing whether every scene could really happen. You can become
      so involved in a book that you lose track of time. You can become
      absorbed in a difficult programming problem, a piece of music, a
      video game, or an idea that fascinates you. Hypnotic techniques provide ways of deliberately working with this
      same flexibility of attention and experience. Hypnosis Doesn't Require Relaxation Hypnosis is often associated with relaxation, and relaxation can
      certainly be useful. A comfortable and relaxed person may find it
      easier to reduce distractions, focus attention, and become absorbed
      in an experience. But relaxation isn't the definition of hypnosis. Attention can become highly focused under many different emotional
      conditions. Curiosity, excitement, anticipation, fascination,
      love, fear, anger, frustration, and other emotional states can all
      dramatically affect attention and perception. In fact, if someone is already highly emotional about something,
      their attention may already be intensely focused on it. Rather than
      having to create focused attention from scratch, a practitioner may
      be able to work with the attention and emotional activation that are
      already present. The useful question isn't necessarily "How relaxed is this person?"
      but rather "How is this person's attention operating right now, and
      how can that attention be used constructively?" Cathy Green - Performing Hypnosis Hypnosis Happens in Everyday Life You don't need a hypnotist to experience the kinds of focused
      attention and absorption associated with hypnosis. Have you ever become so absorbed in a movie that you temporarily
      forgot about everything happening around you? Have you ever lost
      track of time while reading, listening to music, working on a
      project, playing a game, or becoming deeply involved in a
      conversation? These experiences demonstrate how flexible human attention can be.
      Our awareness can become intensely focused on one thing while
      other information fades into the background. Another familiar example is what is commonly called highway hypnosis : driving a familiar route while becoming
      so absorbed in your thoughts that you arrive at your destination
      with little conscious memory of the individual turns and
      landmarks along the way. Daydreaming, intense concentration, creative absorption, and
      familiar automatic routines can all provide useful examples of
      how attention and awareness can operate differently from our
      ordinary conversational state. What Does a Hypnotist Actually Do? A hypnotist doesn't perform an incantation that magically creates
      hypnosis in another person. I think of the hypnotist more as a guide or coach. The practitioner
      provides structure, language, suggestions, imagery, and direction
      that can help a person deliberately focus their attention and
      become more deeply absorbed in an experience. The participant isn't simply sitting there waiting for something
      to happen to them. They are participating in the process. In that sense, hypnosis is something you experience ,
      not something that a hypnotist simply does to you . Cathy Green - In a Hypnosis Session Your Emotions Can Influence You Before You Think One of the most interesting aspects of human experience is that
      our responses aren't always preceded by deliberate conscious
      reasoning. Someone can say something that immediately makes you angry.
      Another person's tone of voice can make you feel safe or
      threatened before you've consciously analyzed what happened.
      A particular smell can suddenly bring back an old memory.
      A familiar song can transport you back to another time. These experiences illustrate how information can influence us
      through attention, memory, emotion, expectation, and association
      before we have consciously decided how to respond. There is an old saying that your spouse may be your best
      hypnotist. It isn't meant literally to suggest that your spouse
      possesses special hypnotic powers. It points toward something
      much more ordinary: people with whom we have strong emotional
      relationships can have an extraordinary ability to influence our
      attention, expectations, interpretations, and automatic responses. Hypnotic work can deliberately explore some of these same
      relationships between attention, expectation, imagination,
      emotion, and response. Dispelling the Myths About Hypnosis Once hypnosis is separated from its Hollywood portrayal, many
      of the familiar myths become much easier to understand. Myth: Hypnosis Is Mind Control Fictional characters such as Svengali helped establish the idea
      that a hypnotist can take control of another person's mind. Hypnosis does not give the hypnotist ownership of another person's
      thoughts or decisions. The person experiencing hypnosis continues
      to have their own values, preferences, thoughts, and ability to
      make choices. Suggestion can influence attention, imagination, perception, and
      experience, but influence is not the same thing as control. There are many Common Myths about Hypnosis Myth: Hypnosis Means Losing Control Hypnosis isn't about handing your will over to someone else. You can generally accept, ignore, reinterpret, or reject a
      suggestion. If you decide you no longer want to participate,
      you can communicate that decision and end the session. The hypnotist provides guidance. The participant remains an
      active part of the process. Myth: Hypnosis Can Make You Do Anything Stage hypnosis can make this misconception particularly
      convincing. Performers can appear to make participants behave
      in remarkably unusual ways. But stage hypnosis is also a performance. Participants volunteer,
      expectations are established, and people who are comfortable
      participating in an unusual experience are more likely to
      volunteer and respond enthusiastically. Hypnosis shouldn't be understood as a mechanism that allows a
      hypnotist to simply override someone's fundamental values or
      force them to act against their wishes. Myth: You Can Get Stuck in Hypnosis You cannot become permanently trapped in hypnosis. Hypnosis isn't a mysterious place that someone enters and
      cannot leave. Attention naturally shifts, and a person can
      return to ordinary alertness. Someone who appears reluctant to emerge from a deeply relaxed
      state may simply be enjoying the experience. A trained
      practitioner can provide appropriate guidance for bringing
      the session to a close. Myth: Hypnosis Gives You Magical Powers Hypnosis isn't magic and it doesn't give someone supernatural
      abilities. What can sometimes appear extraordinary is the degree to which
      attention, expectation, imagination, suggestion, and context
      can influence human experience. These effects don't require a supernatural explanation. Myth: Analytical People Can't Be Hypnotized Being logical, analytical, skeptical, or highly intellectual
      doesn't make someone immune to hypnosis. Hypnosis doesn't require you to stop thinking. In fact, anyone
      who has become completely absorbed in reading, programming,
      solving a difficult problem, making music, creating art, or
      researching something fascinating already knows something about
      the power of focused attention. Different people simply respond to different ways of focusing
      attention and engaging imagination and expectation. What Hypnosis Is Really About Strip away the pocket watches, mysterious music, swinging
      pendulums, and Hollywood mind control, and something much more
      interesting remains. Hypnosis is about the remarkable flexibility of human attention
      and experience. We are constantly responding to information, expectations,
      memories, emotions, environments, and other people. Many of
      those responses happen automatically before we have consciously
      decided how to respond. Hypnotic techniques provide one way of deliberately working with
      those processes. The goal isn't to surrender control of your mind. The goal is to become more aware of how your mind already works
        and discover where you may have more flexibility and choice
        than you realized. Hypnosis and Personal Transformation Lasting change usually involves more than simply deciding that
      we want something to be different. We develop habits, emotional
      associations, expectations, beliefs, and automatic responses
      over time. Hypnosis provides one way of deliberately working with some of
      those processes rather than relying exclusively on conscious
      effort. It can be combined with mindfulness, visualization, behavioral
      techniques, cognitive approaches, and other methods to create a
      broader framework for understanding and changing patterns. Hypnosis and Addiction & Recovery Addiction provides a particularly interesting example of how
      automatic patterns can develop and become difficult to change. My approach to addiction and recovery is informed by my experience
      with SMART Recovery and by an interest in behavioral science,
      mindfulness, CBT, DBT, and other approaches to understanding
      behavior and change. Hypnosis can be considered as one supplemental tool within that
      larger framework. It isn't a replacement for appropriate medical,
      psychological, or addiction treatment, but it can provide another
      way of exploring attention, habits, associations, motivation,
      and behavioral patterns. Your Path to Transformation Hypnosis is only one part of a broader approach to understanding
      people, behavior, and personal change. If you're interested in hypnosis, I invite you to explore the
      rest of the site as well. You'll find information about
      mindfulness, meditation, addiction and recovery, behavior change,
      emotional regulation, and other approaches to understanding the
      patterns that shape our lives. Learn More About Hypnosis Graphology (Handwriting Analysis) Ever wondered what your handwriting says about you? Addiction Alternatives: A Pathway to Recovery The Challenge of Addiction: A Personal Struggle Issues with Traditional Treatment: Breaking the Cycle Traditional treatment methods, particularly the cycle of Rehab followed by Twelve Step Meetings, prove to be a daunting treadmill. Many addicts, after numerous treatments, find themselves locked into a singular approach. The prevalent emphasis on the Twelve Step / AA / NA process in many Rehab centers often leaves individuals feeling trapped, as if there's no other way to achieve sobriety. Alternative Approaches: Empowering Recovery Thankfully, there exist alternative paths to sobriety. One such transformative approach is SMART Recovery. This method focuses on empowering individuals through Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), Dialectical Behavioral Therapy (DBT), Rational Emotive Behavioral Therapy (REBT), Motivational Interviewing, and Mindfulness. Unlike traditional Twelve Step programs, SMART Recovery emphasizes self-empowerment and does not mandate submission to a higher power. Participants are equipped with practical tools to combat cravings, develop healthier thought patterns, and engage in positive activities. The Power of Hypnosis: Unraveling Subconscious Patterns Hypnosis stands as a potent tool in the journey of addiction recovery. A skilled hypnotist, well-versed in a myriad of modalities, can effectively coach clients into discovering and resolving hidden patterns driving addictive behaviors. Unlike traditional approaches, hypnosis engages the client's subconscious mind, delving into the vast reservoir of their knowledge and experiences. It uncovers subconscious drivers that often lie beyond conscious awareness. Traditional methods, reliant on conscious reasoning, often fall short because the roots of addiction develop long before symptoms manifest. Merely talking about the problem is insufficient; effective hypnotherapy allows the subconscious mind to construct solutions to the addiction. I strongly urge you to explore hypnosis as a modality for your recovery. With proper guidance, your subconscious mind can illuminate a path through your struggles far more effectively than traditional methods. Astrologers then interpret the relationships between those placements to explore personality, tendencies, life themes, relationships, challenges, and possibilities. What is a birth chart? + A birth chart, also called a natal chart, is a map of the sky for a particular moment and location, most commonly the moment of someone's birth. It shows where the Sun, Moon, planets, zodiac signs, houses, and other points were located at that time. Rather than reducing a person to one zodiac sign, a birth chart provides a much more complete picture of the different energies and patterns represented in the chart. Is astrology more than just your zodiac sign? + Yes. Your Sun sign is only one part of your birth chart. A complete chart includes the Moon, Rising sign, planets, houses, aspects, planetary rulers, and many other relationships and placements. Looking only at the Sun sign is like saying you have read a book because you read the cover. It can tell you something, but it leaves most of the story unread. What information is needed to calculate a birth chart? + A precise birth chart normally requires three pieces of information: your date of birth, your exact or reasonably accurate time of birth, and your place of birth. The date determines the general planetary positions, while the time and location are particularly important for calculating the Rising sign and houses. Why does my exact birth time matter? + The sky is constantly moving, and the Earth is constantly rotating. The Ascendant and houses can change relatively quickly, so even a difference of a few hours can significantly change those parts of a chart. The exact effect depends on the individual chart and the technique being used. What if I don't know my exact birth time? + A chart can still provide useful information without a known birth time, although some parts become uncertain. The Rising sign, houses, Midheaven, and other time-sensitive calculations may not be reliable. Some astrologers use techniques such as chart rectification to explore possible birth times, but that is a more specialized practice. Astrology in History How old is astrology? + Astrology has a very long history. Different forms of celestial observation and divination developed in several ancient cultures, including Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, India, China, and others. What we now call Western horoscopic astrology developed through a long exchange of ideas among ancient traditions, particularly in the Hellenistic world. How was astrology practiced in the ancient world? + Ancient astrologers did not have modern computers, calculators, or online chart generators. They relied on careful observations of the sky, mathematical calculations, astronomical tables, calendars, ephemerides, and accumulated traditions. Astrology was closely related to astronomy, calendrical calculation, religion, medicine, politics, agriculture, and questions about events and timing. Was astrology always about personality? + No. Modern astrology often emphasizes personality, self-understanding, relationships, and personal development, but historical astrology was used for many different purposes. Depending on the culture and period, astrologers examined political events, weather, agriculture, relationships, health, elections and timing, mundane events, and questions about individuals. What is an ephemeris? + An ephemeris is a table showing the calculated positions of celestial bodies for particular dates and times. Before computerized astrology software and online calculators, astrologers commonly used ephemerides along with other astronomical tables to determine planetary positions and construct charts. Why is modern astrology so strongly associated with Sun signs? + Much of modern popular astrology was shaped by newspapers and magazines. A complete birth chart requires information such as birth time and location, while someone's Sun sign can be determined simply from a birthday. That made Sun-sign astrology much easier to turn into a short, mass-market column that could be read by millions of people. By the 1930s, the familiar newspaper-style Sun-sign horoscope had become an important part of popular astrology. Was the Rising sign more important before Sun-sign astrology became popular? + The Ascendant has historically been extremely important in many traditions of horoscopic astrology. It is closely connected with the houses and therefore provides the framework in which the rest of the chart is interpreted. Modern popular astrology shifted much of the public's attention toward the Sun sign because it was dramatically easier to determine and communicate to a mass audience. Why does a newspaper horoscope seem so different from a birth chart reading? + A newspaper horoscope is usually written for a broad group of people sharing the same Sun sign, or sometimes another simplified chart factor. A birth chart reading considers an individual's actual planetary placements, houses, aspects, and other relationships. A generic horoscope therefore describes possibilities for a large group, while a natal chart provides a much more individualized framework. What does horoscope actually mean? + The word horoscope has historically referred to a chart or diagram representing the positions of celestial bodies for a particular moment and place. In popular culture, however, the word has become strongly associated with short newspaper and magazine predictions. These are related concepts, but they are not the same thing as a complete individualized birth chart. Types and Systems of Astrology Are there different types of astrology? + Yes. Astrology is not a single universal system. Different cultures developed their own traditions, techniques, calendars, zodiac systems, philosophical assumptions, and methods of interpretation. Western astrology, Vedic astrology, Chinese astrology, Hellenistic astrology, medieval astrology, and many other traditions have their own approaches. What is Western astrology? + Western astrology is a broad family of traditions that developed through ancient Mediterranean and European astrology and continued to evolve over centuries. Modern Western astrology commonly uses the zodiac signs, planets, houses, aspects, transits, progressions, and other techniques. There are also many different schools and approaches within Western astrology. What is Vedic astrology? + Vedic astrology, commonly called Jyotish, is the traditional astrological system associated with India. It has its own terminology, techniques, philosophical framework, and methods of chart calculation. Many forms of Jyotish use a sidereal zodiac and place substantial emphasis on the Moon, lunar mansions called nakshatras, planetary periods, and other techniques that differ from common Western practice. What is Chinese astrology? + Chinese astrology developed within Chinese cultural and philosophical traditions and uses a substantially different framework from Western astrology. It includes systems involving the Chinese zodiac, elemental relationships, yin and yang, heavenly stems and earthly branches, and other methods of analyzing cycles and relationships. What is Hellenistic astrology? + Hellenistic astrology refers to the traditions of horoscopic astrology that developed in the Hellenistic world during antiquity. It is an important historical foundation for many later Western astrological traditions and places substantial importance on the Ascendant, houses, planetary condition, aspects, and the relationship between planets and specific areas of life. What is the difference between Western and Vedic astrology? + Western and Vedic astrology share some historical roots and vocabulary but developed into distinct systems. They can use different zodiac frameworks, house methods, interpretive techniques, terminology, and priorities. A person may therefore receive different planetary sign placements when looking at Western and Vedic charts. A difference does not necessarily mean that one chart was calculated incorrectly; the systems are using different frameworks. Why is my sign different in Vedic astrology? + One major reason is that many forms of Vedic astrology use a sidereal zodiac, while modern Western astrology commonly uses a tropical zodiac. Because of the gradual precession of Earth's axis, the two zodiac frameworks have drifted apart by roughly one sign. This can result in different sign placements for the same birth data. Which type of astrology is the most accurate? + There is no universally accepted way to answer that question. Different astrological systems have different purposes, assumptions, calculations, and interpretive traditions. Rather than treating astrology as one system competing against another, it can be more useful to understand what each tradition is designed to examine and how its practitioners interpret a chart. Are there other forms of astrology besides Western, Vedic, and Chinese astrology? + Yes. There are numerous historical and contemporary traditions, including Hellenistic, Persian, Arabic, medieval, Renaissance, electional, horary, mundane, medical, financial, and various modern psychological and evolutionary approaches. There are also specialized techniques that can be used within a larger astrological system. Zodiac Signs What are the twelve zodiac signs? + The twelve signs are Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. Each sign is traditionally associated with particular qualities, elemental characteristics, modalities, planetary rulerships, and symbolic themes. What do zodiac signs represent? + In astrology, signs describe qualities or styles through which planetary energies are expressed. A planet can be thought of as representing an energy or function, while the sign describes something about how that energy tends to operate. What are the elements in astrology? + The twelve signs are grouped into four elements: Fire, Earth, Air, and Water. Fire is traditionally associated with energy, inspiration, and action; Earth with practicality, stability, and tangible matters; Air with thought, communication, and relationships; and Water with emotion, intuition, sensitivity, and depth. What are the modalities in astrology? + The signs are also divided into three modalities: Cardinal, Fixed, and Mutable. Cardinal signs are associated with initiation, Fixed signs with persistence and stabilization, and Mutable signs with adaptation, transition, and flexibility. Does my zodiac sign determine my personality? + Not by itself. Your Sun sign describes one important part of a chart, but your personality is represented through many interacting factors. The Moon, Ascendant, other planets, houses, aspects, planetary rulers, and the overall balance of the chart can all modify how a particular sign is expressed. Why don't I feel like my birth sign? + Your Sun sign is only one part of your birth chart. You may have a Rising sign that expresses itself very differently from your Sun sign, a Moon sign that describes your emotional nature differently, or strong planetary placements and aspects that create competing or complementary patterns. For example, a difficult aspect such as a square or opposition involving the Sun and Ascendant can symbolize tension between how you experience yourself and how you naturally present yourself to others. Planets and Planetary Energies What do planets represent in astrology? + Planets are commonly interpreted as different functions, drives, or types of energy within a chart. The sign describes how that energy is expressed, while the house describes an area of life in which it tends to operate. What does the Sun represent? + The Sun is associated with vitality, identity, individuality, self-expression, purpose, and the development of one's sense of self. What does the Moon represent? + The Moon is associated with emotions, instincts, habits, reactions, security needs, memory, and the way we respond to experiences on a more personal and immediate level. What does Mercury represent? + Mercury is associated with communication, thinking, learning, observation, reasoning, information, and the way we process and exchange ideas. What does Venus represent? + Venus is associated with attraction, relationships, affection, aesthetics, pleasure, values, harmony, and the things we appreciate or find desirable. What does Mars represent? + Mars is associated with action, motivation, assertion, desire, initiative, competition, physical energy, and how we pursue what we want. What does Jupiter represent? + Jupiter is associated with expansion, growth, optimism, opportunity, philosophy, belief, exploration, learning, and the search for meaning. What does Saturn represent? + Saturn is associated with structure, discipline, responsibility, boundaries, limitations, patience, maturity, and long-term development. What do Uranus, Neptune, and Pluto represent? + Uranus, Neptune, and Pluto are often called the outer or generational planets because their slow movement means that many people born within the same period share their sign placements. They can still become highly personal when they strongly aspect personal planets or important chart points. Uranus is associated with change and independence, Neptune with imagination, ideals and dissolution, and Pluto with transformation, power, and profound change. What are planetary rulers? + In astrology, each zodiac sign has a traditional planetary ruler. For example, Mars traditionally rules Aries, Venus rules Taurus and Libra, Mercury rules Gemini and Virgo, and so on. The ruler of a sign can provide another layer of interpretation when examining where that sign appears in a chart. Understanding the Birth Chart What is the Rising sign? + The Rising sign, or Ascendant, is the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the time and location of birth. It is especially important because it establishes the starting point for the houses in many astrological systems. It is also commonly associated with one's outward style, first impressions, approach to life, and the way one initially engages with the world. What is the difference between my Sun sign, Moon sign, and Rising sign? + These three placements describe different dimensions of a chart. The Sun is commonly associated with identity, vitality, and self-expression. The Moon relates to emotional needs, instincts, and reactions. The Rising sign describes the Ascendant and the way a person approaches the world and may initially appear to others. None of these three should be treated as the entire personality by itself. Why is the Rising sign so important? + The Ascendant is important because it establishes the framework for the houses in many house systems. It therefore affects where the signs and planets fall throughout the chart. In traditional astrology, the Ascendant is also a major indicator of the individual and the beginning point of the horoscope. What are houses in astrology? + Houses divide the chart into twelve areas associated with different areas of life and experience. While signs describe qualities and planets describe energies or functions, houses describe where those energies are expressed. What do the twelve houses represent? + The twelve houses are traditionally associated with themes including identity, possessions and values, communication, home and family, creativity and self-expression, work and service, partnerships, shared resources and transformation, higher learning and worldview, career and public life, friendships and groups, and the inner or hidden dimensions of experience. What does it mean to have a planet in a house? + A planet in a house suggests that the function represented by that planet has an important relationship to the area of life represented by the house. For example, Venus in the seventh house would bring Venus themes into the area of partnerships, while Mars in the tenth house could emphasize action, ambition, and drive within career or public life. What does it mean when a planet rules a house? + The sign on a house cusp determines its planetary ruler in systems that use sign-based house rulership. The location and condition of that ruling planet can provide additional information about how the affairs of that house may operate in the chart. What is a house cusp? + A cusp is the boundary where one house begins and another ends. The sign located on that boundary is particularly important when determining the ruler of the house and interpreting the house's themes. Aspects and Planetary Relationships What is an aspect in astrology? + An aspect is an angular relationship between two planets or other significant points in a chart. Aspects describe how different planetary energies interact with one another. They can indicate areas where energies cooperate easily as well as areas where they create tension, challenge, or pressure for development. What is a conjunction? + A conjunction occurs when two planets or points are close together in the zodiac. Their energies are combined and intensified, although the way the conjunction operates depends on the planets, signs, houses, and other factors involved. What is a square? + A square is an aspect of approximately 90 degrees. It is traditionally associated with tension, friction, challenge, and the need to reconcile different drives. Squares are not necessarily negative; they can create motivation, strength, and opportunities for development. What is an opposition? + An opposition occurs when two planets or points are approximately 180 degrees apart. It can symbolize polarity or tension between two areas of life, often creating a need to find balance between seemingly opposing forces. What is a trine? + A trine is an aspect of approximately 120 degrees. It is traditionally considered harmonious and can indicate energies that work together naturally or easily. What is a sextile? + A sextile is an aspect of approximately 60 degrees. It is generally considered supportive and can indicate opportunities for cooperation, learning, development, and constructive interaction. Are squares and oppositions bad aspects? + Not necessarily. It is tempting to label aspects as good or bad, but real charts are more complicated. Challenging aspects can represent friction, but friction can also create awareness, motivation, resilience, and growth. Harmonious aspects can provide natural strengths, but they can also be taken for granted. What are orbs? + An orb is the amount of allowable distance from an exact aspect. Different astrologers and traditions use different orb ranges. Generally, a tighter aspect is considered more exact, while a wider aspect may be interpreted as weaker or more subtle. Intermediate Chart Interpretation What are intercepted signs? + An interception occurs in certain house systems when an entire zodiac sign falls inside a house without appearing on a house cusp. Some astrologers interpret intercepted signs as energies that may be less immediately accessible or require additional development and awareness. What are decans? + Each zodiac sign contains 30 degrees and can be divided into three sections of ten degrees called decans. Decans provide another layer of symbolic differentiation within a sign and can be used to add nuance to an interpretation. What is a stellium? + A stellium is a concentration of several planets or important chart points in the same sign or house, depending on the definition being used. It can make the themes represented by that area particularly prominent. What does it mean to have a strong planet? + A planet can be considered strong for many different reasons depending on the astrological tradition being used. Its sign placement, house, rulership, angularity, aspects, dignity, and relationship with other chart factors can all contribute to how prominently its energy is expressed. Why can't you interpret a planet by itself? + A planet's meaning changes depending on its sign, house, aspects, rulerships, and relationships with the rest of the chart. Reading one placement in isolation can produce an interesting description, but reading the relationships between placements provides a much richer interpretation. Why can two people with the same Sun sign be completely different? + Because two people born under the same Sun sign can have very different Moon signs, Rising signs, planetary placements, houses, aspects, and overall chart patterns. Even people born on the same day can have substantially different charts when their birth times and locations differ. Advanced Astrology What are house systems? + A house system is a mathematical method for dividing the horoscope into twelve houses. Different systems can place house cusps differently, particularly at higher latitudes, and astrologers may choose different systems based on their tradition or approach. What is the Placidus house system? + Placidus is one of the most widely used house systems in modern Western astrology. It is a quadrant house system that calculates houses using time-based divisions of the diurnal movement of the sky. What is the difference between Placidus and Whole Sign houses? + Placidus and Whole Sign are different ways of dividing the horoscope. In Whole Sign houses, each zodiac sign becomes an entire house. In Placidus, house cusps are calculated using a time-based geometric method. The same birth chart can therefore produce different house placements depending on the system used. Why do different house systems produce different readings? + Different house systems divide the sky differently. This can move a planet from one house to another or change the exact house cusps. The planetary positions in the zodiac do not necessarily change; rather, the framework used to interpret where those planets operate can change. What are degrees in astrology? + Each zodiac sign contains 30 degrees, making 360 degrees around the entire zodiac. The exact degree of a planet can matter when examining aspects, conjunctions, house cusps, decans, and other specialized techniques. What are transits? + Transits describe the current or future movement of planets in relation to the positions in a natal chart. They are commonly used to explore periods of change, opportunity, pressure, development, and other recurring planetary cycles. What are progressions? + Progressions are a symbolic timing technique used to explore personal development over time. One common Western technique is secondary progression, in which each day after birth symbolically corresponds to approximately one year of life. What is a progressed chart? + A progressed chart is a chart calculated using a progression technique to examine how the symbolic planetary picture develops over time. Progressions are often used alongside the natal chart and transits rather than as a replacement for the birth chart. What are Chiron, Lilith, and the Part of Fortune? + These are examples of additional chart points used by some astrologers. Chiron is often associated with themes of vulnerability, healing, and integration. Black Moon Lilith is used in several different ways depending on the tradition and calculation. The Part of Fortune is a calculated point with a long history in traditional astrology and is interpreted in relation to topics such as circumstances, resources, and flourishing. What Can Astrology Be Used For? What can a birth chart tell me? + A birth chart can be used as a framework for exploring personality, tendencies, motivations, emotional patterns, relationships, strengths, challenges, and areas of potential development. I approach the chart as a map of tendencies and energies rather than a simple list of predetermined outcomes. Can astrology help me understand my personality? + Yes. A chart can be examined as a collection of interacting tendencies. Rather than asking "Which sign am I?", a more useful question is often "What combination of energies am I working with, and how do they interact?" Can astrology identify areas I may want to work on? + A chart can be used to identify patterns that may be worth exploring, including tensions between different parts of the personality, recurring challenges, underdeveloped qualities, or energies that may feel difficult to access. The purpose is not to label someone as defective, but to provide another perspective for self-reflection. Can astrology help me understand my strengths? + Yes. Harmonious aspects, prominent planets, strong sign placements, house emphasis, and other chart patterns can suggest areas where certain energies may feel particularly accessible or natural. What does it mean when an energy is difficult for me to access? + Some chart patterns can suggest that certain qualities do not come naturally or are expressed indirectly. Other patterns can indicate that an energy is extremely strong but difficult to regulate. Exploring both the accessible and challenging parts of a chart can create a more balanced picture of personality. Can astrology answer specific questions? + Astrology can be approached through several question-oriented techniques. A question can be explored in relation to the natal chart, current transits, progressions, or other techniques depending on the nature of the question. The chart provides context rather than a simple yes-or-no answer to every possible question. What is synastry? + Synastry is the comparison of two birth charts to explore the relationships between them. It can be used to examine attraction, communication, emotional compatibility, tension, shared strengths, and the ways two people's planetary patterns interact. Can astrology be used for relationships? + Yes. Relationship astrology can include synastry, composite charts, individual natal charts, and timing techniques. These approaches can be used to explore how two people interact rather than simply assigning a compatibility score based on their Sun signs. What is location astrology? + Location-based astrology examines the relationship between astrology and geographic places. Depending on the technique, this can include examining a person's chart in relation to different locations, as well as exploring the astrological history or symbolism associated with a particular city, region, or place. What is astrocartography? + Astrocartography is a location-based technique that projects planetary positions from a birth chart onto a world map. It is commonly used to explore how different geographic locations may emphasize different planetary themes in an individual's chart. What is mundane astrology? + Mundane astrology is concerned with larger collective subjects such as countries, governments, political events, social trends, and other developments involving groups or societies rather than only individual birth charts. What is electional astrology? + Electional astrology is the practice of selecting a favorable time for beginning an activity or event. The underlying idea is that the astrological conditions surrounding the beginning of something can be considered when choosing a time to initiate it. What is horary astrology? + Horary astrology is a question-oriented branch of astrology in which an astrologer constructs a chart for the time and place when a particular question is asked and then interprets that chart according to horary techniques. How I Approach Chart Interpretation How do you interpret a birth chart? + I look at the chart as an interconnected system rather than a list of isolated meanings. I consider the signs, planets, Rising sign, houses, planetary rulers, aspects, and other relevant chart factors and then look for patterns. The goal is to understand which energies appear naturally accessible, which may be more challenging, and how different parts of the chart interact. Do you just tell me what my signs mean? + No. Sign descriptions are a useful starting point, but they are only one layer of astrology. A personalized reading looks at where the planets are located, what houses they occupy, what aspects they make, what signs rule important houses, and how those pieces fit together. What do you mean by "energies"? + When I use the word energies, I am referring to the symbolic qualities traditionally associated with planets, signs, houses, and their relationships. For example, Mars can be associated with action and assertion, while Venus can be associated with attraction, values, and harmony. The chart shows how these different symbolic energies are combined. Can the same placement have both positive and difficult expressions? + Absolutely. A planetary placement is not necessarily good or bad. The same energy can be expressed in different ways depending on the rest of the chart and the circumstances of the individual. One of the most useful parts of interpretation is exploring both the strengths and challenges of a particular pattern. Does astrology say that my future is predetermined? + I do not approach astrology as a rigid statement that everything is predetermined. I see a chart more as a map of tendencies, patterns, possibilities, and cycles. How a person responds to those patterns remains an important part of the picture. Can astrology replace professional advice? + No. Astrology can be used for reflection, exploration, and personal insight, but it should not replace qualified medical, psychological, legal, financial, or other professional advice. Astrology Readings and Services Do you offer individual astrology readings? + Yes. Individual readings provide a more personalized opportunity to explore a complete birth chart, including personality patterns, accessible and challenging energies, relationships between different chart factors, and areas that may be useful for personal reflection or development. What happens during a general birth chart reading? + A general reading looks at the overall structure of your birth chart. Rather than focusing on one isolated placement, we can explore your major planetary energies, Sun, Moon, Rising sign, houses, aspects, strengths, challenges, and the ways these different pieces interact. Can I ask a specific question during a reading? + Yes. A reading can be organized around a particular question or area of interest. The question can then be considered in relation to your natal chart and, when appropriate, current planetary cycles or other techniques. Do you offer relationship or synastry readings? + Yes. Synastry readings compare two birth charts to explore the interaction between two people. This can provide a much richer perspective than simply comparing two Sun signs. Do you offer progressed chart readings? + Yes. Progressed chart readings can be used to explore longer-term developmental themes and changes in the symbolic chart over time. Progressions can also be considered alongside the natal chart and current transits. Do you offer astrology at parties and events? + Yes. I offer brief, entertaining birth chart insights for parties, corporate events, community functions, gatherings, and other events. These are designed to be engaging and accessible rather than lengthy private consultations. What are astrology readings like at an event? + Event readings are generally short, conversational, and designed to give each participant an interesting glimpse into their chart. They can spark conversations and provide guests with something personal and memorable to take away from the event. Do you teach astrology? + Yes. I teach astrology through seminars, workshops, and groups. The material can range from introductory concepts to more intermediate and advanced subjects depending on the group. What do you teach in an introductory astrology seminar? + Introductory material can include the twelve signs, their elements, modalities, energies and traits, planetary meanings, planetary rulers, and the basic structure of a birth chart. The goal is to give students a vocabulary for understanding astrology rather than simply memorizing Sun-sign descriptions. What do you teach at the intermediate level? + Intermediate material can include the houses and their meanings, house rulers, planets in houses, aspects such as conjunctions, squares, oppositions, trines and sextiles, interceptions, and the interpretation of the outer and generational planets. What can an advanced astrology class cover? + Advanced subjects can include different house systems such as Placidus and Whole Sign, degrees, decans, aspect orbs, additional chart points such as Chiron, Lilith and the Part of Fortune, progressions, transits, synastry, and other specialized techniques. Can you teach astrology to a group with no previous experience? + Yes. Astrology can be taught progressively, starting with the basic vocabulary of signs and planets and gradually introducing houses, aspects, rulerships, timing techniques, and more advanced interpretation. Can astrology be part of a corporate or community event? + Yes. Short astrology readings can work well as an interactive activity at corporate events, community functions, parties, social gatherings, and other events. The format can be adapted to the type of audience and amount of time available. title: About Hypnosis | Adam Fistler | South Jersey Hypnosis & Addiction Recovery Consultant
description: Adam Fistler offers specialized behavioral consulting, mindfulness, and hypnosis, and addiction & recovery help in South Jersey. Transform habit loops and tackle addiction recovery. I'm local to Camden, Gloucester, Burlington, and Atlantic Counties
content:
Search: Hypnosis Experience, Training & Approach As the former owner and primary hypnotist at Baltimore Hypnosis
            Center, I bring years of experience working with hypnosis,
            mindfulness, visualization, and other approaches to personal
            transformation. Now based right here in the South Jersey and Philadelphia area, I work with clients throughout Camden County, Gloucester County, Burlington County, and Atlantic County. I became a Board Certified Hypnotist through the
            National Guild of Hypnotists (NGH) in 2007 and have continued to
            build on that foundation through experience, study, and exploration
            of different approaches to behavior and change. My training includes the structured 5-PATH approach to hypnosis,
            which provides a systematic framework for conducting a hypnotic
            session and working with the patterns that may be involved in a
            person's particular concern. I also draw from mindfulness,
            visualization, NLP, Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), Dialectical
            Behavior Therapy (DBT), and other behavioral and contemplative
            approaches. These approaches give me a broader toolkit rather than a single
            formula that has to work for everyone. Whether someone in our local community is working
            on a habit, stress, confidence, behavior change, personal
            development, or another challenge, the approach can be adapted to
            the individual and the goal. My work with hypnosis has included concerns such as weight
            management, smoking cessation, stress, fears, habits, and other
            areas where changing established patterns may be useful. I also
            have a particular interest in the relationship between hypnosis,
            mindfulness, behavior, and addiction and recovery. Hypnosis isn't a replacement for appropriate medical or mental
            health care, nor is it a magic solution to every problem. I see it
            as one practical tool that can be incorporated into a larger
            approach to understanding ourselves and creating meaningful change. If you'd like to learn more about my professional experience,
            training, and work at Baltimore Hypnosis Center, you can read my Hypnosis Professional Experience page. Hypnosis is Often Misrepresented by Hollywood Hypnosis: Not as Mysterious as It Seems The word "hypnosis" can make the subject sound far more mysterious
            than it really is. Movies and television often portray hypnosis as something
            mysterious: a hypnotist waves a pocket watch, says a few carefully
            chosen words, and somehow takes control of another person's mind. That's a great premise for a movie. It isn't a very good description
            of hypnosis. Much like computers, medicine, psychology, and many other subjects,
            hypnosis has been represented in popular culture in ways that don't
            necessarily correspond to how it works in real life. My view of hypnosis is considerably less mysterious. I see hypnosis
            as a useful term for a collection of ordinary human processes,
            including focused attention, absorption, imagination, expectation,
            suggestion, emotion, perception, and the way we respond to
            information and context, that can be deliberately harnessed for
            personal change. These processes aren't unique to hypnosis. We experience them
            throughout everyday life. What makes hypnotic work interesting is
            that we can deliberately structure and direct these natural
            capacities toward a particular purpose. Hypnosis Is Something You Experience, Not Something Done to You A hypnotist doesn't magically create hypnosis inside another
            person's mind. I think of the hypnotist more as a guide or coach. The practitioner
            provides structure, language, suggestions, imagery, and direction
            that can help a person deliberately focus their attention and
            become more deeply absorbed in an experience. The person experiencing hypnosis remains an active participant.
            Their expectations, interpretation of the experience, willingness
            to participate, attention, imagination, and response to suggestion
            all matter. This is one reason the relationship between the hypnotist and
            client is important. A hypnotist can have tremendous technical
            skill, but if a client doesn't trust the practitioner, doesn't
            understand the process, or believes that hypnosis cannot work for
            them, simply performing a technically perfect induction isn't
            likely to accomplish very much. Hypnosis isn't a magic trick that works independently of the person
            experiencing it. It is an interaction between the practitioner,
            the participant, the context, and a collection of psychological
            processes that are already part of being human. Focused Attention and Selective Thinking One of the central ideas in my approach is that hypnosis involves
            more than simply "going into a trance." It involves changes in how
            attention is directed and how information is processed and
            interpreted. When attention becomes highly focused, some information becomes
            more prominent while other information fades into the background.
            Our thinking can also become more selective. We may temporarily
            give greater attention and significance to certain ideas,
            sensations, memories, images, or possibilities while paying less
            attention to others. This happens all the time without anyone calling it hypnosis. You can become completely absorbed in a movie and temporarily stop
            analyzing whether every scene could really happen. You can become
            so involved in a book that you lose track of time. You can become
            absorbed in a difficult programming problem, a piece of music, a
            video game, or an idea that fascinates you. Hypnotic techniques provide ways of deliberately working with this
            same flexibility of attention and experience. Hypnosis Doesn't Require Relaxation Hypnosis is often associated with relaxation, and relaxation can
            certainly be useful. A comfortable and relaxed person may find it
            easier to reduce distractions, focus attention, and become absorbed
            in an experience. But relaxation isn't the definition of hypnosis. Attention can become highly focused under many different emotional
            conditions. Curiosity, excitement, anticipation, fascination,
            love, fear, anger, frustration, and other emotional states can all
            dramatically affect attention and perception. In fact, if someone is already highly emotional about something,
            their attention may already be intensely focused on it. Rather than
            having to create focused attention from scratch, a practitioner may
            be able to work with the attention and emotional activation that are
            already present. The useful question isn't necessarily "How relaxed is this person?"
            but rather "How is this person's attention operating right now, and
            how can that attention be used constructively?" Cathy Green - Performing Hypnosis Hypnosis Happens in Everyday Life You don't need a hypnotist to experience the kinds of focused
            attention and absorption associated with hypnosis. Have you ever become so absorbed in a movie that you temporarily
            forgot about everything happening around you? Have you ever lost
            track of time while reading, listening to music, working on a
            project, playing a game, or becoming deeply involved in a
            conversation? These experiences demonstrate how flexible human attention can be.
            Our awareness can become intensely focused on one thing while
            other information fades into the background. Another familiar example is what is commonly called highway hypnosis : driving a familiar route while becoming
            so absorbed in your thoughts that you arrive at your destination
            with little conscious memory of the individual turns and
            landmarks along the way. Daydreaming, intense concentration, creative absorption, and
            familiar automatic routines can all provide useful examples of
            how attention and awareness can operate differently from our
            ordinary conversational state. What Does a Hypnotist Actually Do? A hypnotist doesn't perform an incantation that magically creates
            hypnosis in another person. I think of the hypnotist more as a guide or coach. The practitioner
            provides structure, language, suggestions, imagery, and direction
            that can help a person deliberately focus their attention and
            become more deeply absorbed in an experience. The participant isn't simply sitting there waiting for something
            to happen to them. They are participating in the process. In that sense, hypnosis is something you experience ,
            not something that a hypnotist simply does to you . Cathy Green - In a Hypnosis Session Your Emotions Can Influence You Before You Think One of the most interesting aspects of human experience is that
            our responses aren't always preceded by deliberate conscious
            reasoning. Someone can say something that immediately makes you angry.
            Another person's tone of voice can make you feel safe or
            threatened before you've consciously analyzed what happened.
            A particular smell can suddenly bring back an old memory.
            A familiar song can transport you back to another time. These experiences illustrate how information can influence us
            through attention, memory, emotion, expectation, and association
            before we have consciously decided how to respond. There is an old saying that your spouse may be your best
            hypnotist. It isn't meant literally to suggest that your spouse
            possesses special hypnotic powers. It points toward something
            much more ordinary: people with whom we have strong emotional
            relationships can have an extraordinary ability to influence our
            attention, expectations, interpretations, and automatic responses. Hypnotic work can deliberately explore some of these same
            relationships between attention, expectation, imagination,
            emotion, and response. Dispelling the Myths About Hypnosis Once hypnosis is separated from its Hollywood portrayal, many
            of the familiar myths become much easier to understand. Myth: Hypnosis Is Mind Control Fictional characters such as Svengali helped establish the idea
            that a hypnotist can take control of another person's mind. Hypnosis does not give the hypnotist ownership of another person's
            thoughts or decisions. The person experiencing hypnosis continues
            to have their own values, preferences, thoughts, and ability to
            make choices. Suggestion can influence attention, imagination, perception, and
            experience, but influence is not the same thing as control. There are many Common Myths about Hypnosis Myth: Hypnosis Means Losing Control Hypnosis isn't about handing your will over to someone else. You can generally accept, ignore, reinterpret, or reject a
            suggestion. If you decide you no longer want to participate,
            you can communicate that decision and end the session. The hypnotist provides guidance. The participant remains an
            active part of the process. Myth: Hypnosis Can Make You Do Anything Stage hypnosis can make this misconception particularly
            convincing. Performers can appear to make participants behave
            in remarkably unusual ways. But stage hypnosis is also a performance. Participants volunteer,
            expectations are established, and people who are comfortable
            participating in an unusual experience are more likely to
            volunteer and respond enthusiastically. Hypnosis shouldn't be understood as a mechanism that allows a
            hypnotist to simply override someone's fundamental values or
            force them to act against their wishes. Myth: You Can Get Stuck in Hypnosis You cannot become permanently trapped in hypnosis. Hypnosis isn't a mysterious place that someone enters and
            cannot leave. Attention naturally shifts, and a person can
            return to ordinary alertness. Someone who appears reluctant to emerge from a deeply relaxed
            state may simply be enjoying the experience. A trained
            practitioner can provide appropriate guidance for bringing
            the session to a close. Myth: Hypnosis Gives You Magical Powers Hypnosis isn't magic and it doesn't give someone supernatural
            abilities. What can sometimes appear extraordinary is the degree to which
            attention, expectation, imagination, suggestion, and context
            can influence human experience. These effects don't require a supernatural explanation. Myth: Analytical People Can't Be Hypnotized Being logical, analytical, skeptical, or highly intellectual
            doesn't make someone immune to hypnosis. Hypnosis doesn't require you to stop thinking. In fact, anyone
            who has become completely absorbed in reading, programming,
            solving a difficult problem, making music, creating art, or
            researching something fascinating already knows something about
            the power of focused attention. Different people simply respond to different ways of focusing
            attention and engaging imagination and expectation. What Hypnosis Is Really About Strip away the pocket watches, mysterious music, swinging
            pendulums, and Hollywood mind control, and something much more
            interesting remains. Hypnosis is about the remarkable flexibility of human attention
            and experience. We are constantly responding to information, expectations,
            memories, emotions, environments, and other people. Many of
            those responses happen automatically before we have consciously
            decided how to respond. Hypnotic techniques provide one way of deliberately working with
            those processes. The goal isn't to surrender control of your mind. The goal is to become more aware of how your mind already works
              and discover where you may have more flexibility and choice
              than you realized. Hypnosis and Personal Transformation Lasting change usually involves more than simply deciding that
            we want something to be different. We develop habits, emotional
            associations, expectations, beliefs, and automatic responses
            over time. Hypnosis provides one way of deliberately working with some of
            those processes rather than relying exclusively on conscious
            effort. It can be combined with mindfulness, visualization, behavioral
            techniques, cognitive approaches, and other methods to create a
            broader framework for understanding and changing patterns. Hypnosis and Addiction & Recovery Addiction provides a particularly interesting example of how
            automatic patterns can develop and become difficult to change. My approach to addiction and recovery is informed by my experience
            with SMART Recovery and by an interest in behavioral science,
            mindfulness, CBT, DBT, and other approaches to understanding
            behavior and change. Hypnosis can be considered as one supplemental tool within that
            larger framework. It isn't a replacement for appropriate medical,
            psychological, or addiction treatment, but it can provide another
            way of exploring attention, habits, associations, motivation,
            and behavioral patterns. Your Path to Transformation Hypnosis is only one part of a broader approach to understanding
            people, behavior, and personal change. If you’d like to explore how hypnosis can help you examine and transform unwanted or unhelpful behavioral patterns, work through overwhelming or intrusive emotions, overcome fears, phobias, and anxiety, or process the effects of difficult past experiences, Contact me . Hypnosis can also be used to help you work with urges and cravings associated with overeating, smoking, alcohol, or substance use, and to explore ways hypnosis can support your recovery. If you’re tired of automatically reacting to anger and would like to learn how to pause, release it, and let it go instead—or if you simply want to lose weight, stop smoking, or change an unwanted habit—contact me and let’s explore how hypnosis may be able to help.
