content: Search: Hypnosis Frequently Asked Questions Frequently asked questions about hypnosis, hypnotic experience, behavior change, memory, regression, and my approach to hypnosis. The Basics What is hypnosis? + Hypnosis is a way of deliberately working with naturally occurring human processes such as focused attention, absorption, expectation, imagination, suggestion, emotion, perception, and response. These are processes that we experience in everyday life, rather than something mysterious that only appears when a hypnotist begins a session. In personal growth and transformation work, hypnosis uses these naturally occurring processes and deliberately focuses and directs them toward the client's desired goal. The purpose isn't to create some entirely foreign state of consciousness, but to use the flexibility of attention, imagination, awareness, and response in a purposeful way. The hypnotist provides structure, guidance, suggestions, imagery, and direction, while the person experiencing hypnosis actively participates in the process. Hypnosis is therefore something you experience and participate in, rather than something that is simply done to you. Is hypnosis a special state of consciousness? + Hypnosis can involve experiences that feel different from ordinary conversation, but I don't think it is necessary to think of hypnosis as one single, mysterious state that everyone enters in exactly the same way. Human attention and awareness are highly flexible. Hypnotic techniques provide ways of deliberately directing that flexibility toward a particular purpose. In this sense, I don't think of hypnosis as a special state of consciousness so much as the deliberate use of everyday states and processes of attention, imagination, awareness, and experience for personal growth, change, and transformation. Focused attention, absorption, imagination, expectation, emotional responses, and changes in awareness are not abilities that suddenly appear when a hypnotist begins a session. You have already experienced many of these processes countless times in ordinary life. This is one reason you may not immediately recognize that you are experiencing hypnosis. You may simply feel like you are sitting there listening, imagining, thinking, or experiencing something. A skilled hypnotist can demonstrate changes in your attention, imagination, perception, or responses through exercises and suggestions, helping you recognize what is happening rather than simply telling you, "Now you're hypnotized." So while hypnosis can certainly feel different from your ordinary conversational state, I don't think of it as a dramatic new state of consciousness that you suddenly enter. It is more like deliberately using and directing processes that already occur naturally, and focusing them toward personal growth, change, and transformation. What does hypnosis feel like? + There isn't one particular feeling that proves someone is hypnotized. Some people experience deep relaxation, while others notice focused attention, absorption, changes in perception, vivid imagination, emotional responses, physical sensations, or simply a different quality of attention. The experience can vary considerably from person to person and from session to session. Do I have to relax to experience hypnosis? + No. Relaxation can make it easier for many people to focus their attention and become absorbed in an experience, but relaxation isn't the definition of hypnosis. Attention can become highly focused during curiosity, excitement, anticipation, fear, fascination, emotional experiences, and many other states. Relaxation and hypnosis sometimes become coupled together because relaxation is simply an easier state to work with for self-development and transformation than states such as anger, frustration, or intense agitation. A relaxed person may have fewer distractions competing for their attention, making it easier to direct that attention toward the work of the session. Your hypnotist may therefore ask you to focus on relaxation, not because relaxation itself creates hypnosis, but because it can be one of many doorways into a hypnotic experience. Once your attention is focused and directed, the hypnotist can use that state to work with visualization, suggestion, imagination, and other processes involved in the session. Do I have to close my eyes? + No. Closing the eyes can reduce visual distractions and make it easier for some people to focus inward, but hypnosis does not require closed eyes. The important issue is what is happening with attention and experience, not whether someone's eyes happen to be open or closed. Your hypnotist may ask you to close your eyes because doing so can be useful to the transformation process. It can make visualization easier, reduce distractions from the surrounding environment, and help keep your attention directed toward the thoughts, images, and experiences you are working with during the session. Closing your eyes is therefore a useful technique, not a requirement for hypnosis. There may also be times when keeping your eyes open is useful, depending on the exercise, the goal of the session, and what works best for you. How do I know if I'm hypnotized? + There isn't necessarily one dramatic sensation that tells you that you're hypnotized. You may notice changes in attention, absorption, imagination, perception, emotion, physical sensations, or your response to suggestions. You may also feel that you are simply participating in an interesting experience. A skilled hypnotist can demonstrate to you that you are experiencing hypnosis by using exercises and suggestions that allow you to notice changes in your attention, imagination, perception, or responses. This can be particularly useful because hypnosis is a natural process that makes use of abilities and experiences you have already had many times in ordinary life. Because you have already moved in and out of these kinds of focused and absorbed states countless times, you may not immediately recognize, "Yes, I am hypnotized." You may simply feel like you are sitting there listening, imagining, thinking, or experiencing something. This is also why I don't think of hypnosis as a dramatic new state of consciousness that you suddenly enter. It is more useful to think of hypnosis as deliberately using and directing processes that already occur naturally in everyday life, and applying them toward personal growth, change, and transformation. The usefulness of hypnosis therefore does not depend upon experiencing something dramatic. What matters is whether the focused attention, imagination, suggestion, and other processes involved are helping you accomplish the purpose of the session. Is the hypnotic state the same for everyone? + No. The experience of hypnosis can vary considerably from person to person. Some people experience a profound state of physical and mental relaxation. Others experience something much less dramatic, and for some people it may simply feel like sitting comfortably with their eyes closed while becoming absorbed in what they are hearing and imagining. And that's important to understand: relaxation isn't hypnosis itself. Relaxation can be a useful state because it may make it easier to focus attention and become absorbed in the experience, but hypnosis does not require a particular level of physical relaxation. What matters more is that your attention becomes more focused and directed, along with your responsiveness to suggestion. You don't necessarily have to feel dramatically different or experience some unmistakable "trance" before you can benefit from hypnosis. Your hypnotist is skilled at observing how you respond during the session and can use various suggestions and experiences to determine whether you are responding to the process and, when appropriate, help you deepen the experience. There isn't one universal hypnotic experience that everyone has to achieve. Your experience may be quite different from someone else's, and even your own experience may differ from one session to another. What matters isn't whether hypnosis feels a particular way, but what you are able to experience and accomplish with it. Will I be awake during hypnosis? + Yes. In the work that I do, your conscious mind remains awake and alert throughout the experience. You will be able to hear and understand what is happening, know what is being said and done, and remain aware of your experience throughout the session. Hypnosis does not require unconsciousness or sleep. In fact, I want you to be an active participant in the process. Your attention may become highly focused, and your awareness of the surrounding environment may change, but you are not unconscious or unaware of what is happening. You should also expect to remember the experience. There is no need for you to lose your memory or have gaps in your awareness for hypnosis to be useful. Most importantly, the choice always remains with you. You can respond to a suggestion, choose not to respond, ask a question, change your mind, or stop participating. Hypnosis is something you experience and participate in, not something that is simply done to you. Will I remember what happens during hypnosis? + Yes, in the work that I do, you should expect to remember the experience. Your conscious mind remains awake and alert throughout the session, and you remain aware of what is happening. Hypnosis is not like general anesthesia, where consciousness is intentionally suspended during the procedure. Because hypnosis works with processes that already occur naturally in everyday life, I think of it as being more like deliberately directed daydreaming, focused attention, and other forms of absorption than like being unconscious. You are still conscious and participating, but your attention is being directed toward the experience and the work of the session. The way people remember a hypnotic experience can still vary from client to client. Someone who becomes particularly relaxed and deeply absorbed may not remember every detail of the session, while another person may remember virtually everything from beginning to end. Not remembering every detail does not mean that you were unconscious during the process. You can remain conscious and aware while experiencing a very deep level of relaxation or absorption. Most importantly, you remain an active participant throughout the experience. You know what is happening, you can respond to what is being said, and the choice to participate always remains with you. Can I get stuck in hypnosis? + No. Hypnosis isn't a place from which you can become permanently trapped. This idea largely comes from television, movies, and sometimes from what people see in stage hypnosis. Occasionally, someone may appear reluctant to come out of hypnosis or open their eyes. There are several perfectly ordinary explanations for this. A stage participant may intentionally refuse to respond because they are playing along, trying to be funny, or creating a scene for the audience. In a therapeutic setting, someone may simply be experiencing such a profound and comfortable state of relaxation and absorption that they don't particularly want to leave it quickly. In either case, they aren't actually stuck. They are making a choice about how they are responding to the experience. They remain conscious and aware, even when deeply relaxed or absorbed. A skilled hypnotist knows how to recognize and appropriately handle these situations and can provide guidance for bringing the experience to a comfortable close. Hypnosis is not a state that takes control away from you or prevents you from returning to ordinary alertness. Participation, Expectation & Responsiveness Can anyone be hypnotized? + People differ in how readily they respond to different hypnotic experiences, and different people have different levels of suggestibility. There also isn't one technique that works identically for everyone. Attention, expectations, willingness to participate, imagination, trust, context, and the relationship with the practitioner can all influence the experience. But in general, almost anyone can use hypnosis as a tool for personal growth, change, and transformation. The question of whether someone "can be hypnotized" often comes down to what they think hypnosis actually is. If you believe hypnosis means surrendering control, entering a mysterious or special state of consciousness, or allowing someone else to control your mind, then it is understandable that you might think you cannot be hypnotized. But those ideas come largely from assumptions and portrayals of hypnosis in movies, television, and popular culture rather than from what hypnosis actually involves. Hypnosis is not surrendering control. It is not mind control, a battle of wills, or a way of forcing you to do something you do not want to do. It works with processes you already experience in everyday life, such as focused attention, imagination, absorption, expectation, emotion, and response, and deliberately directs those processes toward a particular goal. For personal growth and transformation, hypnosis is therefore less about asking whether you can enter some mysterious state and more about learning how to use the natural flexibility of your attention, awareness, imagination, and responses in a purposeful way. Do I have to believe in hypnosis for it to work? + You don't have to believe in hypnosis for it to work, and you certainly don't have to believe in any supernatural theory about hypnosis. What is much more important is understanding what hypnosis actually is and having enough confidence in the process to participate openly. Being educated about hypnosis before the process can dramatically improve the experience. Many people come to hypnosis with ideas they have picked up from television, movies, stage performances, or other sources. If you believe hypnosis means losing control, being put to sleep, or allowing someone else to control your mind, those misconceptions can interfere with your ability to understand and participate in the process. A skilled hypnotist will normally conduct what is called a "pre-talk" before beginning the hypnosis work. This is an opportunity to explain what hypnosis is, address common misconceptions, describe how the hypnotist's particular process works, and answer any questions the client may have. You don't need to arrive as a believer. You can arrive curious, skeptical, or simply willing to find out what the experience is like. Understanding the process and knowing what to expect allows you to participate more fully and gives you a much better foundation for using hypnosis for personal growth and transformation. Can skeptical or analytical people be hypnotized? + Being analytical or skeptical does not make someone immune to focused attention or absorption. People who become deeply absorbed while reading, programming, solving a difficult problem, making music, or researching something fascinating are already familiar with some of the ordinary processes that hypnotic techniques can deliberately engage. Can skeptical or analytical people be hypnotized? + Yes. Being analytical or skeptical does not make someone immune to focused attention, absorption, imagination, or other processes involved in hypnosis. In fact, asking whether an analytical person can be hypnotized is somewhat like asking whether an analytical person can become absorbed in a movie, experience highway hypnosis, fall in love, or become completely caught up in an argument. Highway hypnosis is the familiar experience of driving a well-known route while becoming absorbed in your thoughts or the routine of driving, sometimes arriving at your destination with little memory of the individual turns or landmarks along the way. You were not unconscious while driving. Your attention was simply being directed differently from your ordinary conversational state. The same principle applies to other ordinary experiences. A skeptical person can become deeply absorbed in a movie while simultaneously noticing every implausible detail and thinking, "That would never happen." Being analytical doesn't prevent absorption; it simply means that analytical thinking may continue to be part of the experience. Hypnosis is not a special or unique state of consciousness that requires you to stop thinking or abandon your skepticism. It uses everyday processes such as focused attention, imagination, expectation, absorption, emotion, and response, and deliberately directs them toward a particular purpose. A proper consultation before beginning hypnosis can also help determine whether a client is a good candidate for the particular hypnosis process being offered. The goal isn't to convince someone to stop being skeptical. It is to make sure they understand the process, know what to expect, and are willing to participate in it. Can I reject a hypnotic suggestion? + Yes, absolutely. A suggestion is not the same thing as a command. You remain a conscious, aware, and active participant in the process, and you can respond to, reinterpret, ignore, or reject a suggestion. If something is inappropriate, uncomfortable, or simply doesn't fit with what you want, you can choose not to accept it, communicate that to your hypnotist, or end the session. This is one reason the preparation before a hypnosis session is so important. A skilled hypnotist will gather background information about what you have already tried, what problems or concerns are affecting your life, how those concerns are interfering with your personal, emotional, and other goals, and what you would like to accomplish through hypnosis. It is also useful to explore what you expect to gain from making the desired change. What would be different in your outside world? What might change in your inner or emotional world? What would you be able to do, experience, or enjoy that is more difficult for you now? This information helps the hypnotist develop suggestions that are relevant to your actual goals and circumstances. Good hypnotic suggestions aren't simply generic statements that are delivered to everyone. A suggestion that makes perfect sense for one client might be completely irrelevant to another and could be met with an immediate, "Yeah, right," or "That's not going to happen." The more closely suggestions fit the person's goals, experiences, expectations, and desired changes, the more useful they can be. So yes, suggestions can be rejected. In fact, the possibility of rejection is one reason the hypnotist should take care in developing suggestions that are appropriate for the individual client. Even if a hypnotist were to give an unrelated or unwanted suggestion, you remain conscious, awake, and aware of what is happening. You can simply reject the suggestion, tell the hypnotist that you don't want to continue, or choose to end the session and leave. Inductions & Hypnotic Techniques What is a hypnotic induction? + An induction is a structured exercise used to help focus attention and establish the conditions and expectations for a hypnotic experience. Different inductions may use relaxation, imagery, attention exercises, conversation, physical responses, surprise, or other methods. Why do hypnotists use inductions? + An induction can provide a clear transition into the session, reduce distractions, focus attention, establish expectations, and help the participant become more absorbed in the experience. It can also give the client a familiar structure for understanding what is happening. Is the induction the most important part of hypnosis? + Not necessarily. An induction is one tool within a larger process. Once someone understands what hypnosis is and becomes familiar with the experience, a lengthy formal induction may not be necessary. The useful part of the work may be what happens after attention has been focused: exploring perceptions, emotions, expectations, imagery, suggestions, beliefs, or behavioral patterns. Why might you use different inductions with different people? + People differ in how they naturally focus attention and become absorbed in an experience. An approach that works well for one person may be unnecessary or less useful for another. I prefer to treat hypnotic techniques as tools rather than as a single formula that must be followed identically with everyone. What is a hypnotic deepener? + A deepener is a technique traditionally used to increase the depth of a hypnotic experience. In practical terms, this may involve increasing absorption, focused attention, imagery, expectation, responsiveness, or the sense that the experience is becoming more vivid or immersive. I don't consider "depth" to be a single simple measurement of how useful a session will be. Hypnosis in Everyday Life Can hypnosis happen naturally? + Many of the processes involved in hypnosis occur naturally in everyday life. People become absorbed in movies, music, books, conversations, games, creative work, memories, and thoughts. Attention can become highly focused while awareness of other information fades into the background. Hypnotic techniques provide a way of deliberately working with some of these ordinary human capacities. What is highway hypnosis? + Highway hypnosis is the familiar experience of driving a well-known route while becoming absorbed in thoughts or other mental activity and later realizing that you have little conscious recollection of each individual turn or landmark. It is a useful everyday example of how attention can become focused while routine behavior continues. Is getting absorbed in a movie similar to hypnosis? + It can illustrate some of the same processes. When you become deeply absorbed in a movie, your attention may become concentrated on the story while you temporarily pay less attention to your surroundings. Emotional responses can also become very real even though you know the events on the screen are fictional. Hypnotic techniques can deliberately work with similar capacities for attention, imagination, absorption, expectation, and emotional involvement. Control & Common Myths Is hypnosis mind control? + No. The image of hypnosis as mind control owes much to fiction, especially Svengali, the hypnotist in George du Maurier's 1894 novel Trilby. Later movies, television programs, stories, and conspiracy theories repeated the idea of a hypnotist who can take over another person's mind. It is a dramatic plot device, not a realistic account of hypnosis. As discussed elsewhere in this FAQ, hypnosis works with ordinary human processes such as focused attention, imagination, expectation, absorption, emotion, and response. The person remains conscious, aware of what is happening, and able to think, choose, question, or stop participating. Hypnosis may influence an experience or a response, but influence is not the same as taking ownership of another person's mind. Research does not support the claim that hypnosis is a special means of compelling a person to violate their values or beliefs. In a classic experiment, Orne and Evans (1965) found comparable apparent compliance with troubling experimental requests among hypnotized participants and participants asked to simulate hypnosis, showing that social expectations and the situation—not hypnosis alone—were central to the behavior. See Orne and Evans, "Social Control in the Psychological Experiment: Antisocial Behavior and Hypnosis," Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1, 189-200. People can be pressured, deceived, or abused in many settings, and those concerns should always be taken seriously. But hypnosis itself is not a power that can force or make someone act against their will. While mind control works well as a story device, actual hypnosis cannot turn a person into someone else's puppet. Can a hypnotist make me do something against my will? + No. A hypnotist cannot take over your mind or use hypnosis as a special power to make you act against your values, beliefs, judgment, or wishes. You remain conscious and aware during hypnosis, and you remain able to think, choose, ask questions, decline a suggestion, or stop participating. Hypnosis works with ordinary human processes such as focused attention, imagination, expectation, absorption, emotion, and response. A hypnotist can offer suggestions and provide structure, but you are still an active participant in the experience. Influence is not the same as control, and a suggestion is not an order that overrides your judgment. Research does not support the idea that hypnosis itself compels people to violate their values. In the classic Orne and Evans (1965) experiment, hypnotized participants and participants asked to simulate hypnosis showed comparable apparent compliance with troubling requests, highlighting the importance of social expectations and the situation rather than a hypnotist gaining control over someone else. Movies, television, stories, and conspiracy theories often portray hypnosis as a way to force people to act like puppets. That makes for an effective plot device, but it is not how hypnosis works in real life. People can be pressured, deceived, or abused in many settings, and those concerns should always be taken seriously; hypnosis itself, however, is not a mechanism for forcing someone to act against their will. Is hypnosis a truth serum? + No. Hypnosis is not a truth serum and does not provide a special way to determine whether someone’s statements are objectively true. People can misremember, misunderstand, imagine, interpret, or reconstruct experiences during hypnosis just as they can in ordinary life. Hypnosis does not take away a person’s choice, autonomy, judgment, or ability to decide what to say. You remain conscious, awake, and aware during the process. You can think, question a suggestion, choose not to answer, correct yourself, or stop participating. As discussed elsewhere in this FAQ, hypnosis is a word we use for deliberately working with everyday human processes and states such as focused attention, imagination, expectation, absorption, emotion, perception, and response. In personal growth and transformation work, those processes are focused toward a person’s own goals for change; they do not become a mechanism for extracting guaranteed facts or overriding someone’s agency. For that reason, hypnosis should not be used as a way to establish the truth of a memory, obtain a confession, or decide whether a person’s account is accurate. A statement made while hypnotized still needs the same careful evaluation and corroboration as any other statement. Can hypnosis make me reveal secrets? + No. Hypnosis does not take away your autonomy, judgment, or ability to choose what you say. You remain conscious, awake, and aware during hypnosis, and you can decline a suggestion, refuse to answer a question, change the subject, ask questions, or stop participating. As explained in the answers about mind control and acting against your will, hypnosis is not a mechanism for overriding a person’s values, wishes, or choices. A hypnotist can offer suggestions and ask questions, but you remain an active participant. Influence is not the same as control, and a suggestion is not an order that compels you to disclose information. Hypnosis works with ordinary processes such as focused attention, imagination, expectation, absorption, emotion, and response. It may help a person explore their own experiences, but it does not function as a truth serum or a method for extracting private, objectively verified information. Movies and television often portray hypnosis as a way to uncover secrets, but that is a dramatic plot device rather than an accurate account of hypnosis. Can stage hypnosis really make people do strange things? + Stage hypnosis can make it easier for willing participants to set aside the part of the mind that says, “No, you’ll look silly,” “That is ridiculous,” or “That will never happen.” Hypnotists often call this doubting or evaluating process the critical factor. By reducing that immediate self-doubt, hypnosis can heighten suggestibility: a person may become more open to engaging with an idea, image, or suggestion. This is also one reason hypnosis can be useful for personal growth and transformation. When someone wants to change a habit, develop a new response, or work toward a goal, setting aside the automatic belief that change is impossible can make it easier to imagine, practice, and respond in a new way. That openness remains the person’s choice; it is not compulsion or force. In a stage setting, volunteers are generally people who are already interested in the show, willing to participate, and comfortable being the focus of attention. To a participant, it may feel as though they are simply playing along with the hypnotist—and in an important sense, that willingness to engage is part of heightened suggestibility. It should not be confused with the hypnotist taking control of the person’s mind. Stage hypnotists do not usually select volunteers at random. Many first invite audience participation or use informal responsiveness exercises, then choose people who appear engaged, responsive, and eager to take part. Someone who is highly skeptical, uninterested, or unwilling to participate is not a good fit for a stage performance, because hypnosis cannot force someone to join in or make them do something against their will. The unusual behavior in a stage show can be genuine, while also being shaped by the volunteer’s expectations, the social setting, the performer’s suggestions, and the shared understanding that everyone is participating in entertainment. It is not evidence that the hypnotist has made the participant into a puppet. Memory, Regression & Earlier Experiences Can hypnosis accurately retrieve a memory? + Not as a historically exact recording of an event. Memory is not like retrieving a video file from a computer. Even ordinary recall is a reconstruction: each time we remember, the memory can be influenced by our current emotional state, later information, changing understanding of what happened, expectations, and personal beliefs. Hypnosis does not turn memory into a perfect record or guarantee that a recalled event happened exactly as described. It can sometimes help a person focus on memories, sensations, images, and impressions, but a vivid or emotional recollection is not, by itself, proof that every detail is historically accurate. A person may also misremember, imagine, interpret, or confabulate details during hypnosis, just as they can during ordinary remembering. For this reason, a skilled hypnotist working with memories uses careful, non-leading questions. Non-leading questions are open and do not assume that a particular event, detail, person, or object was present. They invite the person to describe their own experience rather than supplying information that could shape the memory. A hypnotist may use carefully worded yes-or-no or binary questions to establish baseline perceptions, such as whether the person recalls it being light or dark, indoors or outdoors, or whether they recall anyone else being present. These questions should allow for uncertainty or no recollection and should not assume that a particular detail occurred. Asking whether a particular person or object was present, for example, can introduce information that may shape later recall. Forensic hypnosis is a specialized area concerned with obtaining the most careful possible account of a witness’s recollection. Its emphasis is on neutral interviewing, avoiding suggestion, documenting the process, and distinguishing what the person remembers from what may have been introduced later. Even with those safeguards, hypnosis cannot guarantee an accurate reconstruction of the past, and any account should be evaluated alongside independent evidence. What is age regression? + Age regression is a hypnotic approach used to explore the perceptions, beliefs, emotions, and responses connected with experiences from earlier periods of a person’s life. In this context, it is not a search for a single hidden event that explains everything, and it is not a method for recovering a historically exact record of the past. An unwanted behavior, reaction, or pattern often develops through a web of experiences rather than one event. What begins as a helpful coping response can provide temporary relief from uncomfortable emotions or beliefs. Over time, similar situations may trigger familiar emotional and behavioral responses, even when that response is no longer helpful. For example, sadness, fear, loneliness, or stress may become associated with eating, craving chocolate, smoking, drinking, or using another substance. A once-useful coping strategy can then become maladaptive. The phrase “neurons that fire together wire together” is a simplified way of describing how repeated experiences and responses can become strongly associated. It should not be taken literally as one part of the brain storing a complete, time-stamped file containing memories, beliefs, and emotions. Memory and emotion involve networks across the brain. The hippocampus is important for episodic memory, while the amygdala helps process emotional significance and can influence how emotional experiences are remembered; the prefrontal cortex also helps with interpretation, regulation, and retrieval. Age regression can be a useful model for examining the web of meanings, perceptions, beliefs, and emotions that may contribute to a present unwanted outcome. The goal is to develop more realistic or helpful ways of understanding those experiences, reduce the emotional force of outdated responses, and support new choices in the present. It is not necessary for a person to identify one perfect “root cause” for that work to be useful. Some early experiences that contribute to a later pattern may have seemed ordinary or insignificant at the time and may not be readily available to conscious awareness. That does not mean they are hidden historical facts waiting to be uncovered. It means that a current pattern can have multiple influences, including learned associations, repeated experiences, relationships, coping strategies, and the meanings a person has made of events over time. For this reason, age regression should be approached carefully and should not be treated as a way to prove what happened in the past. Hypnosis can increase the vividness and emotional impact of recalled material without guaranteeing its accuracy. A skilled practitioner avoids leading questions, does not present imagined material as fact, and keeps the focus on the person’s present goals and wellbeing. Research reviews describe age regression as a potentially useful adjunct in some settings, while also emphasizing the limits of the evidence, memory-accuracy concerns, informed consent, and appropriate clinical training. Does age regression literally take me back in time? + No. Age regression does not take you back in time. It is better understood as a therapeutic model for exploring present perceptions, beliefs, emotions, associations, and patterns that may be connected with earlier experiences. A vivid experience of an earlier period can be meaningful without being literal time travel or a perfect recording of the past. Are memories experienced during hypnosis historically accurate? + No. Age regression does not recreate an earlier event as a literal, historically exact experience. It is better understood as a useful therapeutic model for exploring present perceptions, beliefs, emotions, associations, and patterns that may be connected with earlier experiences. There is no single part of the brain that stores memories, beliefs, and emotions as complete files with a reliable date-and-time stamp. Episodic memory depends in part on the hippocampus, while the amygdala helps process emotional significance; the prefrontal cortex and other brain networks also contribute to interpretation, regulation, and recall. Remembering is reconstructive, which means that recall can be influenced by current emotion, later information, expectations, and the meanings a person has made of an event over time. A person may enter age-regression work convinced of a particular perception of an event, whether or not every detail is historically accurate. What can be useful for the hypnotist and client is examining how that perception has influenced the person’s feelings, beliefs, expectations, and choices. Those meanings and emotional responses may help maintain an unwanted behavior, reaction, or pattern in the present, regardless of whether the recalled event can be verified in every detail. During age regression, a person may experience images, emotions, bodily sensations, beliefs, or impressions that feel vivid and meaningful. The value of that material does not depend on locating one perfect root cause or treating it as a factual record. Instead, the work can support more realistic and helpful ways of understanding experience, reducing the influence of outdated responses, and building new choices in the present. For that reason, age regression should not be used to establish historical facts, prove an allegation, or decide exactly what occurred in the past. Any event that needs to be treated as an actual account of what happened should be independently verified through appropriate outside sources. A skilled practitioner avoids leading questions and keeps the focus on present goals, wellbeing, and informed choice. Can hypnosis recover forgotten memories? + Sometimes a person may recall thoughts, images, emotions, impressions, or details that were not previously in conscious awareness. However, hypnosis cannot reliably retrieve a forgotten memory on demand, and a memory that emerges during hypnosis should not automatically be treated as historically accurate. Memory is reconstructive, and hypnosis can increase the vividness or emotional force of recalled material without guaranteeing that every detail is true. If the purpose is to recover information for a historical, legal, or investigative matter, it is important to seek an appropriately trained forensic professional and to follow the relevant legal and interviewing standards. Hypnosis should not be used casually to establish facts, prove an allegation, or create a record of what occurred; any account that matters as historical evidence needs independent corroboration. If the goal is personal change, it is usually more helpful not to assume that a forgotten event is the source of a current problem or unwanted behavior. A careful assessment can explore the person’s present beliefs, perceptions, emotions, coping patterns, and associations. Hypnotic age-regression work can be one way of examining those patterns, but it should not begin with the assumption that a hidden memory must be found. An earlier event may be relevant to a current issue, or it may not be. When a meaningful memory, perception, or emotional association does emerge, the useful therapeutic question is how it relates to the person’s present experience and goals—not whether it supplies a perfect historical explanation. A skilled practitioner uses non-leading questions, avoids presenting imagined material as fact, and keeps the focus on informed choice and current wellbeing. What is an affect bridge? + An affect bridge is a technique that follows a current emotional experience toward other experiences, memories, images, beliefs, or associations connected with that feeling. It can be useful for exploring patterns without assuming that there is necessarily one original event that caused everything. Does every problem have one root cause? + Not necessarily. Human behavior is often more like a network than a single chain of cause and effect. A habit or recurring problem may involve many overlapping experiences, emotions, beliefs, expectations, associations, environmental cues, and learned responses. Sometimes useful change comes from working with several parts of that network rather than discovering one hidden event. It can be helpful to think of this as a web of snowballs that develops over time. An early experience may shape a perception, belief, emotion, or coping response; later experiences that feel similar can add to and reinforce that pattern. What begins as a useful way to obtain temporary relief from discomfort can gradually become an unwanted or maladaptive response when it continues after it is no longer helping. For example, a person may develop patterns around eating, smoking, alcohol, other substances, avoidance, anger, or withdrawal because those responses once offered relief from stress, fear, loneliness, or other uncomfortable feelings. The present pattern may involve many linked experiences and meanings, not simply the first time the person engaged in that behavior. This is why age-regression work should not be treated as a search for one perfect root cause. It can instead provide a way to examine the perceptions, beliefs, emotions, and associations that may be contributing to the unwanted outcome now. The goal is to understand the pattern well enough to develop more realistic, helpful responses and support change in the present. The value of exploring the experience is therefore in understanding what is meaningful and useful for the person now. Hypnosis & Behavior Change Can hypnosis change habits? + Hypnosis can be used as one tool for examining and changing habitual patterns. Hypnotic techniques can help bring some of these processes into focused awareness and create opportunities to practice different responses. Is willpower enough to change a habit? + Willpower can be useful, but behavior is influenced by much more than deliberate effort. A broader approach can sometimes make change easier than relying on willpower alone. Can hypnosis change emotional responses? + Emotional responses can be influenced by attention, interpretation, epectation, memory, association, and context. Search: I Provide Hypnosis Services for a Wide Range of Issues I have experience working with a vast array of issues. Below is a list of
            some of the common issues I handle.
            Hypnosis can be successful for you! If you do not see the issue you are interested in
            working on listed below, Contact me and I can help you
            be successful with your issue. All sessions are one-on-one and confidential. Adderall Abuse Addiction Alcohol Abuse Alcoholism Anger Anxiety Bad Habits Benzodiazepine Abuse Bruxism (Teeth Grinding) Cocaine Abuse Confidence Crack Abuse Diabetes Emotional Eating Exercise Habits Fatigue Fear of Failure Focus Forgiveness Grief Issues Guilt Headaches Heroin Abuse Heroin Addiction Hopelessness Hydrocodone (Vicodin) Abuse Irrational Fears (Phobias) Irritability Klonopin Abuse Laziness Methamphetamine Abuse Migraine Headaches Mood Swings Nail Biting Nose Picking Opiate / Opioid Abuse Oxycodone (Percocet) Abuse Pain Control / Pain Management Panic Attacks Procrastination Relationship Issues Relaxation Road Rage Self Discipline Self Esteem Self Image Self Sabotage Skin Problems Smoking Cessation Social Anxiety (Shyness) Stress Stuttering Substance Abuse Tension Test Anxiety Tiredness Trust Issues Weight Loss Worry Worthlessness * All hypnosis involving medical conditions, such as managing 
              pain, is always done under the supervision of a physician, 
              or by referral. If you want to use hypnosis to help you with a medical 
              condition, give me a call. I am experienced in working with physicians and 
              know how to set up the referral. Is Hypnosis Effective for My Issue? Hypnosis is a highly effective tool for creating lasting personal change. 
            Whether you want to shift automated habits, resolve uncomfortable emotional patterns, 
            or overcome internal resistance, hypnosis works directly with the subconscious 
            processes that drive behavior. A growing body of modern clinical research supports hypnosis as a powerful 
            modality for managing anxiety, stress, chronic pain, and habit change. 
            Rather than relying on continuous conscious effort or willpower alone, hypnosis helps 
            align your subconscious beliefs and emotional responses with your conscious goals. Contact me to discuss how I can apply hypnosis to your specific situation. How Does My Hypnosis Process Work? My approach to hypnosis focuses on resolving the root causes behind unwanted behaviors and 
            emotional patterns—what is happening "under the hood." Rather than simply attempting to suppress a 
            symptom, I systematically address the underlying beliefs, emotional triggers, and learned associations. When you schedule your initial session, I begin with a brief preliminary conversation 
            about what you would like to accomplish. This helps me establish the focus for our first meeting. Your First Visit: Explanation & In-Depth Intake When you arrive for your first appointment, I sit down directly with you to demystify the process. 
            I explain exactly what hypnosis is, what it isn't, and address common misconceptions. 
            You will understand that hypnosis is a collaborative, conscious state where you remain aware, 
            in control, and active in your own change process. Next, I gather comprehensive background information to map out the issue: Your Goals: What success looks like to you and what you want to achieve. Past Attempts: What you have tried in the past and where conscious effort or willpower fell short. The Impact: How this issue is currently affecting your life—personally, emotionally, socially, and professionally. The Meaning of Change: What making this change will mean for your future, as well as the personal cost of remaining stuck in the old pattern. From this evaluation, I outline what hypnosis can realistically accomplish, how I will address 
            the problem, and what your role in the process will be. Phase 1: Establishing the Foundation During your initial hypnosis work, my goal is to build a solid foundation for long-term success. 
            I guide you into the appropriate level of hypnosis required for deep psychological work. 
            Once the proper depth is achieved, I perform a convincer—demonstrating directly to your 
            conscious mind that you are in hypnosis. With the foundation set, I introduce initial reframing of existing blockages, build foundational 
            motivation, and begin shifting the behavioral aspects of the issue. When you emerge, I review 
            the experience with you, gather your feedback, and establish awareness goals for the week ahead. Phase 2: Resolving Beliefs, Emotions, and Root Causes In subsequent sessions, I move into the heart of the work. This is where I address the web 
            of connections driving the behavior: Uncovering and releasing limiting core belief systems (e.g., self-sabotage, unworthiness, or fear). Separating false hunger, false cravings, or urges from underlying emotional triggers using The Secret Language of Feelings . Resolving stored guilt, shame, anger, or resentment tied to the issue or past quit attempts. By systematically resolving the emotional and psychological drivers, the need for the old behavior 
            naturally dissipates. Phase 3: Custom Motivation & Reinforcement Because the underlying emotional drivers are cleared during the core work, many of my clients find that 
            their habits have naturally shifted and require minimal additional push. However, if further 
            structure, specific dietary/exercise motivation, or habit reinforcement is needed, I customize 
            this final phase to fit your individual goals. Contact me today to schedule an appointment and begin restoring control over your habits, emotions, and life. content: Search: My  Apporach to Weight Loss I understand that in order to achieve effective long term weight loss, it requires more than just simple changes in behavior. I understand the complex behavioral, mental and emotional issues that contribute to keeping unwanted weight. Inspired by the teachings of Calvin Banyan, M.A., Certified Hypnosis Instructor, Fellow of the National Guild of Hypnotist, and his 5-PATH approach to hypnosis I have developed a unique approach that not only helps you easily change your behavior but un-plants the negative seeds that drives unnecessary physical hunger, false hunger, the lack of desire for exercise and much, much more. As you continue to read about our approach, I am sure you will become excited at the new possibilities that you may have not yet considered. Incorporating our philosphy and apporach I are sure you will agree that I have South Jersey's most unique approach to getting rid of unwanted weight. Our approach is not to help you lose weight, but to get rid of weight, now and in the long term. My Philosophy Regarding Weight Loss The problem with losing weight is that there is a sense of loss, deprivation, either conscious or subconsciously. When you decide you are going to rid of the weight, once and for all you do it to satisfy your self. Traditional weight loss programs, be it diets or forced exercise programs are about depriving your self. Either depriving your self of the foods you like or making you do a type of exercise program that you aren't comfortable with. There are all kinds of different diets, low carb, low fat, restricted calorie, just about everyone knows about just about all of those diets. Worse yet, 'being on a diet' requires lots of mental attention and focus, once you begin to lose your focus, you find your old habits returning. As you already know, over the long run dieting and exercising without neutralizing the source of false, unnecessary physical hunger or unwanted habits is not easily maintainable. Our approach to getting rid of unwanted weight is about satisfaction. It's about both keeping the foods that satisfy you and satisfying the feelings that drive false hunger. You may not have been aware of it but unsatisfied feelings often contribute to the physical feelings people confuse with true physical hunger. Often times a feeling will come up and a person will associate that with being hungry. The feelings can be anything, boredom, sadness, anger, guilt, loneliness, any feeling can drive that false sense of hunger. Once a person feels these feelings, he or she eats and the feeling goes away, at least temporarily. Eating in response to those feelings is just distracting from those feelings. In a short time those feelings will return and thus that person will feel hungry again. This is why some people can eat and feel hungry again a half hour to an hour later. Then he or she will eat something else and distract from the feeling again. Over time, that person begins to feel frustrated. That person will again eat to distract from that feeling of frustration. Over more time that person might begin to feel depressed because what they have tried to do in the past to lose weight hasn't worked, so they're mind is telling them to take a break for a little while. Then they eat out of that feeling of depression. I call this cycle the over eaters rut. Our approach to hypnosis breaks this cycle and satisfies the feelings that cause false hunger, thus eliminating false hunger. Another overlooked aspect of weight loss is stress. Stress contributes to physical hunger. In the physiology of the body, when stress levels goes up our liver releases more sugar into our body. This release of sugar is used to drive the fight or flight mechanism, to give us the energy to deal with a truly dangerous situation. But in our society if you are cut off in traffic or overworked, there is no way for this sugar to be burned off naturally. So when that sugar isn't used your body then releases insulin. Insulin is the hormone the body releases to store that sugar back into the body's cells. That unused sugar is then stored in our body cells, causing us to gain weight. Another byproduct of that insulin release is that an increase of insulin in our body causes physical hunger. If I were in an actual fight or flight situation, I would need to replace that used energy. But being stressed now that insulin release makes us physically hungry causes us to eat more. This cycle put together with unchecked stress can cause us to eat more than I really need to. Our approach to hypnosis allows our clients to better handle stress by helping eliminate the emotional cause of stress, and teaching our clients better relaxation techniques. My approach to getting rid of unwanted weight takes approximately four to six sessions, however everyone is different so certain clients make take longer. Our process is a supplement to a healthy diet and exercise program. This means that any diet within reason will help you lose weight and you must be willing to do some sort of exercise program. This does not mean you have to give up the foods you love, I will help you eat less. In the beginning you will need to make a conscious effort to eat less and enjoy it more and exercise. It is not necessary to follow any type of diet program. However it is best to consult your doctor before you change your diet or begin a new exercise program. It is also a good idea to get a check up from your doctor to determine if there are any physical causes that would inhibit weight loss, such as a thyroid condition or certain medications. Ask your doctor before stopping or changing any medications you are on. Sessions Structure On your first session, I will begin by having you fill out paper work. This will allow use to get a little background information on your situation. I will also then give you a copy of our client bill of rights, privacy policy and explain our code of ethics. After you have filled out your paper work, I will then show you two brief videos. The first video will explain all about hypnosis and answer any questions or lingering doubts that you may have about hypnosis. The second video will explain how emotions contribute to weight gain and how hypnosis will help. You will then be greeted by your hypnotist who will then answer any questions you may still have, and gather a little bit more background information. Our first session deals with the behavioral aspects of your situation. In this session I will help any family training issues in regards to food. These include guilt over not cleaning your plate, taking too much and feeling compelled to eat everything, the quality of the food you eat and much more. I will also target exercise motivation and portion control. After our first session your hypnotist will suggest that you only eat in one place, whether that be the table. He will suggest that you do not eat in the car, or in front of the TV, as distracted eating causes us to eat more than I realize. Your input on the first session will be vital, so it is a good idea to begin to think about the areas of weight loss that are a challenge to you, and together I will address these to help you get on the high road to success. It is important to realize that our approach to getting rid of weight is a process. Every session builds on the last session. In the beginning I focus on building a solid foundation that is necessary for lasting success. After each session it you will find it will become easier and easier to get rid of that unwanted weight. However it is our aim to give our client's realistic expectations. I find that when our clients have realistic expectations their rate of success is much greater. Although the first session will address a great many issues, you can't expect that everything will be solved after just one session. The first session prepares you for the rest of the process. Before doing this powerful process, it is important to decide whether you are going to stick to and complete this whole process. You can expect that over time that you will begin to achieve your goals, but sometimes people experience what they perceive as set backs. For example they have in mind they want to reframe for eating a certain food, and when they do they think they.re whole week is blown. I want you now to give yourself permission to be human and know that by choosing to do this process that over time, your worst day will become better than your best day is today. Give your self permission to look back and see all the things that you have done that you are proud of. All the little things you do towards you goal adds up to one big difference. From the second session onward, I deal with the mental and emotional aspects that drive false hunger. Using advanced hypnotic techniques I target and neutralize those feelings, returning your control to be who you want to be. If you are finally ready to get rid of false hunger and over eating, this is for you. I also deal with eliminating and controlling stress, reducing unnecessary physical hunger. I will neutralize all the feelings driving your false hunger; fear, anger, guilt, loneliness, boredom. I will also beck how the behavioral aspect is going and work on any additional aspects that need to be worked on. Another important overlooked aspect is weight loss is forgiving your self. The burden of troubling your self with not physically being the way you want, and beating yourself up because of it contributes to the stress that holds on to that weight. I find that once I neutralize the primary causes that prevent you from getting rid of that weight, its helpful to remove any anger or guilt that you may feel towards you self. In doing so you will become self confident, happier and much more in control of many aspects of your life, including your weight. Think about what it will feel like to release that. In our experience this goes a long way. Change Your Life As you can see, our approach to getting rid of unwanted weight is thorough and complete. I believe if you are willing to work with us, letting us be your hypnotic guide I can help you achieve your goal. It takes commitment and a little effort but with your willingness and our expertise you can succeed. Contact me and schedule your appointments! content: Search: Release Your Anger Forever... TRANSFORM Your Life by Releasing Your Anger, not just Managing it. Welcome... Even if you tried different anger management techniques before and failed, our hypnosis process can help you. I can help you release your anger because I understand anger. I believe that all feelings when they are based in reality. It is how one reacts to a feeling that makes the response to that feeling either good or bad. I have a unique and specialized hypnotic process that doesn.t just give you new techniques to bury your anger, our process releases anger, so you can begin to respond better. I Understand Anger All feelings are good. Anger is a good feeling. Anger tells us that something isn't fair and to take action to make the situation fair. In fact there have been many good things come as a result of anger. In fact, our country was founded by a group of angry men, who wanted freedom and felt they were being treated unfairly. Anger is a feeling and all feelings are good when they are based in reality. It is when a feeling isn't based in reality when they begin to cause problems. This can happen with any feeling. For example some people begin to experience feelings of fear that aren't based in reality, so they develop phobias. So now that little spider becomes perceived as a huge threat. This can also happen with anger. Some time long ago, for whatever reason you may have been in a situation where you were treated unfairly and at the time there was nothing you could do about it. Sometimes people remember what it was sometimes they don.t. But over time every time that person got angry it was like pouring that anger into a cup. Every time that person gets angry that cup fills more and more. So every time when that person gets angry that person begins to experience and feel that anger from all those situations in the past where they were anger. So now even in a situation where someone would only be a little bit annoyed, this person feels all that anger from the past as well as the present which causes them to experience it as if the situation was really, really unfair. This is called emotional resonance. When that person feels that angry, they might explode and yell at that person or do things that they might regret. After the situation passes they make a promise that they will never react that way again. But the next time they get angry, all that anger from the past begins to come up again causing them to react in the same way. Each time it happens they put more and more anger into that cup. This makes it easier for that cup to overflow with just a little provocation. The Hypnosis Process That Really Works Some people begin to seek out anger management techniques which teach you not to express your anger, but to bury. These techniques work for a while but every time that person buries that anger it fills that cup more and more. Perhaps you have tried some of these techniques and they have not worked. Now that you know, you can begin feel better now since now you can begin to use the right tool to release your anger. Search: Does Hypnosis Work? You might know or have heard of someone who has received results by using hypnosis.  
            You may even be considering using hypnosis to lose weight, stop smoking, overcome a 
            fear or to obtain another result.  Even though you are considering the benefits of 
            hypnosis, you begin to wonder, "Does hypnosis really work?" or maybe you think, 
            "I have tried everything!How can hypnosis help me with this?"
            After trying so many different ways to get the result you want, 
            it's easy to become skeptical when considering a new approach to an old problem.  
            As you begin to open yourself and start to learn what hypnosis really is, you 
            might find yourself becoming fascinated as you discover all the ways you can use 
            hypnosis, and how the mind works.  You may even become amazed as you learn why what 
            you have done in the past to accomplish your goal has not worked, or wasn't long lasting.  
            When you discover what's possible, you will agree that hypnosis is the right choice for you. What is Hypnosis? To answer the question, "Does hypnosis work?", you must first understand what hypnosis really is.  
            If you are like most people, most of what you know about hypnosis comes from Hollywood.  While they
            may be entertaining, most of what you see on TV, in the movies or read in a novel simply isn't true.  
            Consider a few movies that has a portrayal of your profession.  Was that portrayal accurate?
            Ask anyone who has worked around computers.  They know that Hollywood's portrayal of computers is 
            far for accurate.  Now take what you know about hypnosis, and set it aside and open yourself as 
            we set aside common misperceptions people have about hypnosis and learn what hypnosis really is. Hypnosis is the optimal state to make changes in your life.  Imagine setting aside that part of 
            you that keeps you from making the changes you want.  Set aside that part of you that nags at you, 
            and tells you that things aren't possible.  Set aside that part of you that keeps you from 
            accomplishing the things you want.  When you do hypnosis with us, you can set that part aside.  
            That part is called the critical factor.  It's the part of you that keeps you from changing.  
            It's the part that re-enforces limiting beliefs the part that keeps you stuck.  We set that
            aside when we do hypnosis.  We do this by the establishment of acceptable selective thinking.  
            The establishment of acceptable selective thinking simply refers to the process of guiding
            someone into hypnosis by using a hypnotic induction. Hypnosis is not mind control.  This popular misconception has been popularized via movies and TV.   
            As we discussed above, the hypnotic state is achieved by the establishment of acceptable selective
            thinking.  That means that suggestions being given must be acceptable to you, the client.   
            That means at any time during a hypnosis session, if there is a suggestion given you don't like,
            you can either simply disregard the suggestion or you may even emerge from hypnosis.  
            Hypnosis is a state of inner focus and control for you, the client.  You can begin to feel confident
            that in hypnosis you have control of what you accept or what you reject. In hypnosis, you are awake and aware.  Hypnosis is not a form of sleep.  The thought of hypnosis 
            as sleep can be traced back to Dr.   James Braid back in the mid 1800s.  James Braid was a physician
            and surgeon.  He observed that eye fatigue, starting at an object to tire the eyes, induced hypnosis.  
            From this he theorized that hypnosis was a sleep like state.  Thus in 1843, Dr.   Braid coined the 
            term hypnosis.  Hypnos is the Greek word for sleep.  After later realizing that hypnosis wasn't a form 
            of sleep, he tried to change the name to be more descriptive.  He chose the word monodeism, meaning 
            a single focus, but it was too late and the term hypnosis stuck and it has been used ever since. Hypnosis is not sleep.  In hypnosis you are awake and aware.  In hypnosis you are aware of all the
            suggestions being given and you are in control of what you accept and what you reject.  
            When you emerge from a hypnosis session, you will be aware of what happened.  The belief that you 
            will not remember anything about your hypnosis session is simply not true. Hypnosis is not a truth serum.  Since you are awake, alert and in control, no one, not even your 
            hypnotist can compel you to reveal anything that you don't want to reveal. Hypnosis is not relaxation.  Hypnotists commonly use relaxation as a doorway to entering the 
            hypnotic state, however being relaxed does not equal being in hypnosis. All hypnosis is self hypnosis.  Hypnosis is a state that you must enter into yourself.  
            Your hypnotist is more like a guide or a coach.  In order to enter into the hypnotic
            state and achieve the results you want, you must have a willingness to follow your 
            hypnotist's instructions.  Your hypnotist has the training and experience and 
            knows exactly what to do to help you achieve your goal.  However hypnosis is like a dance,
            it requires the cooperation of both the client and hypnotist, you can't dance very
            will if your partner is not willing to follow your lead. Now that you know what hypnosis really is and know the truth about the common misperceptions 
            that people have about hypnosis, you can feel safe and confident that hypnosis is the right
            choice for you.  However hypnosis is not a magic pill.  It takes a special type of person
            to be a good candidate for hypnosis.  It takes someone that is committed to accomplishing 
            their goal, it takes someone who is willing to follow the hypnotist's instructions
            and it takes someone who is ready to make that change.  Are you ready to achieve what
            before you could only dream about accomplishing? Can I be Hypnotized? You may still object, "I can't be hypnotized.  " or maybe you even said,"I'm too smart to be hypnotized.  " 
            These are common assertions but they come from a misunderstanding of hypnosis .  You have been 
            hypnotized many times before, even though you may not be aware of it. "I can't be hypnotized.  "If you have ever watched a TV show, or read a book and gotten absorbed into it, 
            maybe it was because you were hooked and just couldn't wait to find out what happens next, but what ever 
            it was you were drawn in.  Or if you have even driven a car, and got lost in a though or in a day dream,
            then all of the sudden you look up and you've missed your exit, or not sure of where you are, or even 
            wonder how you got where you are you were in hypnosis.  If any of these have even happened to you, 
            you have already been hypnotized and are quite capable of being hypnotized. "I'm too smart to be hypnotized.  "Being hypnotizable has nothing to do with your level of intelligence.  
            What this usually means is that I'm too smart to let people control me.  This is a misperception that
            hypnosis is a form of mind control.  As we've discussed above, hypnosis is not mind control.   
            You are the one who has the control of whether or not you want to proceed with your session.  
            All that is required to do hypnosis is the ability to follow instructions, the willingness to follow 
            those instructions and a desire to change.  Ask your self, "Can I follow instructions?"
            If you answered "Yes" then you can be hypnotized. You may have heard that only a certain percentage of people are hypnotized.  This is true for hypnotists 
            that rely on lengthy old fashioned hypnotic inductions.   This used to be the case in the past when there
            was less of an understanding about hypnosis.  This assertion is no long true.  A hypnotist that is
            trained in the latest and most advanced techniques can hypnotize any willing candidate that
            is ready to follow instructions. You now know that you are quite capable of doing hypnosis.  Being in the hypnotic state is much like that
            inner focus of watching TV or daydreaming.  Since you may not even be aware that you are in hypnosis, a 
            skilled hypnotist will convince you and show you that you are in hypnosis, so that you may receive
            your maximum benefit.  You do hypnosis all of the time, you are good at it.  
            Are you ready to use hypnosis to improve your life? Cathy Green in a Hypnosis Session What Does Hypnosis Feel Like? Hypnosis is a state of inner focus that allows you to make the inner changes to improve you life.   
            Hypnosis by itself really doesn.  t feel like anything, any more than daydreaming or watching TV 
            feels like anything.  Hypnotists commonly use relaxation as a doorway to entering the hypnotic 
            state so it may feel relaxing.  However everybody's experience is different, some people feel lighter, 
            some people feel heavier, some people feel floaty, and some people don't feel any differently.  
            Your hypnotheapist knows exactly how to determine if you are in hypnosis and knows how to
            show you that you are in hypnosis. How Can I Use Hypnosis to Help Me? What you have done in the past hasn't work.  You've gotten all of the information you could find about 
            the problem you want to overcome.  You've received the well meaning advice from your friends and family.   
            If you wanted to lose weight, you hear all you have to do is cut back on your eating, or just walk a
            little bit each day.  For smokers it could be "My uncle went stopped cold turkey, why can't you?", or 
            "Try the gum, or patch.  "Some people even tell you that you have no "will power" or "self control".   
            You hear the advice and each time you hear it you become more and more frustrated.  
            If it was as simple to do as that, you would have done it already.  Maybe you even made up your mind,
            and thought this was really the time I was going to lose weight, stop smoking or break that bad habit.  
            So you make up your mind and stick to it.  You may find that you are able to start losing a bit of weight, 
            or stop smoking, for a short time but then it all comes back.  After so many times of making up your mind
            you just give up hope, you figure I'll just accept the fact that I'm overweight, or I'm going to be a smoker
            and will just live with all the consequences.  You tell yourself that you are happy and that you accept yourself
            as you are.  But secretly you want to lose that weight, or stop smoking or just break that bad habit. The problem is that you are trying to out will the problem.  You are trying to use the conscious mind to 
            over power a belief that is generating feelings from the subconscious mind.  The problem with will power 
            is that it you have to constantly keep thinking about your problem and will power is easily defeated.  
            Will power goes away when you are hungry, angry, tired, lonely or tempted in another way.  Just think of 
            the last time you were really hungry, or saw a piece of cake, candy or something else that you really
            wanted and said "Oh well, I can start that diet starting tomorrow.  "Or when you really got stressed out
            or something happened where you just had to have a cigarette.  Will power takes a lot of though and
            energy to maintain.  Worse yet when using will power you constantly are thinking about the thing you
            want to will away.  The subconscious mind can't process a negative, so all of that time you spend trying 
            to not think about eating or have a cigarette you are actually reinforcing the behavior you want to
            get rid of.  It's like asking someone not to think about pink kittens.  Even people who are successful
            with will power for a time can get complacent and start to slow revert to their old ways because using
            will power alone does not get rid of the cause of the problem. Talking about the problem doesn't remove the problem.  It may feel good for a time to talk about 
            losing weight, breaking a bad habit, or quitting smoking or another problem.  You've tried it and it 
            has not worked.  Over and over you friends all tell you the same thing and what has worked for them 
            and in the end it just ends in frustration.  Some people spend years talking about their problem 
            and see little to no results.  You are trying to use the conscious mind to overcome a problem that 
            is stored in subconscious mind.  The conscious mind only focuses on what you are currently 
            thinking about at the time, it's analytical and likes to rationalize.  Consciously you know all the
            things that you should do to overcome your problem. The subconscious mind is where the change needs to happen.  Your subconscious mind stores all of the
            information that you have ever been exposed to in your life, it stores your beliefs and generates feelings.  
            Your critical factor is what prevents you from accomplishing your goal consciously.  It compares what you
            already know and believe about yourself, it lets in and reinforces what you already believe and rejects 
            anything that doesn't match.  It is what keeps that shy person believing that people don't like them, 
            or what keeps some people thinking only bad things happen to them when to all of the world they see good
            things happening or they know that other people like that shy person.  In these cases, the critical factor 
            only lets in the events that reinforce what that person already believes.   
            Through hypnosis we can set asides the critical factor and finally change behaviors, beliefs and habits. Imagine, we can help you lose weight without cravings, change the way you view exercise, and remove all 
            of the subconscious barriers that prevent you from losing weight.  You can finally begin to build a real 
            sense of hope that this time it will be for real.  Finally, you will no longer need to focus on dieting,
            because the urge and emotions that caused you to over eat will be gone.  Imagine shifting you view of
            exercise from painful, torture, time consuming, punishment to being enjoyable, natural and easy to do, 
            something that you look forward to doing.  Imagine improving your self-esteem, finally losing that weight
            and being able to do it without feeling deprived.  You can do all of that with hypnosis and more. You can stop smoking without feeling stressed out, anxious, sad, or angry.  Some people think of their
            cigarette as their buddy.  We can help you get rid of that buddy and not even miss him.  
            You can do this all without losing weight.  People who quit smoking and gain weight are people who have
            not taken care of the cause of the problem.  Through hypnosis we can take care of those subconscious 
            causes and use powerful hypnotic techniques to break the habit.  You can stop smoking with hypnosis and not gain weight. Are all Hypnotists the Same? Just about any hypnotist can guide you into hypnosis.  But that's where the similarities between hypnotists end.  
            All hypnosis sessions are not the same.  In order to receive long lasting and even permanent results you must 
            choose a hypnotist that uses techniques to remove the true cause of the problem.  Direct suggestion, 
            just giving suggestions to the client, alone does not remove the problem.  Hypnosis by direct suggestion alone 
            generally tends to wear off and needs to be reinforced often.  This happens because subconscious causes of the 
            problem were not taken care of.  This is why when a smoker or weight loss client that has only undergone direct 
            suggestion hypnosis alone runs up against a stressful situation they revert to their old behavior.  Direct suggestion
            hypnosis sessions are usually just one hypnosis sessions, or hotel hypnosis sessions.  Direct suggestion a foundation 
            of successful hypnosis program, however it must be used in a hypnosis program that deals with the cause of the problem.   
            When the subconscious causes of the problems are gone, your desire to continue your old behavior disappears and 
            your subconscious mind accepts all of the suggestions you want permanently.  
            I customize your sessions to your needs and do whatever needs to be done to help 
            you overcome your problem.  I combine direct suggestion and along with advanced hypnotic techniques, and newer modalities to help you get
            rid of that old useless problem.  Now that you know that hypnosis works, that you can be hypnotized and how it will 
            work for you. Contact me and make that change today.
