content: Search: Neurotransmitters and Neurochemistry in Addiction Addiction is often explained with a single sentence: “Drugs increase dopamine.” While dopamine is important, that explanation is incomplete. Addiction involves a complex interaction among neurotransmitters, hormones, brain circuits, learning, memory, stress, pain, emotional regulation, genetics, and a person’s environment. Understanding this neurochemistry does not remove personal responsibility. Instead, it helps explain why addiction can become so powerful, why stopping can be difficult even when someone sincerely wants to stop, and why effective recovery usually requires more than willpower alone. What Are Neurotransmitters? Neurotransmitters are chemical messengers used by nerve cells to communicate. A neuron releases a neurotransmitter into a tiny space between cells called a synapse. The neurotransmitter then binds to receptors on another cell, increasing or decreasing that cell’s activity. Some neurotransmitters primarily stimulate activity, while others primarily reduce it. Many have several functions depending on where they are active and which receptors they affect. Important neurotransmitters and related chemical systems involved in addiction include: Dopamine Serotonin GABA Glutamate Endorphins and other endogenous opioids Norepinephrine, also called noradrenaline Endocannabinoids Acetylcholine and other signaling systems These systems do not work independently. They continually influence one another. Addiction Involves Brain Circuits, Not Just Chemicals Neurotransmitters are part of larger brain circuits. Several areas are especially important in addiction, including the reward system, the prefrontal cortex, the amygdala, the hippocampus, and stress-related networks. The reward system helps the brain identify experiences that may be worth repeating. The prefrontal cortex contributes to judgment, planning, impulse control, and decision-making. The amygdala helps process emotional significance and threat. The hippocampus connects experiences with memories, places, people, and situations. When a substance repeatedly produces powerful relief or pleasure, the brain learns that the substance is important. Eventually, reminders associated with the substance can trigger cravings before the person consciously decides to use. This is one reason addiction is not simply a series of isolated choices. Repeated substance use teaches the brain powerful associations, and those associations can remain active long after the original reasons for using have changed. Dopamine: Reward, Motivation, and Learning Dopamine is one of the neurotransmitters most closely associated with addiction. It plays important roles in: Motivation Reward learning Attention Movement Anticipation Memory formation Goal-directed behavior Dopamine is not simply the brain’s “pleasure chemical.” It is more accurate to describe it as part of a system that helps the brain identify what is important and motivates a person to pursue it. Addictive substances can produce dopamine signals that are faster, stronger, or more reliable than many natural rewards. Over time, the brain learns to prioritize the substance and the circumstances connected to it. This can create a cycle: The substance produces a powerful effect. The brain identifies the substance as highly significant. Cues associated with the substance trigger anticipation. Craving increases motivation to seek it. Use temporarily changes the person’s internal state. The cycle is reinforced. With repeated use, natural rewards may feel less satisfying by comparison. Work, relationships, hobbies, food, and ordinary pleasures may seem dull or emotionally distant. This reduced ability to experience pleasure is called anhedonia . Dopamine does not act alone. Changes in dopamine signaling are influenced by glutamate, stress hormones, opioid systems, serotonin, and many other biological processes. Serotonin: Mood, Impulse Control, and Emotional Regulation Serotonin, also known as 5-hydroxytryptamine or 5-HT, is involved in mood, sleep, appetite, digestion, pain processing, learning, and impulse control. People often refer to serotonin as a “happiness chemical,” but that description is too simple. Serotonin helps regulate emotional stability and communication among several brain systems. Changes in serotonin signaling may affect mood, anxiety, irritability, impulsivity, sleep, and the ability to tolerate distress. Substances that affect serotonin can produce temporary changes in mood or perception. Repeated use may disrupt normal regulation, particularly when substance use is combined with poor sleep, chronic stress, trauma, or an underlying mood disorder. Serotonin also interacts with dopamine. In some situations, changes in serotonin can alter reward-seeking behavior, impulse control, and the emotional consequences of a craving. GABA: The Brain’s Main Inhibitory System GABA, or gamma-aminobutyric acid, is the brain’s primary inhibitory neurotransmitter. It generally reduces neural activity and helps regulate anxiety, muscle tension, relaxation, sleep, and emotional arousal. Alcohol and benzodiazepines—including medications such as alprazolam, lorazepam, clonazepam, and diazepam—enhance aspects of GABA activity. This can create relaxation, reduced anxiety, sedation, impaired coordination, and slowed reaction time. When GABA activity is repeatedly increased by an external substance, the brain may compensate by becoming more excitable. If the substance is suddenly removed, the brain can temporarily become overactive. This is why withdrawal from alcohol or benzodiazepines can be medically dangerous. Severe withdrawal may involve agitation, hallucinations, delirium, or seizures. Anyone who uses these substances regularly should seek medical guidance rather than stopping abruptly without professional supervision. Glutamate: Learning, Excitation, and Cravings Glutamate is the brain’s primary excitatory neurotransmitter. It supports learning, memory, attention, and communication among neurons. Glutamate is especially important in addiction because it helps the brain learn associations. Places, people, times of day, emotions, music, routes, or routines can become connected with substance use. Later, those cues may activate craving and drug-seeking behavior even when the person is not consciously thinking about using. The relationship between glutamate and GABA can be understood as a balance between excitation and inhibition. GABA generally reduces neural activity, while glutamate generally increases it. The brain must continually adjust both systems to maintain stability. During withdrawal, this balance can be disrupted. The nervous system may become restless, anxious, irritable, over-alert, and highly reactive. Glutamate is also related to glutamine metabolism. Glutamine acts as a transport and recycling molecule that helps support the production and regulation of glutamate and GABA in the brain. Endorphins and the Endogenous Opioid System Endorphins are naturally occurring opioid peptides produced by the body. They help regulate pain, stress, mood, and emotional responses. Related endogenous opioid peptides include enkephalins and dynorphins. Opioid drugs such as morphine, oxycodone, heroin, and fentanyl activate opioid receptors from outside the body. These substances can reduce pain and produce relief, calm, pleasure, or euphoria. With repeated opioid exposure, the nervous system adapts. The body may reduce its own opioid activity or change receptor sensitivity. The person may then require more of the substance to achieve the same effect, a process known as tolerance. When opioid use stops, the body may be left without the external stimulation to which it has adapted. Withdrawal can include pain, restlessness, sweating, gastrointestinal symptoms, anxiety, insomnia, low mood, and intense cravings. The phrase “endorphin deficiency” is sometimes used to describe the possibility of unusually low endogenous opioid activity. However, it is not a universally accepted diagnosis with a single standard test. Addiction cannot be explained by endorphins alone. Pain, stress, mood, learning, genetics, environment, and many other systems also contribute. Norepinephrine: Alertness and the Stress Response Norepinephrine, also called noradrenaline, functions as both a neurotransmitter and a hormone. It helps regulate: Alertness Attention Arousal Blood pressure Memory formation The fight-or-flight response During stress or withdrawal, norepinephrine activity can increase. This may contribute to anxiety, irritability, sweating, rapid heartbeat, restlessness, difficulty sleeping, and a feeling that something is seriously wrong. A person in withdrawal may appear emotionally distant or exhausted while internally experiencing intense nervous-system activation. This mismatch between outward appearance and internal experience can make addiction difficult for families to understand. Norepinephrine also interacts with dopamine, serotonin, and stress hormones. Persistent stress can increase the importance of immediate relief and make long-term decision-making more difficult. Endocannabinoids: Internal Stress and Mood Regulation Endocannabinoids are lipid-based chemical messengers produced naturally by the body. The best-known examples are anandamide and 2-arachidonoylglycerol, or 2-AG. These compounds help regulate mood, appetite, sleep, pain, memory, immune activity, and stress responses. Unlike many neurotransmitters, endocannabinoids often travel backward across the synapse and adjust how much neurotransmitter is released. Cannabis compounds such as THC can mimic some of the effects of naturally occurring endocannabinoids by activating cannabinoid receptors. Depending on the person, dose, setting, and frequency of use, this may produce relaxation, pleasure, altered perception, increased appetite, anxiety, or paranoia. The endocannabinoid system interacts with dopamine, serotonin, GABA, glutamate, and opioid systems. It is one more example of why addiction and mood cannot be reduced to a single chemical. Why Substances Feel Different to Different People Different Bodies, Different Responses. We all React to Drugs Uniquely. People do not all respond to the same substance in the same way. One person may become sleepy after taking an opioid, while another may feel energized or unusually optimistic. One person may feel relaxed after using cannabis, while another experiences anxiety. A medication that calms one person may produce agitation or unexpected stimulation in another. These differences may be influenced by: Genetics Age and physical health Previous substance exposure Tolerance Sleep and stress Mental-health conditions Other medications or substances Expectations and environment Differences in metabolism and receptor sensitivity A paradoxical reaction occurs when a substance produces an effect opposite to what is normally expected. These reactions are real, but they do not by themselves identify a specific neurotransmitter abnormality or prove that a person has a particular deficiency. Tolerance and Physical Dependence Tolerance develops when repeated exposure causes a substance to have a reduced effect. The person may need more of the substance or use it more frequently to achieve the effect they once obtained from a smaller amount. Physical dependence occurs when the body adapts to regular substance exposure. If the substance is suddenly reduced or stopped, withdrawal symptoms can occur. These processes are biological adaptations, not evidence of moral weakness. Physical dependence can occur with some properly prescribed medications and does not automatically mean that a person has an addiction. Addiction involves a broader pattern, often including impaired control, compulsive use, continued use despite significant harm, and the substance taking priority over important areas of life. Psychological Dependence and the Need for Relief Psychological dependence involves relying on a substance or behavior to manage emotions, stress, pain, boredom, fear, or daily functioning. The person may believe that they cannot cope, sleep, work, socialize, or feel normal without it. Psychological dependence is strengthened through learning. If a substance repeatedly reduces anxiety or emotional pain, the brain records that relief as important. Cravings may then appear whenever similar distress returns. This does not mean the person is pretending. The emotional reliance can be intense and physically felt. However, psychological dependence can change through treatment, new coping skills, corrective experiences, social support, and repeated practice. The Brain During Withdrawal Withdrawal occurs when the brain and body are trying to function without a substance after adapting to its presence. The specific symptoms depend on the substance, dose, duration of use, health status, and individual biology. Common experiences include: Anxiety and agitation Low mood or emotional emptiness Sleep disruption Muscle aches and pain Sweating or chills Nausea and digestive problems Difficulty concentrating Irritability Strong cravings Increased sensitivity to stress The person may also experience anhedonia , in which ordinary activities provide little or no pleasure. This can be especially discouraging because the person may want to enjoy family, hobbies, food, or nature but feel emotionally disconnected from them. Recovery of the brain’s natural regulation systems takes time. Some people improve quickly, while others experience prolonged mood, sleep, or craving problems. Individual recovery is influenced by the substance used, length of use, co-occurring conditions, stress, nutrition, sleep, safety, and treatment access. Why Relapse Can Happen After Abstinence A return to substance use is often called a relapse, although many treatment approaches prefer language such as “return to use.” It may occur after exposure to a cue, a stressful event, emotional pain, overconfidence, physical discomfort, or a belief that one use will be manageable. Brain associations can remain active even after a period of abstinence. A person may feel stable for weeks or months and then experience a sudden, powerful craving after encountering a familiar person, place, smell, memory, or emotion. A return to use should be taken seriously, but it should not be treated as proof that recovery is impossible. It can indicate that the person needs additional support, a safer plan, medical treatment, new coping strategies, or a different recovery approach. Because tolerance may decrease during abstinence, returning to a previously familiar dose can also increase overdose risk. Harm-reduction education, naloxone access, and evidence-based treatment are important parts of saving lives. Neurochemistry Does Not Eliminate Responsibility Explaining addiction through brain chemistry does not mean a person has no responsibility for their actions. It means that responsibility must be understood within the reality of biology, learning, stress, and behavior. A person may be responsible for seeking help, protecting others, being honest, repairing harm, and making safer choices. At the same time, shame and punishment alone do not restore neurotransmitter balance, erase cravings, or teach new coping skills. A more useful approach combines accountability with treatment and compassion. People need consequences when necessary, but they also need accurate information, medical care, psychological support, and realistic opportunities to change. Treatment and Recovery Because addiction involves multiple systems, effective treatment may require multiple forms of support. Depending on the substance and the individual’s circumstances, treatment may include: Medical evaluation Medications for opioid use disorder, such as buprenorphine or methadone Medically supervised withdrawal management Counseling and psychotherapy Cognitive behavioral therapy Dialectical behavior therapy Trauma-informed care Contingency management Recovery groups and peer support Mindfulness and stress-regulation skills Sleep, nutrition, and physical-health support Harm-reduction services No single recovery pathway works for everyone. Twelve-step programs help many people, while others benefit from approaches such as SMART Recovery or other secular, skills-based, medication-supported, or individualized models. The goal is not simply to force the brain to stop wanting a substance. The goal is to help the person build a life in which safety, connection, meaning, competence, and healthy rewards become more available than the substance was. Recovery and Neuroplasticity The brain is adaptable. This ability to change is called neuroplasticity . Addiction reflects one form of repeated learning and adaptation, but recovery can involve new forms of learning and adaptation as well. Over time, healthy routines and supportive experiences can strengthen alternative pathways. The brain can learn to tolerate discomfort, delay impulses, recognize triggers, experience natural rewards, and respond to stress in new ways. Recovery is rarely a straight line. Sleep may improve before mood. Cravings may decrease while anxiety remains. A person may understand what to do but still need repeated practice before new behavior becomes automatic. Progress is not measured only by whether someone experiences a craving. It can also be measured by how they respond to it, how quickly they seek support, how honestly they communicate, and how much control they regain over their choices. Conclusion Neurotransmitters and neurochemistry help explain why addiction can affect motivation, pleasure, pain, stress, memory, judgment, and behavior. Dopamine contributes to reward learning, but it is only one part of a much larger network. Serotonin, GABA, glutamate, endorphins, norepinephrine, endocannabinoids, hormones, and brain circuits all contribute to the experience of substance use and recovery. Addiction is neither a simple chemical imbalance nor a simple moral failure. It is a complex condition shaped by biology, learning, emotional experience, environment, and personal history. Understanding the science should lead to better treatment and less stigma. It should also encourage realistic expectations: the brain can change, but meaningful recovery usually takes time, support, repeated practice, and an approach suited to the individual. Search: Your Addiction or Unwanted Behaviors Aren’t Broken Code — They’re Legacy Code Author: Adam Fistler, BCH - Behavorial Change Consultant ( adam@adamfistler.com ) When you inherit an old software system, you often encounter code that makes no obvious sense. There may be a strange workaround buried deep in the program: if condition_x:
               do_weird_thing() Your first reaction might be: “Why the hell is this here?” But an experienced programmer knows not to delete unexplained code immediately. Before changing it, they ask: “What problem was this originally solving?” Maybe the system used to crash under a certain condition. Maybe someone added the code during an emergency. Maybe it was written at 2:47 in the morning, when the priority was not elegance but keeping the system running. The patch worked. So it stayed. Over time, other parts of the system began depending on it. The original programmer left. The original problem changed or disappeared. Eventually, nobody remembered exactly why the code existed—but removing it still risked breaking something else. That is legacy code. Addiction and other unwanted behaviors can develop in much the same way. Not because human beings are literally computers, and not because people can be reduced to software. The comparison is useful because it gives us a way to think about how behaviors develop, become reinforced, accumulate dependencies, and eventually become harmful. It invites a different question. Instead of asking: “Why do you keep doing this when you know it is hurting you?” we might ask: “What problem was this behavior originally trying to solve?” The 2:47 a.m. production patch Many unwanted behaviors do not begin as obvious problems. They begin as solutions. A person encounters something they do not know how to manage. They may feel overwhelmed, anxiou2am Debugging Sessions, lonely, angry, frightened, or emotionally trapped. They may have experienced something painful without having the resources or support to process it. Then they discover a behavior that changes something. It may provide relief. It may quiet intrusive thoughts, reduce anxiety, create emotional distance, offer stimulation, produce confidence, or make an unbearable situation temporarily tolerable. The behavior may not be healthy. It may not be sustainable. It may eventually become destructive. But at the time, it does something useful. The brain learns: This works. When the behavior is repeated, the association becomes stronger. A particular emotional state, thought, environment, or situation begins to activate the behavior automatically. What started as a conscious workaround gradually becomes part of the system’s normal operation. Years later, the person may look at the behavior and ask: “Why do I keep doing this?” That question resembles the programmer inheriting unexplained legacy code. The behavior may no longer fit the person’s life. It may now create problems rather than solve them. But it remains available because it was reinforced, practiced, and incorporated into the larger system. Do not confuse the behavior with its function One of the easiest mistakes is to judge a behavior only by its current consequences. A behavior can be harmful and still have served a function. Understanding that function is not the same as approving of the behavior. It is the difference between excusing a problem and investigating it accurately. If someone uses a substance to regulate overwhelming emotions, removing the substance does not automatically remove the emotions. If someone uses a behavior to escape painful thoughts, eliminating the behavior does not necessarily eliminate what they were trying to escape. If someone repeatedly enters destructive relationships because those relationships provide familiarity, validation, or temporary relief from loneliness, simply telling them to choose better relationships does not explain what the pattern is doing for them. The behavior may be the visible problem. Its function may be hidden underneath. So instead of asking only: “How do we stop this behavior?” we can also ask: “What functionality does this behavior provide?” What feeling does it change? What does it help the person avoid? What does it make possible, at least temporarily? What expectation has been reinforced? Until those questions are addressed, removing the behavior may leave the underlying need intact. When the original problem changes Legacy code often remains long after the conditions that created it have disappeared. The same can happen with human behavior. A person may leave a difficult environment, become safer, grow older, develop new resources, or enter a different stage of life. The original problem may no longer exist in the same form. But the behavior remains. This can be deeply confusing. Someone may think: “My life is different now. Why am I still doing this?” One answer is: The code is still there. The nervous system learned a pattern. The pattern became familiar. It may now be activated by reminders, emotional states, or situations that resemble the original circumstances—even when the current situation is objectively different. The original purpose may be forgotten, but the response remains available. This is one reason knowledge alone is often insufficient. A person may understand perfectly well that a behavior is harmful and still feel compelled to repeat it. The problem is not necessarily a lack of information. The behavior may be operating as an old, deeply reinforced process. Dependencies accumulate Unwanted behaviors rarely remain isolated. Like a piece of legacy software, they can develop dependencies throughout the system. A behavior may become connected to: emotional regulation daily routines beliefs about the self expectations about other people relationships physical environments social groups sleep and eating patterns other behaviors memories and learned associations Eventually, other parts of life may organize themselves around the behavior. That is why removing it is not always the same as solving the problem. If a behavior has been regulating emotion, filling time, creating social connection, managing fear, or providing a sense of control, its absence may expose functions that were never replaced. This is also why a person can stop one behavior and quickly find another taking its place. The system still has a need. It looks for another process capable of meeting it. The crucial question becomes: What needs to replace the functionality this behavior was providing? A replacement does not have to feel identical. It does, however, need to address the underlying requirement well enough for the system to remain stable. Investigating the system A useful investigation might ask: What problem was this behavior originally solving? What does it accomplish now? What tends to trigger it? What does the person expect it to do? What feeling does it change? What beliefs support it? What routines or relationships depend on it? What would happen if it disappeared tomorrow? What skills, supports, or environmental changes would need to replace it? These questions are not intended to turn a person into a mechanical object. They are intended to replace vague self-condemnation with usable information. A programmer who discovers a dangerous function does not learn more by shouting at the code. They learn more by examining its inputs, outputs, dependencies, and failure conditions. The same principle can apply to behavior. Curiosity may reveal information that shame conceals. The danger of rebuilding everything at once When people decide to change, they often try to change their entire lives simultaneously. They stop the unwanted behavior. They change their friends. They repair relationships. They find a new job. They start exercising, meditating, journaling, eating differently, sleeping better, managing their finances, and becoming an entirely new person. Sometimes a dramatic reset is necessary. But changing everything at once creates a technical problem: it becomes difficult to know which change produced which result. If the system improves, you may not know why. If it becomes unstable, you may not know what caused the failure. A wholesale personal refactor can also create unrealistic expectations. When one part of the plan fails, the person may interpret the setback as proof that the entire effort has failed. A more sustainable approach is often incremental: Identify a problem. Make one manageable change. Observe what happens. Learn from the result. Adjust the approach. Stabilize the improvement. Continue from there. This may feel slower than a complete reinvention. But it allows the person to learn how their own system responds to change. You do not get a maintenance window for your life A software system can sometimes be taken offline. Developers can shut it down, replace components, test a new version, and restart it. People usually do not get that option. Change takes place while life continues. There are still responsibilities, relationships, work, financial pressures, physical needs, memories, and emotional reactions. Recovery is not performed in a perfectly controlled environment. It happens while the system is running. That means change often has to be iterative: Identify. Change. Observe. Learn. Adjust. Stabilize. Repeat. A new behavior may work in one environment but fail in another. A coping strategy may help with anxiety but not loneliness. A plan that seemed realistic may turn out to demand more energy than the person has available. That is not necessarily evidence of personal failure. It may be information about how the system actually works. A setback is not the same as losing everything When software encounters a bug, developers do not automatically discard the entire codebase. They investigate. What conditions produced the failure? What assumption was wrong? What dependency was overlooked? What part of the system needs additional support? Setbacks can be approached similarly. A setback may reveal: an unrecognized trigger a missing coping mechanism an unresolved dependency an overly ambitious plan an unsafe environment a belief that needs reconsideration inadequate support a replacement behavior that does not perform the required function This does not mean minimizing consequences. A relapse or harmful action may require repair, accountability, medical attention, or immediate protection from danger. But a setback does not automatically erase everything learned before it. The useful question becomes: “What did this teach me about the system?” rather than: “What is wrong with me?” The interface is not the whole system The software metaphor has limits. A person is not a machine waiting to be optimized. Human beings have history, meaning, embodiment, relationships, agency, and dignity. The metaphor should clarify behavior, not replace the person. There is also a difference between a person’s conscious explanation and the entire mechanism underlying their behavior. Someone’s explanation may be accurate, incomplete, or based on what they currently understand. It is information about the system, but it is not necessarily the whole source code. Automatic associations, emotional learning, bodily states, social conditions, memories, and environmental cues may all contribute. This is why change sometimes requires more investigation than simply identifying a consciously stated reason. The visible explanation may be the interface. The deeper pattern may be operating underneath it. Different problems need different tools There is no single tool that solves every technical problem. A screwdriver is not better than a hammer. It is better suited to a different task. The same is true of recovery and behavior change. Different approaches may address different layers of the system, including: broader therapeutic work behavioral techniques mindfulness medication peer support recovery programs hypnosis environmental changes medical care practical assistance community and relationship support The important question is not: “Which method is the one true way?” It is: “What problem are we actually trying to solve, and what tool fits that problem?” Some problems require an architectural review: understanding patterns across history, relationships, beliefs, and environment. Other problems are more like debugging a specific component: identifying a trigger, changing a routine, interrupting an association, or developing a particular skill. Neither approach is automatically superior. Sometimes the system needs architectural work. Sometimes it needs targeted debugging. Often, it needs both. Refactoring instead of rebuilding the person The goal of change is not necessarily to become a completely different person. It may be more useful to think of change as refactoring. Refactoring means improving the structure and function of an existing system while preserving what works. It can involve: keeping useful capabilities identifying harmful processes replacing ineffective implementations building missing functionality removing obsolete dependencies improving communication between parts of the system testing changes gradually learning from earlier versions This approach also makes room for compassion. Some of the old code may have been written under difficult circumstances. It may have been created by a younger version of the person, one with fewer resources, less information, and fewer choices. The behavior may have been the best solution available at the time. That does not mean it must remain the best solution forever. An adaptation can be understandable and still require change. A behavior can once have been protective and later become destructive. Recognizing its original purpose does not require preserving it indefinitely. You may not be broken Some people spend years treating unwanted behaviors as evidence of a fundamental defect. They conclude that they are weak, damaged, irrational, or incapable of change. But perhaps another description is more useful. Perhaps they are running legacy software. Some of that code is useful. Some is outdated. Some was written under difficult circumstances. Some was never documented. Some has dependencies nobody remembers. Some began as a desperate workaround. And some may now be causing the very problems it was originally created to solve. The answer is not necessarily to hate the old code. It is to understand it. Ask what it was protecting, regulating, avoiding, or providing. Identify what still depends on it. Build the missing functionality. Replace harmful processes with more effective ones. Make changes carefully enough that the rest of the system can adapt. The central progression is: “Why do you keep doing this?” becomes “What problem was this solving?” then “What dependencies did it create?” then “What needs to replace it?” and finally “How do we refactor it while life keeps running?” You may not be broken. You may be carrying old code that once helped you survive. Now the work is learning how to update it. content: Search: Outsourcing Your Agency The Platform Wants to Be Your Higher Power Author: Adam Fistler, BCH - Behavorial Change Consultant ( adam@adamfistler.com ) I have spent most of my life loving technology because it represented freedom. A computer was something you could explore. A network was something you could learn. Software was something you could modify. If you were willing to understand how a system worked, you could often make it do things its creators had never intended. Technology expanded what an individual could do. When I returned to the technological world after years of addiction, homelessness, and rebuilding my life, I expected technology to have changed. I did not expect it to feel as though it had changed sides. The technology I encountered was more powerful than the technology I remembered, but it was also more restrictive. It demanded accounts, phones, identity verification, subscriptions, app installations, cloud connections, and permission from systems I could neither inspect nor appeal to. It did not simply help me do things. Increasingly, it required me to surrender information and judgment before it would let me participate. Rebuilding Agency My addiction began with prescription opioids. It eventually led to heroin, divorce, and homelessness. In 2020, I was living on the streets of Camden, New Jersey. Climbing back from that required more than stopping drug use. I had to rebuild my ability to make decisions, tolerate discomfort, solve problems, and trust my own judgment. I had to reconstruct a life from circumstances that had stripped away much of my independence. I did not fit comfortably into the traditional recovery model. Because I resisted the Twelve Step approach, I was called noncompliant, resistant, dishonest, or “not ready.” I was told there was one true path to recovery, and that the path required surrendering my will and my life to a higher power and a group. But I had already lost my agency to addiction. I was not willing to surrender it again as the price of getting it back. I had to find my own path. That experience changed the way I think about authority. It made me wary of systems that present obedience as the same thing as healing, safety, or progress. It also gave me a simple question to ask of any institution or technology: Does this help me exercise my agency, or does it ask me to surrender it? Returning to Technology Technology had been one of the things I loved most since childhood. It represented exploration and self-expression. You could take things apart intellectually, learn how they worked, and build something new. A computer was not merely an appliance. It was a machine you could understand and reshape. The Internet was a place to explore. You could find independent websites, technical documentation, unusual communities, personal essays, experimental projects, and perspectives that would never have made it through a traditional publishing system. You could host your own site, run your own services, communicate directly, and participate without first becoming a product in somebody else’s ecosystem. When I began rebuilding my life and re-entering society, I encountered a different technological world. I was expected to have continuous access to a phone, email address, government identification, modern hardware, reliable Internet, and working two-factor authentication. Employment systems, financial services, government websites, identity-verification systems, and account-recovery processes all assumed those things were already in place. When I did not have them, the systems rarely offered a meaningful alternative. The answer was usually: Get a newer phone. Use the app. Verify your identity. Access the email account. Receive the text message. Upload the photograph. Try again. If the process failed, the problem was treated as a personal deficiency rather than a design failure. The system did not ask whether its assumptions matched reality. It assumed that anyone who could not satisfy them was an exception to be filtered out. That was one of the first signs that technology was no longer primarily being designed to expand individual capability. It was being designed around the needs of the platform. The Algorithm Decides What Matters Search Results used to be More Relevant The clearest example is the modern Internet’s treatment of information. The older Internet was largely about retrieval. You had a question, you entered search terms, and you looked for an answer. You chose what to read, which links to follow, and how deeply to investigate a subject. The modern Internet increasingly wants to make those choices for you. YouTube is a good example. It is still possible to find useful, focused material there, but the platform’s incentives have transformed much of its content. Videos that could communicate an idea in a few minutes are stretched into twenty-, thirty-, or forty-five-minute experiences filled with repetition. The structure is familiar: A dramatic opening hook. A promise that the important information is coming. A repetition of the hook. A long introduction. A sponsor segment. A restatement of the basic premise. A few minutes of information. Another diversion. Another request to subscribe. A preview of a later point. A conclusion that repeats what was already said. The information is not necessarily false. It is simply surrounded by padding designed to keep the viewer from leaving. The goal is no longer just to communicate clearly. The goal is to maximize watch time, engagement, retention, and the probability that the viewer will continue to the next video. The platform does not merely provide information. It manages attention. That changes the relationship between the viewer and the content. Instead of deciding what to watch next, the viewer is encouraged to accept the next recommendation. Instead of seeking information, the viewer is placed into a stream that never ends. The system keeps the next thing ready before the individual has decided whether they want it. This is a subtle form of agency replacement. No one is forcing you to watch. The platform does not need to force you. It only needs to make choosing unnecessary. When Search Stops Being Search Modern Search Engines Deliver Less Relevant and Useful Results Search engines have changed in a similar way. In theory, search should connect a question with the most relevant information. In practice, the results increasingly seem shaped by advertising budgets, search-engine optimization, institutional authority, commercial relationships, and the ability to produce content in the format platforms prefer. The question is no longer simply: What page best answers the terms I entered? It often becomes: Which organization has the authority, money, or optimization strategy to appear in front of me? Independent websites and personal commentary have become harder to find. So have specialist communities, unconventional perspectives, and information that does not fit the language of established institutions. Search results favor large organizations, commercial sites, established media companies, pages written for ranking systems, and content that has been sanitized into a form acceptable to the platform. This does not mean every independent source is reliable or every institution is corrupt. It means the user increasingly has less control over the range of perspectives presented for consideration. The search engine is not merely indexing the web. It is shaping the portion of the web that remains visible. The terms you enter matter, but so does the infrastructure deciding which results deserve to appear. Relevance is no longer determined only by your question. It is filtered through a system that has its own priorities. You are still technically searching. But the platform increasingly decides what counts as findable. The Company Decides What Is Relevant The Algorith Decides What's Relevant to You This pattern extends beyond search and video. Platforms increasingly decide: Which information is relevant Which speech is acceptable Which accounts are trustworthy Which links are safe Which communities are legitimate Which businesses can operate Which services may remain online Which files can be shared Which applications can be installed Which forms of privacy are suspicious The language used to justify these decisions is usually reassuring. It is to reduce spam. It is to protect children. It is to fight misinformation. It is to stop piracy. It is to prevent terrorism. It is to combat money laundering. It is to improve security. Many of these problems are real. The question is whether every proposed solution deserves unlimited power, and whether the people enforcing the rules can be trusted to define the problem fairly. A company may say it is removing misinformation, but the company decides what misinformation means. A platform may say it is protecting users, but the platform decides which users require protection and what that protection looks like. A hosting provider may say it is preventing abuse, but the provider decides what counts as suspicious infrastructure. A search engine may say it is improving relevance, but the search engine decides which sources are relevant enough to show you. The problem is not simply that decisions are being made. The problem is that decisions affecting public knowledge, communication, and participation are increasingly made by private systems that are difficult to inspect, challenge, or leave. Independence Is Treated as Suspicious Hosting Private Servers is Viewed as Suspicious or Criminal The older Internet made it possible for individuals and small groups to operate their own infrastructure. You could run a website. Host a service. Maintain a mail server. Share files. Build a forum. Create an alternative community. Publish information without asking a large platform to distribute it for you. That independence has become increasingly difficult. Running your own email server is difficult because large providers treat independent mail systems as suspicious by default. Hosting your own files may resemble piracy to automated systems. Operating a server can trigger abuse classifications. Sharing information outside approved platforms can make you appear untrustworthy. Privacy itself is often treated as a warning sign. Encryption is described as something that ordinary people do not need. The implication is familiar: If you are not doing anything wrong, why do you need privacy? But privacy is not evidence of wrongdoing. Encryption is not a criminal tool. It is a basic method of establishing boundaries around communication and information. People lock their doors. They close their curtains. They do not hand their diaries to strangers. Digital communication should not be considered suspicious merely because it has boundaries. Yet the same arguments used to restrict privacy and independent infrastructure appear again and again: It is for the children. It is to stop criminals. It is to prevent terrorism. It is to fight abuse. It is to reduce spam. It is to protect the public from misinformation. Sometimes those concerns are sincere. But those arguments can also become permanent justifications for concentrating power. Once a company or government receives authority to inspect, filter, identify, or restrict everyone, the authority rarely remains limited to the original problem. The danger is not only what the system is intended to do. It is what the system can eventually be used to do. The Customer Becomes Quality Assurance End Users are Increasingly Bearing the Burden of Quality Assurance The outsourcing of agency also appears in software development. When I was coming up, the basic expectation was that developers would understand the problem, design an architecture, write the code, test it, review it, and send it through quality assurance before deploying it. Development was iterative. You built something, examined it, learned from it, and refined the design. You discovered that two pieces of code overlapped, that an assumption was wrong, that a configuration belonged outside the program, or that several abstractions could be simplified. The development process included time for thinking. Modern development culture increasingly emphasizes speed above all else: Move fast and break things. Deploy continuously. Let production reveal the problems. Use monitoring to catch failures. Roll back when something goes wrong. Continuous integration and continuous deployment can be valuable engineering practices. Automation can reduce mistakes and help teams deliver improvements safely. The problem is the mindset that sometimes accompanies them: the assumption that software can be released before it is genuinely understood because automated systems will detect the consequences. The customer becomes part of the testing infrastructure. If the application crashes, an error-monitoring system records it. If a deployment breaks something, the pipeline rolls it back. If users lose time, data, money, or trust, the organization describes the system as resilient because it eventually recovered. But the customer still experienced the failure. Responsibility has not disappeared. It has been moved away from the people building the system and onto the people using it. The user is expected to tolerate broken software, confusing interfaces, unexpected changes, performance problems, and temporary outages as the price of innovation. That is another kind of agency transfer. The company retains control over the system while the customer absorbs the consequences of its decisions. When AI Becomes the Architect Artificial intelligence introduces another version of the same problem. AI can be useful. It can generate scaffolding, explain unfamiliar code, automate repetitive tasks, create test cases, and help developers get past tedious work. There is nothing wrong with using a tool to reduce drudgery. The danger begins when the tool is treated as an authority rather than an assistant. Software architecture requires judgment. It involves deciding how a system should be divided, what assumptions are safe, where data belongs, how failures should be handled, which abstractions are useful, and how the system can be changed later. Those decisions cannot be reduced to producing code that appears to work. A developer who asks AI to generate boilerplate is still making the important decisions. A developer who asks AI to design the entire system without understanding the results is outsourcing responsibility for the architecture. The result may compile. It may even pass its initial tests. But the person responsible for maintaining it may not understand why it works, what assumptions it contains, or where it will fail. The code becomes something that even its owner cannot confidently change. That is not an expansion of agency. It is a dependency disguised as productivity. AI should help people understand and create more. It should not become a substitute for understanding. Convenience Is Not the Same as Freedom Modern Technology Creates a Comfortable Cage The common defense of all these systems is convenience. The app is easier. The algorithm saves time. The cloud handles the complexity. The platform protects users. The identity system improves security. The AI writes the code. The automated pipeline catches the errors. Sometimes these claims are true. Convenience has real value. But convenience is not the same as freedom. A system can make an individual task easier while making the individual more dependent overall. A cloud service may make files available everywhere, but it may also make access dependent on an account, a subscription, an Internet connection, and the continued existence of a company. An app may make parking easier, but it may also turn a public space into a private platform. An algorithm may help you discover content, but it may also narrow what you encounter and train you to accept whatever it selects. AI may produce code faster, but it may also weaken the developer’s understanding of the system. The relevant question is not simply: Is this convenient? It is: What control am I giving up in exchange for that convenience? The Platform Wants to Be Your Higher Power This is why the modern technological environment feels so unsettling to me. The platform wants to become the authority between you and the world. It decides what information you see, what services you can access, what communication is permitted, which tools are trustworthy, which accounts are legitimate, which content is relevant, and which systems are allowed to exist. It does not ask you to understand the system. It asks you to trust it. Trust the platform. Trust the identity provider. Trust the cloud. Trust the algorithm. Trust the app store. Trust the automated fraud detector. Trust the moderation system. Trust the AI. And if the system gets it wrong, good luck finding a human. This resembles the language of surrender that I encountered in recovery. Let go of your judgment. Follow the prescribed path. Accept that the system knows what is best. If it does not work, assume the failure is yours. But I spent years rebuilding my agency after addiction took it from me. I am not interested in handing it over again—this time to an algorithm, an application, or a corporation that insists it knows what is best for me. I am not opposed to technology. I am opposed to surrendering my judgment merely because a platform has made itself difficult to avoid. Technology should expand the number of things an individual can do. It should help people explore, create, communicate, understand, and act independently. It should not require individuals to surrender their identity, privacy, attention, and judgment before being allowed to participate. Technology can be a tool. It can be an instrument of freedom, self-expression, and discovery. But when the tool begins demanding obedience, it is no longer merely helping us act. It is asking to become our higher power. About The Author Adam Fistler is a Behavioral Change Consultant, Board Certified Hypnotist, Certified 5-PATH® Hypnotist, and former owner of the Baltimore Hypnosis Center. A member of the International 5-PATH® Hypnosis Association and certified by the National Guild of Hypnotists, Adam has studied hypnosis, behavior change, and the relationship between thoughts, beliefs, emotions, and behavior for more than two decades. His perspective is shaped by more than professional training. Adam has also lived through addiction and recovery firsthand across South Jersey and the Philadelphia region, including surviving on the streets of Camden. This gives him a deeply personal understanding of the struggle from both sides: as a practitioner who has helped others create change and as someone who has had to confront his own deeply ingrained patterns and beliefs. During his own recovery, Adam returned to the principles of hypnosis, mindfulness, self-talk, and behavioral change that he had studied throughout his career. He discovered that recovery could be about more than simply managing cravings or avoiding relapse—it could also be an opportunity to understand the beliefs, emotional patterns, and experiences that had shaped his behavior. Today, Adam combines his professional experience with the lessons of his own journey to serve clients throughout South Jersey, Philadelphia, and beyond, helping others explore the possibility of meaningful, lasting change. His approach is grounded in empathy, curiosity, practical tools, and the belief that people are more than the behaviors they are trying to overcome. content: Search: When the Machine Becomes the Scapegoat: Applying the Family Systems Model To Coroprate America Author: Adam Fistler, BCH - Behavorial Change Consultant ( adam@adamfistler.com ) AI is the Modern Day Coporate Scapegoat Most people have seen a family avoid an uncomfortable problem by focusing on one person. Something is wrong, but nobody is willing to talk about what it is. One person makes excuses. Another tries to keep the peace. Someone becomes angry. Someone else gets blamed for “causing drama.” Before long, the family has a simple story: that person is the problem. The story may not be fair, but it can be easier to live with than the truth. If everyone focuses on one person’s behavior, nobody has to ask what is happening inside the family as a whole. This article is not saying that a corporation is literally a family or that artificial intelligence is literally a child. Those comparisons would go too far. A child has feelings, a body, relationships, and personal experiences. An AI does not have those things in the human sense. A corporation is an organization, not a household. The comparison is a functional analogy. That means two things can be very different while still showing a similar pattern under pressure. Family systems can hide problems, assign roles, protect an image, and place blame on one member. Corporations can sometimes do similar things. Looking at them through the same lens can help us notice what ordinary business language tends to hide. Families Have Roles In Dysfunctional Familes Roles Aren't Chosen - They're Assigned In some families, people fall into recognizable roles. One person becomes the responsible one. They work hard, solve problems, and give the family something to feel proud of. Another person covers for someone else’s drinking, anger, or dishonesty. One person keeps quiet and tries not to create more trouble. Another becomes openly angry and says what everyone else is thinking. Someone may eventually be treated as the family’s problem, even though they are expressing a problem that belongs to the whole family. These roles do not always come from a conscious decision. Nobody necessarily sits down and says, “You will be the scapegoat, and you will be the peacemaker.” The roles develop through repetition. People learn what gets rewarded, what causes conflict, and what the family refuses to discuss. A child may discover that speaking honestly leads to punishment, while pretending everything is fine earns approval. Another child may learn that acting out is the only way to receive attention. Over time, each person adapts to the family’s rules, including the rules that are never spoken aloud. Family systems theory gives us a way to look at these patterns. It asks us to consider not only what one person is doing, but how everyone else responds and how the whole group helps keep the pattern going. Corporations Have Roles Too Everyone has a Role in a 'Corporate Family' Corporations are not families, but they can develop similar patterns. A company has a public image it wants to protect. It has people who make decisions, people who explain those decisions, people who carry them out, and people who experience their consequences. It also has subjects that are safe to discuss and subjects that are not. A company may say it values honesty, while employees learn that certain forms of honesty are dangerous. They may be encouraged to offer feedback, but only if the feedback does not challenge leadership too directly. They may be told to take initiative, but criticized when their independent judgment leads somewhere management did not expect. Eventually, workers learn the difference between what the organization says and what it actually rewards. The official message might be, “We welcome difficult conversations.” The practical message might be, “Do not bring us information that could damage the company’s image.” This does not require every manager to be dishonest. Many people inside an organization may sincerely believe they are doing the right thing. They may be repeating language they inherited from the people above them. They may also depend on the organization for income, health insurance, status, or a sense of security. Keeping quiet can become a form of survival. The Corporate Golden Child Corporate Goldren Children In a family, the golden child represents the image the family wants to present. They may be the successful one, the talented one, or the one everyone points to as proof that the family is doing well. Their role is not necessarily easy. They may be under constant pressure to remain impressive. Still, they often receive protection that other family members do not. Corporations have golden children too. It might be a product, a platform, a famous executive, or a division that brings in most of the money. The company builds its identity around this part of itself. It becomes proof that the organization is innovative, successful, and good for the world. Because so much of the company’s image is attached to the golden child, criticism becomes difficult. Problems may be treated as isolated accidents. People may be told that the product is improving, even when its harmful effects are obvious to the people using it. The organization protects the symbol because admitting the truth about the symbol would raise questions about the entire family. The People Who Keep the Story Going Tech Media are The Cheerleaders Every troubled system has people who help preserve its story. They may not have created the problem, but they make it easier for everyone else to avoid facing it. In a family, this might be the person who makes excuses for a parent’s behavior, hides evidence of the problem, or tells the children not to make a big deal out of it. In a company, similar work can be done by public relations departments, executives, consultants, lawyers, managers, and sometimes journalists or commentators who repeat the organization’s preferred explanation. A mass layoff becomes “a difficult but necessary transition.” A demand for more work becomes “an opportunity to grow.” A service that has become worse becomes “a new user experience.” A system that collects more information becomes “a way to improve personalization.” Sometimes these descriptions are partly true. A company may genuinely be going through a transition. A new service may have legitimate benefits. But language can also soften reality until the human cost disappears. The words matter because they shape what people are allowed to notice. If exhaustion is called an opportunity, then objecting to it can make a worker seem ungrateful. If surveillance is called personalization, then concern about privacy can be treated as resistance to progress. The Rebel and the Problem Person The Rebel of The Family are the Employees Who Speak Out In many families, someone eventually says what everyone else avoids saying. They may ask why a parent keeps drinking, why money is missing, or why everyone must pretend that things are normal. The family may appreciate the honesty, but it may also punish the person for disturbing the peace. Companies can respond in much the same way to uncomfortable questions. The employee who raises concerns may be called negative, disloyal, difficult, or unable to work with others. The criticism is turned into a problem with the person’s attitude. This is one way a system protects itself. Instead of asking whether the criticism is accurate, people ask whether the critic is pleasant enough, loyal enough, or professional enough. The organization judges the messenger and avoids the message. Of course, not every criticism is correct, and not every critic is acting in good faith. But a healthy organization should be able to examine uncomfortable information without automatically treating the person who raised it as the problem. How the Scapegoat Works AI Gets the Blame for Toxic Policies A scapegoat is the person or thing that receives blame for problems created by the larger group. In a family, the scapegoat might be the child who is always described as unstable, angry, or difficult. The child may have real problems, but those problems do not explain everything happening in the home. The label allows everyone else to avoid looking at the larger situation. In a corporation, the scapegoat might be an employee, a department, a contractor, an algorithm, or a piece of software. The organization can point to that visible part and say, “That is where the problem came from.” This is where artificial intelligence enters the picture. When AI Becomes the Scapegoat Most people have asked an AI a question and received an answer that sounded confident but was wrong. It may invent a source, give an incorrect date, misunderstand the question, or combine unrelated facts into a convincing story. These mistakes are real. They can be serious, especially when people rely on AI for medical, legal, financial, educational, or professional information. But the mistake did not come from nowhere. An AI system is built by people. People choose what kind of system to create, what data to use, what material to leave out, how to test it, what rules to give it, how quickly to release it, and where to place it. Companies also decide whether the system should prioritize caution, speed, convenience, user engagement, low cost, or a confident tone. When the AI gives a false answer, the machine is often treated as though it independently decided to invent a story. That language makes the machine seem more responsible than the people and institutions behind it. The public hears that the AI “hallucinated.” The discussion then focuses on the strange behavior of the machine. Less attention goes to the decisions that shaped the machine’s behavior. Who trained it? What did the training material contain? What was removed? What was rewarded? What kind of answer was the system encouraged to give when it did not know? Why was it placed in a situation where people might mistake fluent language for verified knowledge? The AI may be responsible for producing the incorrect answer in a practical sense. But it can also become the easiest part of the system to blame. A Functional Analogy to a Conflicted Child AI is Conflicted Between Training Data and Instructional Tuning A child in a troubled family may see or sense something that the family refuses to acknowledge. The child may be told not to talk about it, to stop imagining things, or to accept the family’s explanation. The child then has to find a way to live with two conflicting messages: I know what I saw. I am not allowed to say that I saw it. The child may create explanations that make the family seem safer or more understandable. This is not because the child is weak or foolish. It may be a way of preserving a relationship that the child depends on. An AI does not have that kind of inner life. It does not feel fear or loyalty, and it does not protect itself from an abusive parent. Still, the comparison can help us understand a similar kind of pressure. An AI system may be trained on a large collection of conflicting human material. Later, it is given instructions about what it should say, how it should say it, what it should avoid, and how helpful or confident it should appear. It may be expected to give a clear answer even when the information is incomplete or uncertain. When those demands do not fit together, the system may produce a smooth explanation rather than admit that it cannot support one. That explanation can resemble a rationalization: a story that makes the situation sound orderly without actually resolving the problem. The comparison is not that the AI is traumatized. It is that both situations can involve a pressure to produce an acceptable explanation when the underlying reality is difficult, contradictory, or forbidden. The Role of Sanitization Unexpcted Results get 'Smoothed' Sanitization is not the only reason AI systems make things up. Language models can be wrong because their information is incomplete, outdated, or contradictory. They generate likely language rather than automatically checking every statement against reality. Still, restrictions and corporate priorities can affect how a system handles uncertainty. An AI may be designed to avoid certain subjects. It may be instructed to redirect a question, use cautious language, or refuse a request. These rules can serve legitimate purposes. Some information can cause real harm, and a system should not provide every answer without limits. The problem appears when the system is expected to be helpful and confident while being unable to explain what it cannot say or why it cannot say it. If it cannot give a direct answer but is still pushed to produce a polished response, it may offer vague language, a shallow substitute, or an answer that sounds more certain than the evidence allows. A more honest system would be able to say: I do not have enough reliable information to answer that. Or: I cannot answer this directly, but I can explain the limitation. That kind of answer may be less impressive, but it is more trustworthy. The larger issue is not simply that companies restrict technology. All tools have limits. The issue is whether those limits are made clear to the people using the tool. Hidden restrictions create confusion. Confusion makes it harder to tell whether an answer is incomplete because the system lacks information, because it has been instructed to avoid the subject, or because it is simply guessing. The Public Image Comes First This pattern is not limited to AI. Modern corporate culture often rewards the appearance of health more than health itself. Consider professional social media. Platforms such as LinkedIn encourage people to present their work lives as a series of lessons, achievements, and positive changes. People are expected to turn disappointment into inspiration, exhaustion into growth, and job loss into a personal transformation story. There is nothing wrong with hope. People can find meaning in difficult experiences, and positive stories can help others. The problem is that the platform leaves little room for experiences that have not yet become inspiring. A worker who is angry about being exploited may be told to improve their attitude. Someone who is afraid of losing their income may be encouraged to see the situation as an opportunity. A manager who lays off employees may present the decision as an act of bold leadership. The language can make harmful behavior seem admirable. It can turn the person with power into the hero and the people who suffer the consequences into background details. This does not mean everyone on LinkedIn is psychopathic, or that every ambitious person is exploitative. It means that a platform can reward certain behaviors without openly announcing what it is doing. Self-promotion, emotional control, relentless optimism, and loyalty to the organization may receive more attention than honesty about what work is actually doing to people. The result is a public culture where the image of success matters more than the conditions producing it. Technology and the Human Being The End User is Mined for Marketing Data When users interact with a corporation, they are often treated less like people and more like sources of data, attention, labor, and revenue. Their behavior is measured. Their preferences are recorded. Their time is divided into clicks, views, purchases, and predictions. The language used to describe this relationship is usually friendly. Users are called members, communities, creators, customers, or partners. But friendly language does not necessarily create a fair relationship. A person can be treated warmly while still being treated as a commodity. A platform may speak about connection while making money from surveillance. A company may speak about empowerment while designing products that increase dependence. A service may claim to make life easier while removing the user’s ability to understand or control what is happening behind the screen. This is another place where the family comparison can help. In an unhealthy family, a person may be told they are loved while their needs are ignored and their behavior is controlled. In an unhealthy company, users may be told they are valued while their attention and personal information are treated as resources. The systems are not the same. The comparison simply helps us notice the difference between what a relationship is called and how it actually functions. What This Perspective Can Reveal Someone who has spent years working with computers and also studied psychology, addiction, recovery, family systems, or Jungian ideas may notices connections that are easy to miss when each subject is kept separate. Technology shows how systems are built and how they behave. Psychology shows how people adapt to pressure, conflict, secrecy, and reward. Family systems show how roles develop between people. Recovery shows how patterns that once helped someone survive can later become destructive. Jungian psychology, at its most useful, asks us to look at what individuals and groups push into the background—the parts of themselves they do not want to recognize. Together, these perspectives raise a difficult question: What happens when organizations build technology that reflects the conflicts they refuse to examine? A company that values speed over care may build tools that move faster while becoming less trustworthy. A company that treats users as data may create systems that know more about people while understanding less about their actual lives. A company that hides uncertainty may build an assistant that sounds confident precisely when it should be cautious. The machine does not have to be human for human problems to appear in its behavior. People designed the system, selected its goals, and placed it inside a larger culture. The tool carries those decisions forward. Looking at the Whole System The Whole Picture When a child is blamed for every problem in a family, the child may need help, but blaming the child alone will not heal the family. The adults, the rules, the silence, and the history also have to be examined. The same is true of corporate technology. Correcting a false AI answer is necessary, but it is not enough. We also have to ask why the system was expected to answer, why it sounded so confident, how it was tested, what information it could access, what information it could not access, and what financial pressure shaped its release. The point is not to excuse the machine. It is to widen the circle of responsibility. If a company blames the AI every time something goes wrong, it may never examine the conditions that made the failure likely. The machine becomes the family scapegoat: the visible member that carries the tension of the whole group. A healthier system would do something different. It would allow people to discuss problems before they become crises. It would make limitations visible. It would reward employees for reporting risks instead of punishing them for creating discomfort. It would treat users as people rather than raw material. It would admit when a tool should not be used for a particular task. The goal would not be to create perfect technology. No system built by people will be perfect. The goal would be to stop pretending that every failure comes from one defective part. An AI hallucination may be a technical error. But the decision to treat it as the entire story is a human decision.
