content: Search: Everything Is RadioShack Now How Big Tech Is Like RadioShack Asking for Your Name and Address to Buy Batteries Author: Adam Fistler, BCH - Behavorial Change Consultant ( adam@adamfistler.com ) Remember RadioShack? You could walk into the store for something completely ordinary—usually batteries, a cable, or some other small electronic necessity—and leave feeling as though you had applied for a mortgage. The joke was that RadioShack wanted your name, address, phone number, and possibly every other detail about your life before allowing you to buy a couple of batteries. It was absurd because the transaction was so simple: You gave RadioShack money. RadioShack gave you batteries. The interaction should have ended there. At the time, that kind of data collection seemed excessive enough to be funny. Now it feels less like a joke and more like a preview. Welcome to the Modern RadioShack Today, you may need to identify yourself before doing almost anything. Want to read a restaurant menu? Scan this QR code. The menu opens in your browser, perhaps after asking you to accept cookies, enable location access, or visit a website designed primarily to collect information about you. What used to be a laminated piece of paper sitting on the table has become an invitation to enter a company’s digital system. Want to park your car? Download the app, create an account, enter your license plate, provide your payment information, and allow the service to know where you are parked. Want the advertised price at a grocery store? Join the loyalty program. Want a discount at a fast-food restaurant? Download the app. Want a digital receipt? Give the store your email address. Want to use public Wi-Fi? Provide your email, phone number, or social-media account. The transaction itself may take seconds. Establishing your identity takes longer. The Account for the Twenty-Second Task The same thing happens online. Suppose you need to convert a JPEG into an AVIF file. It is a small, uncomplicated task. The sort of thing that used to be handled by a simple utility: Upload the file. Convert it. Download the result. Now the process may look more like this: Create an account. Verify your email. Accept the cookie settings. Provide a phone number. Upload the file. Discover that the free version has limitations. Wait for the conversion. Download the result. Receive marketing emails. The file conversion may take twenty seconds. Joining the service takes five minutes. The same pattern appears when you want to resize an image, compress a PDF, remove an image background, extract a page from a document, print a file, or use some other small online utility. The Internet used to be full of tools that let you perform a task and leave. Increasingly, those tools have become services that want you to register before they will help. You are not merely using the tool anymore. You are becoming a user. When the Store Wants More Than the Sale There is nothing especially strange about a business wanting to sell you something. That is the basic arrangement. The problem is the growing expectation that every transaction should become the beginning of an ongoing relationship. The grocery store does not simply want to sell you groceries. It wants your identity connected to your purchases. The restaurant does not simply want to serve you food. It wants you to order through its app. The parking company does not simply want to collect payment. It wants your license plate, location, phone number, payment details, and continued participation in its platform. The website does not simply want to convert your file. It wants an account, an email address, and the opportunity to bring you back. The result is that ordinary life increasingly involves a series of small negotiations: Can I do this without registering? Can I pay without installing an app? Can I read this without accepting tracking? Can I receive the ordinary price without joining a loyalty program? Can I use this tool without giving away my email address? Can I complete this task without creating another password that will eventually need to be recovered through my phone? These used to be simple interactions. Now they are often conditional. The Physical World Is Becoming an App The most noticeable change is that activities that used to require nothing more than showing up increasingly require a phone. Parking meters need apps. Public transportation systems use apps and digital tickets. Gyms use apps for entry. Apartment buildings use apps for access. Hotels encourage or require mobile check-in. Events distribute tickets through digital accounts. Charging stations require registration. Laundry machines accept payments through apps. Even some vending machines want a phone between you and the thing you are trying to buy. The issue is not that apps are always bad. Some are convenient. Some genuinely improve a service. The issue is what happens when the app stops being an option and becomes the entrance. The physical world may still be there, but access to it increasingly depends on participation in a digital platform. You do not simply park. You become a parking-app customer. You do not simply enter the building. You authenticate through the building’s system. You do not simply buy the item. You identify yourself to receive permission, access, or the advertised price. A Tool or a Relationship? There is an important difference between a tool and a service ecosystem. A tool helps you perform a task. You use it, accomplish what you came to do, and move on. A service ecosystem wants an ongoing relationship. It wants an account, a profile, a history, a way to contact you, and a reason for you to return. This is why such small requirements can feel disproportionate. The service is asking for a relationship when you only wanted to complete a transaction. You wanted to read a menu. It wanted your browser activity. You wanted to park. It wanted your license plate and account information. You wanted to convert an image. It wanted to turn a one-time task into a registered user. You wanted batteries. RadioShack wanted your name and address. The difference is that RadioShack’s demand was once ridiculous enough to become a cultural joke. Today, the same basic demand is often presented as convenience, personalization, security, or modernization. Sometimes those explanations are legitimate. Sometimes they are not. But the result is similar: a simple interaction becomes an opportunity to identify, classify, track, and retain the person performing it. Everything Is RadioShack Now The old RadioShack joke was funny because it exposed a mismatch. The store was treating the purchase of batteries as though it were a meaningful personal relationship. The amount of information being requested did not match the importance of the transaction. That mismatch has become normal. A menu requires a website. A parking space requires an account. A discount requires a profile. A receipt requires an email address. A file converter requires registration. A printer requires an app. A public service requires a phone. None of these individual examples is necessarily the end of the world. But taken together, they describe a broader change in the way ordinary tasks are organized. Simple transactions are increasingly being converted into persistent digital relationships. You no longer just buy the batteries. You become a customer profile that happens to receive batteries. And that raises a larger question: what happens when technology stops being a tool we use and becomes a system we must participate in before we are allowed to do ordinary things? That is a much bigger subject—one involving privacy, centralization, dependence, and the gradual outsourcing of human agency. It is also the subject of another set of articles. Search: A Fresh Approach to a Persistent Challenge Breaking the Cycle: Beyond the Rehab Revolving Door Addiction, a relentless adversary, leaves devastation in its wake, 
            shattering lives and tearing apart families.
            It's a scourge that has left countless individuals desperate, desperately seeking solutions. Even the most deeply entrenched addict, or the most stumbling alcoholic on the streets, 
            has likely found themselves in the confines of a rehabilitation center at some point.
            There's a common aspiration among them all: the desire to break free from the clutches of addiction and lead a meaningful life.
            Yet, the bitter truth they face is the cyclical nature of rehab.
            Seeking help often means being ushered back into the same routine: more treatment, more 12-step meetings, and a repetition of the methods that have failed them in the past. Outdated Methods in Modern Rehab: A Flawed Approach In the landscape of addiction rehabilitation, many centers continue to 
            rely on outdated models that fail to meet the diverse needs of those struggling with addiction.
            The predominant approach often involves group therapy, educational sessions, 
            and the antiquated 12 Step model, a method rooted in a book penned in 1938 and left largely unchanged since then.
            In a standard 28-day rehab stint, the emphasis remains on group therapy 
            sessions and a strong push toward life-long attendance of 12 Step meetings. Misleading Claims and Limited Practicality: The Reality of Rehab's "Evidence-Based" Approaches When rehab facilities claim to employ evidence-based approaches such as 
            Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) and Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT),
            their advertisements often paint an illusion of comprehensive support.
            However, the truth behind these claims is often deceptive. Beyond Short-Term Solutions: The Limitations of Skill-Based Approaches Learning new skills and techniques is challenging for anyone, even those without substance abuse disorders.
            In group or seminar settings, people are introduced to valuable tools, but the reality is,
            applying these skills consistently requires immense effort and discipline.
            Skills demanding constant repetition often fade away with time, making them unreliable for long-term recovery. Empty Promises and Deceptive Claims: The Reality Behind Rehab's Support for Diverse Approaches Many rehabilitation centers claim to endorse a variety of pathways to recovery, 
            asserting their support for alternatives beyond the conventional 12-step method.
            These affirmations often populate their advertisements and phone conversations, 
            serving as enticing bait to attract individuals seeking help.
            However, once within the confines of these centers, the stark truth emerges. Breaking the Chains of 12-Step Dominance: A Call for True Recovery Options Traditionally, addiction rehabilitation centers have been ensnared in the grip of the 12-Step model,
            a framework tightly intertwined with the origins of Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) and Hazelden, 
            one of the pioneering alcohol rehab centers in the United States.
            Hazelden, founded by AA members, laid the foundation for what became the Minnesota model of recovery.
            As rehab facilities sprouted nationwide, they adopted this model. Demystifying 12-Step Meetings: The Reality Behind the Misconceptions A common misconception among those unfamiliar with addiction recovery is the belief 
            that 12-Step meetings resemble classes or educational sessions.
            In reality, these meetings lack the structured learning environment one might expect.
            Contrary to the term "12 Step Classes" or "AA Classes," 12-Step meetings are not classes,
            and attendees don't receive formal education during these sessions. Aftercare: Balancing Life and Recovery Following completion of rehabilitation, individuals often transition into an aftercare program, 
            typically involving Partial Hospitalization Programs (PHP) or Intensive Outpatient Programs (IOP).
            While these programs play a crucial role in the recovery journey, they often pose significant challenges, 
            particularly in managing time and responsibilities. Beyond Surface Solutions: Addressing the Roots of Addiction The complexity of addiction goes far beyond the surface level.
            Research underscores that addiction's roots are deeply embedded in the subconscious mind,
            entwined with unbalanced emotions, distorted belief systems, and other subconscious drivers.
            Traditional methods like group therapy and the 12-step approach,
            though widely practiced, often fall short in delving into these intricate layers. A Revolutionary Approach to Addiction Recovery: Unleashing the Power of Hypnosis Traditional methods often fall short in tackling the intricate web of addiction.
            The subconscious mind, a treasure trove of experiences, emotions, and the very essence of one's being,
            holds the key to understanding addiction at its core.
            Hypnosis emerges as a transformative intervention, 
            offering a direct route to this subconscious realm, where the genesis of the problem resides. Revolutionizing Addiction Recovery with Hypnosis The time for change is now.
            The conventional methods of addiction recovery have proven ineffective, 
            leaving countless individuals trapped in a cycle of despair.
            It's time to shatter the chains of addiction with a revolutionary approach—hypnosis. Spread Awareness: Share this knowledge far and wide.
            Let your friends, family, and community know that there's a groundbreaking solution available.
            Educate others about the power of hypnosis in dismantling addiction at its core. Demand Better Solutions: Advocate for accessible, evidence-based treatments like hypnosis.
            Challenge outdated approaches and demand comprehensive, effective strategies for addiction recovery.
            Let policymakers, healthcare providers, and institutions know that the status quo is unacceptable. Support Research: Contribute to research initiatives focused on hypnosis and addiction recovery.
            The more we understand the science behind this transformative method, the more lives can be saved.
            Support organizations and studies that explore the potential of hypnosis in combating addiction. Empower Those in Need: If you or someone you know is struggling with addiction 
            and is ready to break free from the cycle of failure with traditional approaches, embrace hypnosis. Contact me to set up a free consultation.
            Seek out qualified hypnotists experienced in addiction recovery.
            Empower yourself with knowledge, understanding that there's a solution that goes straight to the heart of the problem. Break the Stigma: Challenge the stigma surrounding addiction and mental health.
            Emphasize that seeking help is a sign of strength, not weakness.
            By fostering a compassionate environment, we can encourage more individuals to explore innovative solutions like hypnosis without fear of judgment. Together, we can revolutionize addiction recovery.
            Let's make lasting change a reality.
            Embrace hypnosis and pave the way to a future where addiction no longer dictates lives but becomes a battle successfully fought and won.             bad choice. From the outside, it can be difficult to understand why someone would
            continue doing something that is obviously damaging their health, relationships,
            career, finances, and future. But addiction is rarely that simple. A person struggling with addiction generally isn't making a conscious decision to
            destroy their life just to get high. They may make decisions that cause enormous
            harm, but the behavior and the person are not the same thing. Addiction can profoundly
            alter motivation, reward, learning, stress responses, habits, emotional regulation,
            and the way a person responds to substances or behaviors that have become associated
            with relief or reward. Understanding this does not mean excusing harmful behavior. It means trying to
            understand what is actually happening so that something more useful than shame can
            take its place. The Cost of Addiction Is Real Addiction can be devastating. The person experiencing it may lose their health, employment, financial stability,
            relationships, housing, opportunities, self-respect, and sometimes their life.
            Families and friends can experience fear, anger, betrayal, financial hardship,
            exhaustion, uncertainty, and grief. Children can be affected by instability and by
            watching someone they love repeatedly struggle. The effects extend beyond the individual and their immediate family. Communities
            bear costs through medical emergencies, accidents, lost productivity, homelessness,
            strained treatment systems, and premature deaths. Acknowledging addiction as a disorder does not make these consequences disappear.
            It simply gives us a better framework for understanding them. There is a difference between understanding why something happens and approving of what happens . We can hold people accountable for harmful behavior while still recognizing that
            addiction is not a character defect. The Person Usually Isn't Trying to Hurt You One of the most painful aspects of addiction is that the person struggling with it
            can genuinely love the people they are hurting. A parent can love their children and still continue drinking. A husband or wife can
            love their partner and still relapse. A successful professional can care deeply
            about their career and still lose it. This creates one of the most painful questions families ask: "If you love me, why do you keep doing this?" Sometimes the honest answer is simply: "I don't know." Or: "I know I'm hurting you, but I can't seem to stop." That isn't a satisfactory answer to the person being hurt. But it can be an honest
            description of what addiction feels like from the inside. Addiction can become a deeply conditioned pattern. What initially begins as pleasure,
            experimentation, recreation, curiosity, self-medication, or relief can eventually
            become something very different. Addiction Is More Than "Wanting to Get High" It is tempting to think that addiction is fundamentally about pleasure. Sometimes it begins that way. A substance may initially provide euphoria, relaxation, confidence, energy, pain
            relief, emotional relief, or an escape from an otherwise unbearable state. But over time, the motivation can change. The person may no longer be chasing an especially pleasurable experience. They may
            be trying to escape withdrawal, anxiety, physical pain, stress, craving, depression,
            or an increasingly uncomfortable internal state. There is a tremendous difference between: "I want to get high." and: "I feel terrible, and this is the only thing I know that will make me feel
            normal again." Sometimes those experiences overlap. Sometimes they don't. This is one reason addiction cannot be adequately explained by dopamine alone.
            Addiction involves interactions among reward and motivation systems, learning,
            stress, pain, emotional regulation, memory, conditioning, and biological adaptation. I've explored some of these mechanisms in greater detail elsewhere on this site. Famous People Don't Get a Special Version of Addiction One reason I find the stories of public figures useful is that they expose another
            misconception about addiction: Addiction does not care how successful you are. It can affect actors, musicians, athletes, artists, businesspeople, and people whose
            names are known around the world. Money doesn't make someone immune. Talent doesn't make someone immune. Intelligence doesn't make someone immune. A successful career doesn't make someone immune. Fame certainly doesn't make someone immune. Sometimes success can even make addiction more difficult to recognize. A person may
            have enough money to hide the consequences for years. People around them may protect
            them from consequences. Organizations may work to keep their problems private. Eventually, however, biology doesn't care about celebrity status. Neither does withdrawal. Neither does overdose. Neither does the damage addiction can do to relationships. The people below represent different experiences with addiction, recovery, relapse,
            loss, and advocacy. They are not presented as interchangeable stories. Each provides
            a different perspective on the larger problem. Actors Robert Downey Jr. Robert Downey Jr. experienced years of serious drug addiction, including periods of treatment, arrest, incarceration, and professional collapse. He eventually achieved sustained recovery and rebuilt both his personal life and career.
  His story represents long-term recovery, rebuilding, and the possibility that addiction does not have to become a person's permanent identity.
  Downey has spoken openly about his addiction and recovery and has used his public position to discuss substance use, treatment, and the importance of support. Jamie Lee Curtis Jamie Lee Curtis has openly discussed her addiction to prescription pain medication and alcohol and has remained in recovery since 1999.
  Her story illustrates how addiction can remain hidden behind professional success and how recognizing one's own behavior as a problem can become a turning point.
  Curtis has spoken publicly about recovery and has used her visibility to reduce the shame surrounding addiction. Philip Seymour Hoffman Philip Seymour Hoffman maintained sobriety for roughly two decades before relapsing and eventually dying from an accidental overdose in 2014.
  His history demonstrates that addiction can remain a vulnerability even after many years of successful recovery. Relapse does not erase the years of recovery that came before it.
  Hoffman's story also illustrates the potentially fatal consequences of relapse after a long period of abstinence, when tolerance may have changed significantly. Matthew Perry Matthew Perry openly discussed years of alcohol and opioid addiction, repeated treatment, periods of sobriety, and relapse. He wrote extensively about his experiences and became an outspoken advocate for people struggling with addiction.
  Perry died in 2023 from the acute effects of ketamine, with drowning and other contributing factors identified by the medical examiner.
  After his death, the Matthew Perry Foundation was established to support people affected by substance use disorder and advance addiction recovery. Musicians Elton John Elton John experienced serious cocaine and alcohol addiction during the height of his career before entering recovery in 1990.
  His story demonstrates that enormous success and wealth do not protect someone from addiction. He has remained open about his recovery and the role addiction played in his life.
  Through the Elton John AIDS Foundation and other philanthropic work, he has supported public health, harm reduction, treatment access, and efforts to reduce stigma. Eminem Eminem developed a serious addiction to prescription drugs and experienced a near-fatal overdose in 2007. He entered recovery and has publicly discussed the difficulties of rebuilding his life afterward.
  His recovery has included major changes in lifestyle and exercise, and his music has documented addiction, relapse, recovery, and the psychological process of rebuilding a life.
  His public discussion of addiction has also helped make recovery part of the conversation surrounding his career rather than something that had to remain hidden. Amy Winehouse Amy Winehouse experienced highly publicized struggles with alcohol and drug use and died in 2011 from alcohol poisoning.
  Her story illustrates the destructive interaction between addiction, fame, public scrutiny, and relapse. It also demonstrates how addiction can become increasingly difficult to separate from a person's public identity.
  The Amy Winehouse Foundation was established in her memory and provides programs addressing substance use, emotional wellbeing, resilience, and recovery for young people. Eric Clapton Eric Clapton experienced serious addictions to heroin and alcohol during the height of his career. He eventually entered treatment and achieved long-term recovery.
  His story demonstrates how addiction can affect even someone who is extraordinarily successful and how recovery can involve rebuilding both personal and professional life.
  Clapton later established the Crossroads Centre in Antigua, a treatment facility focused on helping people recover from alcohol and drug addiction. Athletes Andre Agassi Tennis champion Andre Agassi has publicly described developing an addiction to crystal methamphetamine during his younger years and hiding it while continuing his professional career.
  His story demonstrates that addiction can exist behind exceptional athletic achievement and public success.
  Agassi later became known for extensive philanthropic work through the Andre Agassi Foundation for Education, illustrating how a difficult personal history can coexist with a substantial commitment to helping others. Josh Hamilton Major League Baseball player Josh Hamilton experienced severe addiction to alcohol and cocaine, entered recovery, returned to professional baseball, and later experienced relapse.
  His career demonstrates both the possibility of recovery and the reality that relapse can occur even after years of stability and extraordinary achievement.
  Hamilton's story has been discussed publicly in the context of addiction, recovery, relapse, faith, and the pressures surrounding professional sports. Lamar Odom Former NBA player Lamar Odom experienced serious addiction and nearly died following an overdose in 2015. He subsequently entered recovery and has spoken publicly about addiction and rebuilding his life.
  His story illustrates how addiction can continue beneath professional success and how surviving a medical crisis does not automatically resolve the underlying problem.
  Odom has since used his public platform to discuss recovery and encourage others struggling with addiction. Dwight Gooden Major League Baseball pitcher Dwight Gooden experienced serious addiction to cocaine and alcohol during and after an extraordinary professional career.
  His struggles included relapse, treatment, legal problems, and periods in which addiction threatened both his career and his personal life. He has also experienced periods of sustained recovery.
  Gooden's story illustrates how addiction can coexist with extraordinary talent and achievement while demonstrating the importance of continued recovery and support. Business and Professional Life Advocates and Influential Figures Danny Trejo Actor Danny Trejo has spoken extensively about his history of heroin addiction, incarceration, and recovery. He has remained in recovery for decades and has frequently used his public position to encourage people struggling with addiction.
  Trejo's life demonstrates that recovery can involve a profound reconstruction of identity, relationships, career, and purpose.
  He has also worked with recovery communities and people facing addiction and incarceration, using his own history as part of his message of recovery and second chances. Samuel L. Jackson Samuel L. Jackson has openly discussed his history of cocaine and heroin addiction and his recovery. He entered treatment in 1991 after his family discovered him unconscious following drug use.
  Jackson achieved sustained recovery and subsequently rebuilt his career, becoming one of the most recognizable actors in the world.
  His story is a powerful example of how addiction can coexist with talent and ambition while also demonstrating that treatment and recovery can provide an opportunity to rebuild a life. Russell Brand Russell Brand has publicly described his history of addiction to heroin, alcohol, and other drugs and his long-term recovery.
  He has made addiction and recovery major subjects of his public work, discussing his own experiences with treatment, twelve-step recovery, spirituality, and behavioral change.
  His public advocacy has reached a large audience and demonstrates how personal experience with addiction can become a platform for discussing recovery and changing attitudes toward people struggling with substance use. Carrie Fisher Carrie Fisher openly discussed her experiences with cocaine, alcohol, and prescription drugs and became an important public voice for reducing the stigma surrounding addiction and mental illness.
  Rather than hiding her struggles, Fisher incorporated them into her writing, acting, and public speaking. Her memoirs and performances frequently explored addiction, recovery, family dysfunction, and the complexity of living with personal difficulties in public.
  Fisher died in 2016. Her openness about addiction remains part of her lasting influence and helped demonstrate that a person can discuss addiction publicly without reducing their identity to the disorder. Babylon 5 and Addiction There is one group of stories I want to treat separately. Babylon 5 was enormously influential on me personally. When I was in 11th and 12th grade, I was working as a college-level intern at
            AlliedSignal Aerospace in Columbia, Maryland. Socialization was extremely difficult
            for me at the time. I was very shy and had a great deal of difficulty figuring out
            how to enter conversations and connect with people. There happened to be a number of Babylon 5 fans working there. That gave me something I desperately needed: a shared language. I could talk about Babylon 5. I could debate characters, episodes, politics,
            technology, philosophy, religion, and the direction of the story. I didn't have to figure out how to manufacture a conversation from nothing. I
            already had something to talk about. For someone who struggled profoundly with social interaction, that mattered. Why Season Three Mattered The period when I was working there overlapped with the heart of Babylon 5's
            third season, which was particularly fertile ground for discussion and debate. By that point, the show had spent years establishing characters, political conflicts,
            personal histories, and long-running mysteries. Season three began paying many of
            those elements off while simultaneously creating new questions about power,
            authoritarianism, loyalty, war, morality, identity, and the consequences of
            choosing sides. Episodes such as Messages from Earth , Point of No Return , and Severed Dreams gave fans an enormous amount to discuss. The conversations weren't simply: "Did you like the episode?" There were much bigger questions. Was Sheridan justified? How much power should an individual be allowed to exercise? When does resistance become terrorism? Can an authoritarian system be defeated without becoming authoritarian yourself? What does loyalty mean when the institution you serve has become corrupt? What happens when people who have spent their lives fighting each other discover that they have a common enemy? For a teenager who found ordinary social interaction difficult, having a universe
            like that to talk about was enormously valuable. Babylon 5 gave me something to connect with other people through at a time when
            connecting with other people was difficult. Babylon 5 Took Addiction Seriously Addiction was not simply used as a joke or as a convenient character flaw on
            Babylon 5. The series repeatedly explored addiction and recovery through its characters. Michael Garibaldi was an alcoholic whose history included sobriety and relapse.
            Dr. Stephen Franklin developed a dependence on stimulants while trying to cope
            with overwhelming stress and workload. Other characters also carried histories
            involving addiction and recovery. The important thing was that these characters were not portrayed as stupid or
            incompetent because they struggled with addiction. Garibaldi was highly capable. Franklin was highly capable. Addiction could exist alongside competence, intelligence, responsibility, and
            genuine concern for other people. That is a very different message from: "Bad people use drugs." Instead, Babylon 5 repeatedly suggested something much closer to reality: Human beings can develop destructive patterns, and those patterns can
            become extraordinarily difficult to escape. JMS and the Personal Experience Behind Garibaldi J. Michael Straczynski was not himself an alcoholic, but he has written about
            extensive firsthand exposure to alcoholism within his family. In discussing alcoholism and Michael Garibaldi, Straczynski described alcoholism
            extending through at least four generations of his family and explained that he had
            more personal experience with alcoholism than he cared to recount. That background helps explain why Garibaldi's alcoholism does not feel like a
            generic television character defect. His addiction is intertwined with stress, guilt, trauma, relationships, identity,
            and attempts to cope with overwhelming circumstances. More importantly, the series does not treat sobriety as a magical transformation
            into a permanently fixed person. Addiction remains part of Garibaldi's history.
            Relapse has consequences, and those consequences affect other people. That is much closer to the messy reality of addiction than the convenient television
            story in which someone goes to treatment and is permanently "cured." Giving People Another Chance There is another part of the Babylon 5 story that has always stood out to me. Jeff Conaway, who played Zack Allan, had a very public history of addiction involving
            cocaine, alcohol, and prescription painkillers. He later appeared on Celebrity Rehab . Claudia Christian, who played Susan Ivanova, has also spoken openly about her
            alcohol dependence and recovery using naltrexone and the Sinclair Method. She
            subsequently became an advocate for medication-assisted treatment. Jerry Doyle, who played Michael Garibaldi, also struggled with alcoholism and died
            in 2016. The coroner reported complications from chronic alcoholism as a contributing
            factor in his death. These three people ended up with very different stories. One died after years of addiction and health problems. One became an outspoken recovery advocate. One portrayed an alcoholic character whose story became one of the show's most
            sustained explorations of relapse and recovery. And that is precisely the point. There isn't one addiction story. There isn't one recovery story. There isn't even one definition of what success looks like. Sometimes recovery means decades of sobriety. Sometimes it means finding a treatment that finally works after other approaches
            failed. Sometimes it means trying again after relapse. And sometimes the person doesn't survive. The fact that the outcomes are different does not mean the people who struggled
            were morally different kinds of human beings. Jeff Conaway — Zack Allan Jeff Conaway, best known for Grease, Taxi, and Babylon 5, publicly struggled with cocaine, alcohol, and prescription painkillers. His addiction became particularly intertwined with severe back pain and long-term use of pain medication.
  Conaway played Zack Allan on Babylon 5 and later appeared on Celebrity Rehab. He died in 2011 following severe medical complications after years of addiction and health problems.
  His story illustrates the complicated relationship between chronic pain, prescription medication, physical dependence, addiction, and recovery. Claudia Christian — Susan Ivanova Claudia Christian played Susan Ivanova on Babylon 5 and later openly described her struggle with alcohol dependence.
  After finding success with naltrexone and the Sinclair Method, she became an advocate for medication-assisted treatment and founded the C Three Foundation.
  Her story is especially relevant because it demonstrates how someone can move from addiction and difficulty controlling alcohol use into recovery and then use that experience to educate others about alternative approaches to treatment. Jerry Doyle — Michael Garibaldi Jerry Doyle played Michael Garibaldi on Babylon 5, one of science fiction television's most sustained portrayals of a recovering and relapsing alcoholic.
  Doyle died in 2016 at age 60. The Clark County Coroner reported that complications from chronic alcoholism contributed to his death.
  Garibaldi's fictional history and Doyle's real-life struggle make Babylon 5's treatment of addiction particularly poignant: the series gave addiction a continuing role in a competent character's life rather than treating it as a temporary plot device. What About the People Left Behind? It is important not to romanticize addiction. Families are not obligated to tolerate abuse because someone has a substance-use
            disorder. Friends are not required to continually rescue someone from consequences.
            Partners can establish boundaries. Parents can protect their children. People can
            walk away from destructive situations. Understanding addiction does not mean surrendering your own wellbeing. But boundaries and condemnation are not the same thing. There is a difference between: "I cannot continue living this way, and I need to protect myself." and: "You are a worthless person because you have this problem." The first is a boundary. The second is shame. Shame rarely makes people healthier. Addiction Is a Human Problem The people represented in this article accomplished extraordinary things. Some created music that changed generations. Some became world-famous actors.
            Some were elite athletes. Some built companies. Some became advocates. Some recovered. Some relapsed. Some died. Their accomplishments did not make them immune to addiction. Their failures did not make them less human. And their addiction did not erase everything they had ever contributed to the world. That is something worth remembering when we talk about anyone struggling with
            addiction—not only famous people. The person sitting across from you may have made decisions you cannot understand.
            They may have hurt you. They may have lied to you. They may have broken promises.
            They may have caused enormous damage. And they may still be a human being who is suffering from a condition they
            don't fully understand and don't know how to escape. Those things can coexist. My Own Perspective I don't write about addiction as an outside observer. My own history with addiction, homelessness, and recovery profoundly changed the
            way I understand these issues. I know what it is like to have your life become organized around a problem you
            never intended to have. I know what it is like to experience shame. And I know
            what it is like to rebuild. That is one reason I resist the idea that addiction should be reduced to moral
            failure. If shame and condemnation were sufficient to solve addiction, addiction would have
            disappeared a long time ago. It hasn't. What we need instead is a willingness to look at the entire system: biology, psychology, learning, environment, trauma, stress, relationships,
              habits, pain, social conditions, and meaning. We need accountability without dehumanization. We need compassion without pretending that harmful behavior isn't harmful. We need boundaries without abandoning people to shame. And we need enough curiosity to ask a better question than: "What's wrong with you?" Sometimes the more useful question is: "What happened, what patterns developed, what is maintaining them, and what
              might help create something different?" That is where recovery begins to become possible. If You or Someone You Love Is Struggling If addiction is affecting you or someone close to you, you don't have to figure
            everything out alone. Treatment can involve many different approaches, and what works for one person may
            not work for another. Medical treatment, behavioral therapy, peer recovery,
            mutual-support groups, medication, harm-reduction approaches, and changes in
            environment can all play different roles. Recovery is not always a straight line. A relapse is not proof that previous recovery was meaningless. And needing help is not a character defect. Addiction is a human problem. Recovery is a human possibility. title: The Slow Descent - How Addiction Hijacks the Mind, Body, and Survival System | Adam Fistler | South Jersey Hypnosis & Addiction Recovery Consultant
description: Adam Fistler offers specialized behavioral consulting, mindfulness, and hypnosis, and addiction & recovery help in South Jersey. Transform habit loops and tackle addiction recovery. I'm local to Camden, Gloucester, Burlington, and Atlantic Counties
content: Search: The Slow Descent How Addiction Hijacks the Mind, Body, and Survival System The Question Behind the Story How can someone with a successful career, a family, intelligence, responsibilities, and—on paper—many reasons to be grateful eventually become addicted and live without stable housing in Camden, New Jersey? It is a question I have had to answer in my own life. I had been a systems engineer. I had a career, a family, and an identity built around competence, responsibility, and problem-solving. Yet my life eventually moved through addiction, treatment, homelessness, and survival on the streets of Camden. That transformation can look inexplicable from the outside. It can be tempting to divide people into two categories: responsible people and addicts, moral people and immoral people, people who make good decisions and people who do not. My experience has taught me that addiction is more complicated than that. It is not a light switch. It is a progression—a gradual interaction between biology, emotion, learning, beliefs, behavior, relationships, and environment. By the time the consequences become obvious, the process may have been developing for a long time. Understanding that process does not excuse harmful behavior. It helps explain how a person can become capable of actions they once would have considered unthinkable—and why recovery requires more than being told to try harder. No One Begins by Choosing Addiction Most people do not begin using drugs or alcohol with the intention of becoming addicted. They begin because the substance appears to solve a problem. It may seem to provide: Relief from anxiety or emotional pain Confidence and social ease Energy and motivation Sleep Focus Escape from shame, grief, loneliness, or fear Temporary freedom from intrusive thoughts A sense of belonging Relief from physical or psychological discomfort < Addicion can Begin as an Escape from Tension and Stress At first, the substance may seem effective. That is part of what makes addiction so powerful. If the experience were immediately destructive, most people would not continue. The early use may feel like a discovery: “This helps me.” “This makes me feel normal.” “This lets me be the person I want to be.” Over time, the person may begin to associate the substance with the best version of themselves. They may believe that alcohol makes them more relaxed, opioids make them more comfortable, stimulants make them more productive, or another drug makes them more confident, creative, social, or capable. Eventually, the belief can reverse: “I am not at my best without it.” Then it can become: “I cannot do ordinary things without it.” Work, sleep, conversation, driving, eating, socializing, handling stress, or simply feeling comfortable in one’s own body may begin to seem impossible without the substance. These beliefs are not always conscious decisions or deliberate deceptions. They can be learned expectations reinforced by repeated experience. The substance changes how the person feels, and the mind begins to treat that change as evidence about what the substance—and the person—can do. From Pleasure to Relief Addiction often develops along two connected tracks: psychological dependence and physical dependence. Psychological dependence begins when the substance becomes connected to emotional regulation. Particular situations start activating an expectation: Stress means I need the substance. Loneliness means I need the substance. The end of the workday means I need the substance. Social discomfort means I need the substance. Feeling sad, angry, bored, or ashamed means I need the substance. The brain learns through repetition. A cue, feeling, place, person, or thought becomes linked with the anticipated relief. The urge can arise before conscious reasoning has fully caught up. Physical dependence develops as the nervous system adapts to repeated exposure. Early on, a person may use a substance to feel better than their ordinary baseline. Later, they may use it simply to avoid feeling worse. The goal changes from pursuing pleasure to escaping distress. That is an important turning point. Someone watching from outside may see continued use and think, “They are choosing the drug over everything else.” The person may experience something closer to, “I need this to get through the next hour.” Drugs Use the Brain’s Existing Systems Drugs do not create entirely new brain systems. They interact with systems the body already uses to regulate pain, reward, arousal, fear, learning, sleep, movement, and emotional state. Different substances have different chemical profiles. They bind to or influence different receptors, transporters, and signaling networks. Opioids interact strongly with opioid receptors and resemble some effects of the body’s natural endorphin system. Alcohol and benzodiazepines affect inhibitory GABA-related signaling and other systems. Stimulants alter dopamine, norepinephrine, and related signaling. Other substances have their own combinations of effects. The important point is that the brain is not simply receiving a foreign chemical and remaining unchanged. It is continually attempting to maintain balance. The Body’s Warehouse Manager < Like a Warehouse Adding Capacity, the Body Creates More Receptors to Handle the Demand Imagine a warehouse manager who receives shipments without knowing why they keep arriving. The warehouse keeps receiving far more inventory than it was designed to hold. At first, the existing shelves overflow. To keep the operation functioning, the manager expands the warehouse, adds storage capacity, changes the workflow, and creates ways to accommodate the increased supply. The brain responds in a comparable way to repeated exposure, although the biology is more complex than a single warehouse analogy. It can change receptor sensitivity and number, alter signaling pathways, adjust natural chemical production, and modify the communication between brain regions. These adaptations are attempts at regulation. The body does not know that the chemicals came from a bottle, a prescription, or a street corner. It only registers that the system is repeatedly receiving an unusually strong signal. The adaptation may reduce the immediate impact of the substance. That can protect against some effects of a particular dose, but it also creates tolerance. The person now needs more of the substance—or more frequent use—to produce the earlier effect or to feel normal. The adaptation that helped the body manage the surplus becomes part of the trap. If the outside supply suddenly stops, the warehouse does not instantly return to its original size. The nervous system may still be adjusted for the substance even though the substance is gone. The result can be withdrawal: not simply a desire, but a body and brain struggling to recalibrate. When the Survival System Is Misled < In Addicton The Survival System is Misled Human beings have powerful systems for responding to deprivation. Hunger is not merely an idea. It is a bodily drive that organizes attention, motivation, memory, and behavior around obtaining food. Severe addiction can create a comparable survival-like focus. The substance becomes highly salient—meaning the brain gives it extraordinary importance. Thoughts, plans, relationships, money, and time may increasingly organize around obtaining and using it. This is not a claim that drug withdrawal is literally identical to starvation. The biology differs. The comparison is useful because it helps explain the intensity of the drive. A person who is truly starving may think about food constantly, take risks to obtain it, become irritable or emotionally blunted, and make decisions that would be unthinkable under ordinary conditions. In severe dependence, withdrawal and craving can produce a similarly narrowed field of attention. The brain begins treating access to the substance as urgently necessary. The addicted mind may not be asking, “Is this consistent with my values?” It may be asking, “How do I end this distress?” That is part of what I mean by a survival-system hijack. The substance is no longer experienced only as a source of pleasure. It has become confused with safety, normality, relief, and continued functioning. Why Endorphin Sensitivity May Have Mattered in My Case In my own case, I have wondered whether differences in endorphin sensitivity or endorphin-system functioning may have played a role in my vulnerability. The body’s endorphin system influences pain, reward, stress, and well-being. Opioid drugs can strongly affect the same general network. I cannot claim that endorphin sensitivity was proven to be the cause of my addiction. Addiction is not explained by one molecule, one receptor, or one event. Genetics, stress, emotional learning, trauma, beliefs, opportunity, social environment, mental health, and repeated reinforcement can all contribute. Still, it is possible that some people experience certain substances as unusually effective or unusually regulating. If a substance produces a powerful sense of relief or normality, the learning signal may be especially strong. The person may not simply think, “I like this.” Their nervous system may learn, “This is important. Remember how to get it.” The Broken Thermostat of Withdrawal The nervous system constantly tries to maintain equilibrium. When an outside substance repeatedly pushes the system in one direction, the body may develop counter-adjustments. For example, opioids can suppress pain and arousal signaling. With repeated exposure, the body adapts in ways that increase opposing arousal systems. Noradrenergic activity, including activity associated with the locus coeruleus, is one part of the opioid-withdrawal picture. When the opioid is removed, the drug’s suppressing effect is gone, but the counter-adjustments do not disappear immediately. The result can include restlessness, anxiety, sweating, rapid heartbeat, agitation, insomnia, and the feeling that the body cannot settle. Alcohol and benzodiazepines involve another especially important balance. GABA-related signaling acts in part like a brake, while glutamate-related signaling is excitatory. With chronic exposure to substances that enhance inhibitory effects, the brain can adapt by reducing inhibitory responsiveness and increasing excitatory drive. When the substance is abruptly removed, the balance can swing dangerously toward over-excitation. This is why abrupt withdrawal from heavy alcohol or benzodiazepine use can cause seizures, delirium, and life-threatening complications. Anyone physically dependent on these substances should seek medical guidance rather than attempting to quit suddenly alone. The body is not simply demanding the drug because a person lacks character. It has adapted to the drug’s presence and is now struggling with the absence of it. Why Cold Turkey Is So Difficult—and Sometimes Dangerous A person may sincerely intend to stop. They may promise themselves, their family, or their treatment team that this time will be different. They may mean it completely. Then withdrawal begins. The person may experience pain, sweating, nausea, restlessness, insomnia, panic, depression, irritability, emotional flatness, cognitive difficulty, or an overwhelming sense that something is terribly wrong. Even after acute withdrawal improves, post-acute withdrawal symptoms—often called PAWS—may continue in waves. Sleep, mood, motivation, pleasure, stress tolerance, and impulse control may remain unstable while the nervous system rebuilds balance. At the same time, the substance may still be associated with relief. The brain remembers: “This ends the distress.” That combination creates a powerful conflict. The conscious mind wants recovery. The body wants immediate relief. Under stress, exhaustion, emotional pain, or withdrawal, the executive functions used for planning and restraint may be less available precisely when they are needed most. This is one reason intention alone often does not solve addiction. It is also why severe alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal should not be managed through unsupervised cold-turkey cessation. Medical detoxification has an important place in recovery and can help manage serious risks safely. Normalization: How the Unthinkable Becomes Ordinary Normalization is the process by which something becomes familiar, expected, and accepted within a person’s everyday environment—even when it once seemed dangerous, unacceptable, or unthinkable. Normalization does not require someone to make a formal decision that harmful behavior is good. It often happens through repetition and comparison. The progression may look like this: “I only use occasionally.” “I use because I am under unusual stress.” “Everyone around me does this.” “This is how we get through the day.” “I need it to work.” “I have to do whatever is necessary to obtain it.” As exposure continues, the person’s reference point changes. Drug use, deception, unsafe environments, and increasingly risky behavior become part of the ordinary landscape. Being around other users can accelerate the process. A group can provide belonging and practical support, but it can also normalize patterns that would appear alarming from the outside. When everyone is focused on supply, money, withdrawal, and immediate survival, the group’s standards may gradually replace the standards the person once used to evaluate their behavior. The question shifts from “Would I ever do that?” to “What else can I do?” The Slow Chipping Away of Morality People sometimes describe addiction as if a person suddenly loses their moral compass. My experience was more gradual. The descent usually occurs through small compromises. A person hides use to protect a relationship. Spends money intended for something else. Misses a responsibility. Tells a partial truth. Accepts help under false pretenses. Makes a promise they already suspect they cannot keep. Each compromise creates discomfort because it conflicts with the person’s self-image. The mind then tries to reduce that discomfort. It explains, minimizes, postpones, or reframes the behavior: “This is temporary.” “I will fix it tomorrow.” “They do not understand what I am going through.” “I had no choice.” “I am only doing what I need to survive.” As the behavior repeats, the emotional alarm may become less intense. What once felt like a major violation becomes familiar. The new behavior becomes the starting point for the next decision. This does not mean the person has no responsibility. It means that responsibility must be understood within the reality of a brain and body increasingly organized around obtaining relief and avoiding withdrawal. The person may not be internally trying to become immoral. The addiction progressively narrows the field of concern until immediate relief dominates long-term values. My Descent: From Systems Engineer to Camden From the outside, a successful professional life can appear to provide protection against addiction. In reality, a career and family can conceal the early stages for a long time. A person may continue working while using. They may compensate, make excuses, hide deterioration, or rely on intelligence and experience to solve problems that the addiction is creating. Their competence becomes scaffolding that temporarily holds up an increasingly unstable structure. But scaffolding can collapse piece by piece. Use takes more time. Money becomes less available. Trust weakens. Responsibilities are missed. Work performance suffers. Relationships become strained. Housing and financial stability deteriorate. The person’s world becomes smaller and more organized around the substance. In my own life, that progression eventually carried me from being a systems engineer with a career and family to addiction and homelessness in Camden. That was not a single decision. It was the cumulative result of many changes—biological, emotional, behavioral, social, and environmental—that reinforced each other over time. Understanding the progression does not erase the harm caused to myself or others. It does, however, make the story understandable. A person is not transformed from “good” to “bad” in one moment. They can become increasingly trapped inside a system that keeps rewarding immediate relief while making every other part of life harder to maintain. When Treatment Environments Teach More Than Recovery I also believe we need to be honest about the limitations of some treatment environments. In my first rehabilitation experience, I learned about the availability of drugs on the streets of Camden and how people navigated that environment to obtain substances. I was exposed to scams and other methods that people used to obtain money and drugs. I am not sharing those details as instructions. I am describing how treatment can sometimes unintentionally expand a person’s knowledge of the very drug culture they are trying to leave. For some people, rehab can become an avenue for learning new contacts, stories, rationalizations, scams, and acquisition strategies. A person may enter treatment with one set of experiences and leave with a larger knowledge base about how other users survive and obtain substances. This does not mean rehabilitation is useless. It means treatment environments need to consider group composition, boundaries, information-sharing, supervision, and the possibility that participants may learn from one another in ways that undermine recovery. In my case, the information I learned in that first rehab experience contributed to my future descent. That is a difficult truth, but honest recovery work requires us to examine what helped and what did not. Two Kinds of Dependence, One Reinforcing Loop Physical and psychological dependence continually strengthen each other. Physical dependence creates withdrawal. Withdrawal creates urgency. Urgency directs attention toward the substance. Using the substance produces relief. Relief reinforces the belief that the substance is necessary. Repeated use deepens physical adaptation. At the same time, emotional cues continue to activate psychological dependence. Stress, shame, loneliness, anger, fear, boredom, or memories can trigger craving even when the person is not in acute withdrawal. That is why simply explaining the consequences may not be enough. The person may already know exactly what the substance is costing them. Knowledge does not automatically dissolve the emotional and physiological learning that keeps the cycle active. Why I Believe Emotional Work Matters Before or Alongside Cessation A substance often begins as a coping mechanism before it becomes an addiction. It may help a person calm anxiety, escape shame, numb grief, feel confident, sleep, socialize, work, or stop thinking about something painful. If the substance is removed without addressing the function it served, the person may be left with the original emotional distress plus withdrawal, PAWS, disrupted sleep, emotional flatness, impulsivity, and fear that they cannot function without it. For that reason, I believe emotional and belief-focused work can sometimes make cessation easier when it is medically appropriate to do so. This is not an argument against detoxification. Detox can be necessary and lifesaving. It is an argument for recognizing that detox and emotional healing address different parts of the problem. The traditional sequence may look like this: Remove or reduce the substance → manage withdrawal → develop coping strategies → address deeper emotional patterns My preferred sequence, when appropriate, may look like this: Address emotions and beliefs → develop internal resources → safely remove or reduce the substance → continue recovery support Both approaches can be valid. Sometimes medical stabilization must come first. Sometimes emotional preparation can begin first. Sometimes both processes occur together. The most useful question is not, “Which approach is universally correct?” It is: What does this person need first in order to have a safe and realistic chance of healing? How I Understand Hypnosis I do not view hypnosis as a mysterious power, mind control, or a loss of consciousness. I see it as a practical way of deliberately working with naturally occurring human processes, including focused attention, absorption, imagination, expectation, suggestion, emotion, perception, and response. People experience these processes every day. They become absorbed in a movie, a book, music, a conversation, a difficult programming problem, or a familiar drive. Attention can become highly focused while other information fades into the background. Hypnosis deliberately structures and directs that flexibility toward a chosen purpose. The hypnotist is a guide, coach, and facilitator. The client remains an active participant—conscious, aware, capable of asking questions, rejecting suggestions, changing their mind, or ending the session. Hypnosis is something a person experiences and participates in, not something simply done to them. Relaxation can be useful, but it is not the definition of hypnosis. Focused attention can occur during curiosity, excitement, fear, anger, fascination, or emotional engagement. The goal is not merely to make someone relaxed. The goal is to use attention and experience constructively. Hypnosis and Addiction Recovery Addiction involves automatic patterns. A person may consciously want one thing while their learned emotional and physiological responses push toward another. Hypnosis can provide a structured context for exploring: What the substance came to represent What emotional state it created or removed What beliefs became connected to using What the person believes they cannot do without it Which situations trigger craving How bodily sensations influence interpretation and behavior What alternatives might become possible Hypnosis is not a machine for installing arbitrary beliefs. It is not a guaranteed solution, and it is not a substitute for appropriate medical, psychiatric, psychological, or addiction treatment. Its potential value is that it can help a person work experientially with patterns that may be difficult to change through intellectual understanding alone. A person may know, “This is harming me,” while still feeling, “I need it.” Hypnotic work can help examine that conflict and create new associations, expectations, emotional responses, and choices. My approach draws from hypnosis and 5-PATH® training, mindfulness, visualization, NLP, CBT, DBT, behavioral approaches, SMART Recovery, and personal experience with addiction and recovery. I do not see these as competing systems where one method must explain everything. I see them as tools that can be adapted to the person, the situation, and the goal. If Traditional Treatment Has Not Worked If you have tried traditional approaches and have not succeeded, that does not automatically mean you lacked commitment, honesty, discipline, or willingness to recover. It does not mean you are constitutionally incapable of change. It may mean that the approach, timing, sequence, treatment setting, or combination of services was not a good fit. Removing a substance can expose the emotional pain, beliefs, and survival patterns that the substance had been temporarily managing. When those issues remain unaddressed, early recovery can become overwhelming. PAWS, emotional flatness, impulsivity, stress, sleep disruption, and the absence of familiar relief can make returning to use feel like the only available option. For some people, the next step is not simply trying harder. It may be finding a different entry point—one that addresses the emotional and belief systems first, while still respecting the need for medically safe cessation when necessary. Detox can help create physical freedom. Emotional healing can help make that freedom livable. Hypnosis may be a powerful tool for beginning that work. Final Thoughts Addiction is not formed in a single moment. It develops through repeated interactions among biology, learning, emotional pain, beliefs, environment, relationships, and behavior. The substance may begin as a solution. It may then become a routine, a requirement, and eventually a survival signal. The body adapts to the outside chemical. The mind adapts to the new normal. The social environment reinforces the pattern. Moral boundaries shift gradually. The person’s world narrows. That process can happen to people who are intelligent, successful, loving, responsible, and deeply committed to their families. It can happen to people who genuinely intend to stop. Understanding addiction as a hijacking of reward, emotion, learning, and survival systems does not remove responsibility. It replaces contempt with a more accurate starting point for change. The person needs safety. The body may need medical support. The mind needs new experiences. The emotions need attention. The beliefs need examination. The coping function needs replacement—not merely removal. Addiction may begin as a solution, become a requirement, and end as a survival drive. Recovery begins when we address not only what the substance does, but what the person has been trying to survive. If you would like to explore whether hypnosis and behavior-change work may be appropriate for your situation, Contact me About The Author Adam Fistler is a Behavioral Change Consultant, Board Certified Hypnotist, Certified 5-PATH® Hypnotist, and former owner of the Baltimore Hypnosis Center. A member of the International 5-PATH® Hypnosis Association and certified by the National Guild of Hypnotists, Adam has studied hypnosis, behavior change, and the relationship between thoughts, beliefs, emotions, and behavior for more than two decades. His perspective is shaped by more than professional training. Adam has also lived through addiction and recovery firsthand across South Jersey and the Philadelphia region, including surviving on the streets of Camden. This gives him a deeply personal understanding of the struggle from both sides: as a practitioner who has helped others create change and as someone who has had to confront his own deeply ingrained patterns and beliefs. During his own recovery, Adam returned to the principles of hypnosis, mindfulness, self-talk, and behavioral change that he had studied throughout his career. He discovered that recovery could be about more than simply managing cravings or avoiding relapse—it could also be an opportunity to understand the beliefs, emotional patterns, and experiences that had shaped his behavior. Today, Adam combines his professional experience with the lessons of his own journey to serve clients throughout South Jersey, Philadelphia, and beyond, helping others explore the possibility of meaningful, lasting change. His approach is grounded in empathy, curiosity, practical tools, and the belief that people are more than the behaviors they are trying to overcome. content: Search: For nearly a century, the mainstream approach to treating alcohol use disorder (AUD) in the Western world has been built on a single core requirement: total, immediate abstinence. Traditional recovery models operate under the premise that an individual must hit "bottom," commit to absolute sobriety, and rely on willpower, social support, or spiritual accountability to maintain it. Yet, for tens of millions of people worldwide, this model yields high rates of relapse. A scientifically validated alternative— The Sinclair Method (TSM) —offers a radically different approach that targets the biological mechanics of addiction rather than relying solely on behavioral restraint. What is The Sinclair Method? Developed in the late 1980s by American neuroscientist Dr. John David Sinclair, The Sinclair Method is an evidence-based, targeted pharmacological treatment for alcohol dependence. Unlike conventional treatments that require patients to stop drinking before starting therapy, TSM actually requires the individual to continue drinking while on the protocol. How It Works: Pharmacological Extinction When a person drinks alcohol, it triggers the brain to release endorphins. These naturally occurring opioids bind to receptors in the brain's reward center, releasing dopamine and creating the euphoric "buzz" or pleasure associated with drinking. Over time, through operant conditioning, the brain builds a powerful, reinforced pathway connecting alcohol to reward, giving rise to intense cravings. TSM disrupts this neural pathway using Naltrexone (or Nalmefene), an FDA-approved opioid antagonist. Targeted Dosing: The patient takes a Naltrexone tablet strictly one to two hours before their first drink of the day. Blocking the Reward: When alcohol is consumed, Naltrexone blocks the endorphins from binding to the opioid receptors. The drinker experiences the motor or intoxicating effects of alcohol, but the neurological "reward" is absent. Un-Learning the Habit: Without the chemical reward, the brain undergoes pharmacological extinction . Over a period of several months, the brain slowly unlearns the connection between alcohol and pleasure. Eventually, cravings decline, alcohol obsession dissipates, and individuals regain control over their drinking—either reducing their intake to moderate levels or choosing voluntary, effortless abstinence. Why Isn't the Sinclair Method Popularized in the United States? Despite clinical studies demonstrating a high long-term success rate—around 78% in clinical trials—TSM remains widely unknown and underutilized in the United States. Several systemic factors contribute to this resistance: Entrenched Abstinence-Only Ideology: American addiction treatment has been heavily shaped by 12-step programs and traditional rehab facilities. The prevailing culture often views alcohol use disorder as a moral or spiritual issue requiring absolute abstinence. The idea of prescribing a pill and instructing a patient to continue drinking runs counter to deeply embedded clinical norms in the U.S. recovery industry. Lack of Financial Backing & Pharmaceutical Incentive: Naltrexone was patented decades ago and is now a low-cost generic medication. Because pharmaceutical companies cannot earn significant profits from generic drugs, there is little financial incentive to fund multi-million-dollar marketing campaigns or educate primary care doctors on targeted Naltrexone protocols. Misunderstanding Medical Protocol: In the U.S., when doctors do prescribe Naltrexone, they frequently instruct patients to take it daily while remaining entirely abstinent. Taking Naltrexone without drinking does not trigger pharmacological extinction, because the brain needs to experience drinking without the endorphin reward to unlearn the craving. This widespread off-label misapplication leads many providers to mistakenly conclude that the drug "doesn't work". Fear of Non-Compliance & Misconceptions: Some clinicians express concern that patients will simply skip taking the pill prior to drinking to get the full euphoric effect. Others worry that medication-assisted treatment (MAT) replaces one dependency with another or fails to address underlying psychological trauma. Claudia Christian’s Advocacy: Bringing TSM to the Public One of the most prominent international champions for The Sinclair Method is actress Claudia Christian , best known for her role as Commander Susan Ivanova in the sci-fi series Babylon 5 . A Personal Turning Point After struggling with severe alcohol dependence for years and trying traditional rehab, detox facilities, and 12-step programs without lasting success, Christian discovered TSM in 2009. Within months of following the protocol, her cravings ceased entirely, an experience she credits with saving her life. The C Three Foundation Driven by the realization that millions were suffering without knowledge of this medical option, Christian founded the C Three Foundation in 2013. The 501(c)(3) non-profit organization is dedicated to: Educating medical professionals and the public about pharmacological extinction. Helping patients find TSM-friendly doctors and resources. Reducing the shame and social stigma surrounding alcohol use disorder. Media and Outreach To expand the reach of TSM advocacy, Christian has authored books (including Babylon Confidential ), produced the award-winning documentary One Little Pill (2014), and delivered a popular TEDx talk titled "How I Overcame Alcoholism" . Through her foundation and public speaking, she continues to push for a paradigm shift in healthcare, advocating for scientific options alongside traditional recovery methods. A Science-Based Option The Sinclair Method represents a shift in how medical science understands and treats alcohol reliance. While it is not a "magic pill" and requires strict adherence to taking the medication prior to drinking, it offers an evidence-based alternative for individuals who have struggled with traditional abstinence-only approaches. For further insight into Claudia Christian's advocacy and her personal recovery story, you can watch her talk How I Overcame Alcoholism . This video provides a direct, firsthand look at how pharmacological extinction works and why she founded her nonprofit to raise awareness.
