content: Search: Early Childhood: Struggles With Extreme, Painful Shyness and Social Awkwardness Author: Adam Fistler, BCH — Behavioral Change Consultant Imagine a child trapped inside himself—desperately longing to connect with other people, yet unable to understand them. To him, people are an enigma. Body language is a puzzle he cannot piece together. He is unaware of basic social behaviors, such as making eye contact, and does not understand the invisible rules that seem to come naturally to everyone else. When another child approaches, terror spreads through his body. The room seems to begin spinning. His chest tightens. He feels suffocated and struggles to breathe. His racing heart feels as though it might pound right out of his chest. His jaw tenses. His fists clench. He is frozen and trapped in panic. “Run away.” “Get out of here.” These thoughts race through his mind. His body is covered in a cold sweat, but he cannot find anything to say. Betrayed by his own mind and his own body, he runs away. Slowly, a strong feeling of frustration and self-betrayal washes over him. Wishing he could disappear, his stomach fills with waves of sickening embarrassment. Anger rises from his chest. He balls his fists, screams silently at himself, and asks: “What is wrong with me?” As he fights back his tears, he has no idea that this struggle will shape much of his childhood. I Was That Child I was that child. I watched life from the outside, trying to find a way in. “Why do other children play with each other and not me?” Those words echoed through the agonizing cries of my childhood. It seemed as though other children possessed a special code—a secret club to which I had not been admitted. They seemed to understand something about friendship, connection, conversation, and belonging that I could not figure out. I felt excluded, but I did not understand why. I lived in the deep, piercing loneliness of being left on the sidelines—the child no one wanted to play with. When Other Children Misunderstand Imagine a child sitting at a table with a large box of crayons and plenty of coloring pages. He is drawing by himself when another child approaches. The child looks up and says: “Hi.” But the other child reacts in an unexpected way. He tenses up. Sweat begins to form. A look of terror flashes across his face. Then, inexplicably, he runs away and moves to another table. The first child is confused: “What’s wrong? What did I do?” He looks around, trying to understand what just happened. Eventually, he reaches a conclusion: “That kid is weird. Maybe he is stuck-up. Something must be wrong with him.” He cannot understand that the other child is experiencing overwhelming fear and confusion. He asks his friends about the situation. “Oh, that kid? He’s a weirdo. He never talks to anyone,” one child responds. “Yeah, he just plays by himself. He’s definitely stuck-up or something,” another adds. At some point, many of the children have tried to approach the other child. The reactions are usually the same: tension, panic, avoidance, and escape. The child is not trying to be rude. He is not trying to make others feel rejected. He is struggling with something the other children cannot see or understand. Growing Up Before Autism Was Well Understood Scenarios like this can be familiar to people on the autism spectrum, especially those who grew up before autism was widely recognized in schools and communities. When I was in elementary school during the 1980s, teachers and school counselors were not trained to identify children on the autism spectrum in the way many professionals are today. Back then, I was simply labeled the “odd child.” Some people assumed I was slow, strange, withdrawn, or socially incapable. Today, I look back and believe it is highly likely that I would have been diagnosed with what was then called Asperger’s syndrome. By the time I sought therapeutic intervention, however, I no longer met the criteria for an autism diagnosis. That does not mean the challenges were imaginary. It means that development, learning, adaptation, and life experience had changed the way those traits appeared. People on the autism spectrum may develop at a different pace in certain areas. The process can take longer. Some skills that appear naturally in others may require conscious learning, repetition, and practice. But taking longer to develop does not mean a person is less intelligent or less capable. In fact, many autistic people grow into exceptionally intelligent, observant, creative, and determined adults. Delayed Speech and Feeling Trapped Inside My childhood difficulties were complicated by delayed speech. I did not begin speaking until I was four years old. Even when I started talking, my speech was difficult to understand. At times, even my parents struggled to comprehend what I was saying. I spent approximately five years in speech therapy throughout elementary school. When you cannot communicate clearly, the world can become even more isolating. You may know what you want to say but be unable to express it. You may have thoughts, feelings, questions, and ideas trapped inside you, with no reliable way to communicate them. Every failed attempt at communication can reinforce the feeling that something is wrong with you. You may begin to expect misunderstanding before you even speak. “This Is Just the Way You Are” As I moved into high school, I was told by school counselors and other people: “This is just the way you are.” “You are always going to be this way.” I can still remember the physical impact of hearing those words. My face began to feel hot and swollen. My nose stung as though I had been slapped. I felt myself falling into the depths of despair. But then something else rose from deep inside me: defiance, anger, determination. I rejected those words with everything inside me. “Bullshit,” I said to myself. “There has to be something out there that can help me. I am going to keep searching until I find it.” I refused to accept a life defined by painful loneliness. I refused to believe that I would forever feel like a ghost walking among other people—able to see them, but unable to communicate with them. My heart felt continually shredded, as if a thousand daggers were piercing my soul. “No more,” I told myself. “I will search everywhere. I will do whatever I can to overcome this.” Beginning the Search I spent my first paycheck on therapy. It seemed like a logical place to begin. And so my journey started. At the time, I did not understand that the foundation was being laid for something much larger. I did not know that I would eventually transform some of my deepest wounds into sources of strength, knowledge, empathy, and purpose. I only knew that I could not continue living the way I was living. I was determined not to let a diagnosis, challenge, obstacle, or life circumstance dictate how I would live. Years of Searching My early attempts centered around traditional therapeutic methods. I attended talk therapy and weekly counseling. I tried to examine my emotions, behaviors, and patterns through the lens of the conscious mind. I gained some useful insights. I learned more about eye contact and began to understand body language somewhat better. I became more aware of social patterns and interpersonal behavior. But overall, I did not feel that years of therapy had produced the results I wanted. I understood more intellectually, but I did not feel substantially different internally. I still felt uncomfortable around people. I still felt socially tense. I still carried the painful expectation that I would be rejected, misunderstood, or humiliated. Eventually, I turned to the internet. I found self-help groups, courses on body language, and material about social anxiety, shyness, communication, emotional patterns, and personal development. I attended seminars and encountered many different schools of thought about emotions, behavior, personality, and the causes of shyness. I developed a great deal of intellectual understanding, but understanding alone was not enough. I was building knowledge, but I still had not achieved what I considered satisfying change. Discovering Hypnosis At some point, I found hypnosis. I had encountered the idea earlier in my search, but the images from television and movies influenced how I thought about it. I assumed hypnosis was strange, mysterious, or perhaps even a little frightening. The problem was that I did not understand what hypnosis really was. Hypnosis was not a mysterious state that someone else forced me into. It was not mind control. It was not magic. It was not a miracle cure. Instead, hypnosis was a term used to describe naturally occurring processes—such as focused attention, absorption, imagination, expectation, emotion, and suggestion—that people experience in everyday life. Hypnosis uses these processes purposefully for personal growth and change. Hypnosis Happens in Everyday Life Hypnosis is Focused Attention. Much like being Asorbed in a Movie When you become deeply absorbed in a movie, your attention becomes highly focused. You are emotionally engaged in the story rather than actively questioning and scrutinizing every detail. You may know that the movie is fictional, but your emotional responses can still be real. A similar process can occur during an argument. Your attention becomes focused on anger, threat, injustice, or the words being exchanged. As the emotional intensity rises, it can become more difficult to think clearly or respond rationally. Being in love can also involve a highly focused state. The words and actions of the person you love may affect you deeply, while those same words or actions from a stranger might have little impact. These are ordinary human experiences involving attention, emotion, expectation, and responsiveness. Hypnosis is not a magical state. It is a structured way of using these natural processes to support inner change and transformation. Setting the Critical Voice Aside Hypnosis does not mean surrendering control. It does not mean someone else takes over your mind. It does not compel you to do something against your values. It does not force you to become a different person. Hypnosis can help you gently set aside the critical and doubting part of your mind—the part that says: “I cannot do that.” “That is impossible.” “I am not worthy.” “I will never get this.” “I am always going to be this way.” “Nothing will work for me.” When that automatic resistance becomes quieter, you may be able to examine your thoughts, beliefs, emotions, and patterns from a more objective perspective. You may become more open to helpful ideas, strategies, imagery, and possibilities that would normally be rejected immediately. In reality, you move through versions of this process every day. You simply may not think of it as hypnosis. Hypnosis is a term used to describe deliberately applying these natural human processes toward personal growth, emotional change, and transformation. Why I Chose the 5-PATH Approach When I discovered hypnosis, I did not approach it blindly. I researched different theories, methods, and schools of hypnosis. Eventually, I chose to study the 5-PATH approach because it was one of the structured hypnosis systems I found that approached personal issues systematically. It offered a thorough process for addressing multiple aspects of a problem rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all suggestion or a single-session promise. There are many schools and philosophies of hypnosis. Some are thoughtful and effective; others are less comprehensive. Because of this, the skill, training, judgment, and quality of the hypnotist matter more than choosing a bargain session or searching for a one-session miracle cure. There is no miracle cure. But there are effective ways to support meaningful and sometimes rapid change. Hypnosis Was the Turning Point Hypnosis became a turning point for me. For the first time, I was able to examine and release some of the old emotions, beliefs, and patterns associated with my painful shyness. The change was like night and day. It was not an instant transformation in which I suddenly became a completely different person. The change developed throughout the hypnosis process, and some of the earliest changes were subtle. I began responding differently to situations without always realizing it at first. I became more comfortable around people. I felt less tense. I did not experience the same level of fear and panic in social situations. The difference was not that hypnosis forced me to become sociable. The difference was that I no longer felt trapped by the same emotional reactions. Hypnosis Restored Choice I am still relatively quiet and reserved. Hypnosis did not turn me into a social butterfly. It did not compel me to seek out people constantly or make me enjoy every social situation. What changed was how I felt around people. Before hypnosis, I often felt fearful, tense, shy, frozen, or desperate to escape. Afterward, I felt more comfortable and at ease. I could choose whether I wanted to socialize or spend time alone. I could decide whether to speak or remain quiet without being controlled by overwhelming panic. That distinction is important. Hypnosis is not about forcing a particular personality or behavior; it is about restoring choice. The Problem With Overpowering Emotional States Overpowering feelings is like hitting the gas to clear a garage door. One mistake people often make when trying to solve personal problems is attempting to overpower one emotional state with another. For example, someone experiencing shyness or social anxiety may try to override fear with confidence. That can work temporarily, but it requires artificial energy. It requires maintaining the confident state and remaining constantly vigilant. You have to stay on guard. I know what that feels like because I tried it myself. Eventually, the artificial confidence fades, and the original emotional response returns. Hypnosis offered a different approach. Rather than forcing confidence over fear, hypnosis helped me release some of the old emotions, beliefs, and patterns that were driving the fear in the first place. When the original emotional drivers are no longer as powerful, you do not need to maintain an artificial state to overpower them. From Client to Hypnotist My experience with hypnosis changed the direction of my life. After hypnosis helped me overcome a lifelong struggle with painful shyness and extreme loneliness, I became inspired to become a hypnotist myself. I spent a very cold winter in 2005 at the Banyan Hypnosis Center for Training & Services in Moundsville, Minnesota. There, I learned to become a hypnotist and passed my initial examination to become a National Guild of Hypnotists Certified Hypnotist. After two years of professional practice, supervision, and peer-to-peer education, I studied for and passed the National Guild of Hypnotists Board Certified Hypnotist examination. I founded the Baltimore Hypnosis Center in Gambrills, Maryland, where I practiced from 2005 through 2009. Eventually, life circumstances led me to South Jersey. During my years of practice, I helped clients with concerns including: Shyness Social anxiety Weight loss Smoking cessation Emotional patterns Personal development Behavioral change Other unique and deeply personal challenges You can read more about my experience at the Baltimore Hypnosis Center on my Professional Experience page. You can also browse testimonials from that period on my Testimonials page. Hypnosis Helped With Comfort—But I Still Needed Skills I Joined Toastmasters to Learn Public Speaking Hypnosis helped me feel comfortable around people and in social situations. The emotional education I gained through my own experiences also helped me understand and incorporate emotional intelligence into my daily life. But hypnosis did not automatically teach me every practical communication skill. Feeling comfortable speaking to people and knowing how to structure an effective speech are not the same thing. While working at Comcast in Center City Philadelphia, I joined my company's chapter of Toastmasters International. Toastmasters is a supportive organization that helps members improve public speaking and leadership skills through structured practice. At that time, I completed the ten-speech Competent Communicator program and received my Competent Communicator award from Toastmasters International in 2016. Hypnosis gave me the ability to feel comfortable speaking in front of groups. Toastmasters gave me practical communication skills and helped me learn how to structure and deliver effective speeches. Both were valuable, but they addressed different parts of the problem. What Hypnosis Can and Cannot Do Hypnosis helped me become more comfortable, but it did not erase my personality. I am still somewhat quiet and reserved. I still enjoy time alone. I am not constantly seeking attention or social activity. What hypnosis changed was the emotional burden attached to social interaction. It helped reduce the fear, tension, and sense of being trapped that had dominated my earlier experiences. It also gave me room to learn. Once I was no longer overwhelmed by panic, I could focus on developing practical skills—such as communication, public speaking, reading social situations, and emotional intelligence. This is an important distinction. Hypnosis may help reduce emotional barriers, but it does not eliminate the need to learn, practice, communicate, or make choices. From Painful Loneliness to Purpose As a child, I was painfully shy, lonely, and isolated from others. I spent years trying to understand why connection seemed so easy for everyone else and so difficult for me. Through relentless determination, research, therapy, education, personal development, hypnosis, and practical experience, I became familiar with many different approaches to change and transformation. The pain did not disappear from my history. Instead, it became part of what helped me understand other people who feel trapped inside themselves. I know what it is like to desperately want connection but feel unable to reach for it. I know what it is like to feel betrayed by your own mind and body. I know what it is like to believe that you are permanently defective because someone tells you, “This is just the way you are.” And I know what it is like to discover that change may still be possible. Your Past Does Not Have to Dictate Your Future Your diagnosis, childhood, social history, challenges, or past experiences do not have to dictate the rest of your life. That does not mean change is always easy. It does not mean every difficulty disappears. It does not mean hypnosis is a miracle cure or that one approach works for everyone. It means that a diagnosis is not the same as a life sentence. A challenge is not the same as an identity. A painful past is not a guarantee of a painful future. Sometimes change begins with a refusal to accept the idea that you are permanently stuck. Sometimes it begins with a question: “What else is possible?” Moving Forward I would not be the person I am today without the challenges I faced as a child. My deepest wounds eventually became sources of strength, determination, empathy, and professional purpose. Hypnosis helped me feel comfortable around people. Therapy and personal development helped me understand myself. Toastmasters helped me build practical communication skills. Continued learning helped me combine different approaches into a broader understanding of behavioral and emotional change. No single method did everything. Each approach contributed something important. If you struggle with extreme shyness, social anxiety, social awkwardness, painful loneliness, or difficulty connecting with others, you do not have to assume that you will always feel this way. You may benefit from therapy, social skills training, mindfulness, communication practice, medical support, behavioral approaches, hypnosis, or a combination of different tools. The most important thing is not finding one perfect system. It is finding an approach that helps you move forward. If you are facing challenges with shyness, social anxiety, confidence, communication, or emotional patterns, then Contact me to discuss how I may be able to help. content: Search: The Next Challenge: From Family Man to Addiction and Recovery After I finally made it through the painful shyness and anxiety that had shaped so much of my early life, I thought the hardest part was behind me. I believed I had solved the problem. I had learned how to function in the world, how to work, how to build relationships, and how to move forward. I did not yet understand that life sometimes waits until one struggle is quiet before introducing another. A Temporary Stay in New Jersey In early 2009, while I was still living in Baltimore, Maryland, I received a call from a former manager I had worked with at Northrop Grumman. He was supporting a Federal Aviation Administration project, and he told me that the contract I had worked on several years earlier had moved to Computer Sciences Corporation in Egg Harbor Township, New Jersey. The assignment was supposed to be temporary. I would travel to South Jersey for three to six months, rewrite the system-development, automation, and logistics system I had helped create, and then finish the contract by flying out of Baltimore-Washington International Airport. On June 8, 2009, I arrived in Egg Harbor Township expecting to be in New Jersey only briefly. But life had other plans. While exploring online dating in the South Jersey area, I met Michele. What began as a temporary work assignment slowly became a new life. On April 10, 2010, Michele and I were married. For a while, I believed I had finally found the stability I had always wanted: a wife, a home, children, and work I was proud of. I was a family man. I had no idea that my next major struggle would begin with a routine medical prescription. The Pill That Made Me Feel Normal About two years into our marriage, I was cleaning the gutters outside our house when the ladder slipped out from underneath me. I injured myself and went to the doctor, who prescribed generic Percocet—oxycodone combined with acetaminophen. No one sets out to become addicted. Whether a person first encounters a substance through a prescription, experimentation, or recreation, they are not imagining the loss of control that may eventually follow. They are simply trying to manage pain, stress, emotion, or life as they understand it at the time. When I took the Percocet, I experienced something I later learned was sometimes called a paradoxical drug effect. Instead of feeling sleepy or sedated, I felt energized, euphoric, and alive. Opiates did not slow me down. They seemed to give me energy, confidence, and emotional lift. For the first time in my life, I felt as if I had discovered something I had been looking for without knowing its name. It was not merely that the pill made me feel good. It made me feel like the version of myself I had always wished I could be. That first prescription did not instantly turn me into an addict. At first, I used the medication only occasionally. Then I began experimenting with it. Eventually, occasional use became monthly use, monthly use became weekly use, and weekly use became daily use. The progression was gradual—so gradual that I could explain away each step as it happened. I did not wake up one morning and decide to destroy my life. I drifted into dependence one decision at a time. Trying to Keep Up With Life Perocet gave me limitless energy.  I could work all day without being tired. Opiates gave me an energy that felt almost limitless. I could play with my children, clean the kitchen, move on to the bathroom, and keep going without feeling tired. From inside my own mind, I felt normal and in control. From the outside, however, I looked increasingly intense and erratic. I had more energy than seemed natural. My movements and behavior became unusual. The difference between how I experienced myself and how other people saw me became wider every day. Eventually, I ran out of the oxycodone I had been prescribed. That was a turning point. I began searching online and found people locally who sold 30-milligram oxycodone pills, often called “the blues.” I had moved from legally obtaining a medication to secretly finding it through people I met on the internet. Outwardly, I was still a husband, father, and technology professional working in Center City Philadelphia. Privately, I was arranging meetings and trying to maintain a habit I could no longer control. I repeatedly told myself that I was going to stop. I would buy a final supply and promise myself that this was the end. But the compulsion to use again was stronger than my promises. I was beginning to learn the difference between wanting to stop and being able to stop. The Person My Family Could Not See My fear of losing my family led me to conseal my use from Michele In 2013, I took a job with Micros in Columbia, Maryland. If you have eaten at a restaurant, you may have encountered a Micros terminal without knowing it. During that period, I traveled from our home in South Jersey to Baltimore on Monday mornings, worked there, stayed with my parents, and returned home on Thursday or Friday. Often, I tried to stop using while I was in Baltimore. I would return home without drugs and begin experiencing withdrawal. Michele saw me come home disengaged, distant, and uninterested. She could not see what was happening inside me. She saw a husband who seemed emotionally absent. I was beginning to experience the physical and psychological consequences of stopping oxycodone. When opiates are removed after regular use, the person may appear cold or checked out. It can look like they no longer care about their family, interests, or life. But underneath that flat exterior, the nervous system may be in turmoil. Pleasure becomes difficult to feel. Motivation disappears. Anxiety and restlessness rise. The ordinary world feels harsh, exhausting, and strangely empty. This is one reason addiction is so difficult for families to understand. The person using may appear to be choosing distance, when internally they are trying to survive a storm they do not know how to explain. Why I Kept It Secret Someone might reasonably ask, “Why didn’t you just tell your wife?” The honest answer is that addiction is not governed by logic alone. It is shaped by fear, shame, and isolation. I was terrified that telling the truth would destroy my marriage, separate me from my children, and expose me as a failure. I believed Michele would reject me if she knew who I had become. I was also ashamed of the lies I had already told. The longer I hid the problem, the more frightening the truth became. In a distorted way, I also believed I was protecting my family. I thought that if I carried the secret by myself, I could preserve the life they knew. Of course, secrecy did not protect anyone. It only allowed the problem to grow in the dark. Shame says, “I am bad.” Guilt says, “I did something bad.” For a long time, I confused the two. I was responsible for my choices and for the damage they caused, but I had also come to believe that I was permanently defective—that I could never make amends or become someone better. I later learned that addiction is not simply a moral failure, a lack of willpower, or a decision to abandon one’s family. Responsibility still matters, but so do compassion and an honest understanding of what happens to the brain and body. Addiction is more complicated than any single explanation. When the Pills Ran Out In January 2014, the people I had been buying oxycodone from became unreachable. I was working in Baltimore and desperately trying to avoid withdrawal when I searched online again. Someone told me, “I don’t have pills, but I have something that won’t make you sick.” That “something” turned out to be heroin. I did not seek heroin because I wanted to become a heroin user. I took it because I was desperate not to become sick. That distinction does not erase the consequences, but it explains how quickly desperation can narrow a person’s choices. Heroin was more powerful than the oxycodone, and it affected my behavior dramatically. From the outside, I became increasingly erratic, irrational, and difficult to recognize. July 4th - The Weekend That Changed Everything Michele was Waiting for me at the Front Door with a Drug Test The weekend of July 4, 2014, became one of the great turning points of my life. Earlier that week, while I was traveling from South Jersey to Baltimore for work, my mother suffered a heart attack. I visited her in the hospital, and by the time I returned home on Thursday, things seemed stable. Waiting for me was Michele. Over time, my strange behavior, frequent flat tires, and increasingly late arrivals had become impossible to ignore. Her friend Judy had correctly guessed that I was addicted. Michele had been searching for another explanation—possibly even narcolepsy—because she did not understand that the “nodding” she saw was related to opiate use. When I came home, Michele was waiting with a drug test. I failed it. I had spent years imagining that discovery as the moment my life would collapse. I expected anger, rejection, and the end of my family. Instead, Michele responded with compassion. She did not lash out or humiliate me. She told me that we would face it together. In the moment I expected to find punishment, I found love. That Sunday, July 7, 2014 Michele and I drove back to Baltimore because my mother was scheduled to have a heart-pump connection removed. My family knew there was a possibility she could die during the procedure, but they had not told me. They were afraid I would not be able to handle it, especially with everything else happening. At first, the procedure seemed to go well. Michele and I went to find something to eat. When we returned, we learned that my mother had gone into cardiac arrest. The medical team kept her alive long enough for my father to call her sisters in Pennsylvania so they could come and say goodbye. And then I saw Michele do something I will never forget. I'll Never Forget how Wonderful Michele Was Conforting my Dying Mother While my mother lay intubated in the hospital bed, Michele sat beside her, held her hand, and talked to her about our sons. She comforted her. She stayed with her. In the middle of a terrifying and heartbreaking moment, she gave my mother tenderness and peace. If anyone ever asked me to describe who Michele truly is, I would point to that moment. She has frustrated me, as I have surely frustrated her, but I will always love her for sitting beside my mother when our family was falling apart. That weekend, my wife learned that I was using drugs, and my mother died within days of one another. It was more grief than I knew how to hold. During the week of the funeral, Michele remained supportive. She was not vindictive or angry. After my mother’s funeral that Friday, she drove me directly from Baltimore to Mirmont Treatment Center in Media, Pennsylvania. That was my first experience with formal drug and alcohol treatment—and the beginning of a long journey through addiction, recovery, education, and change. Learning Beyond the First Answer I've Spent Years Researching Addiction Beyond what is Taught in Rehab My experience in treatment made me want to understand addiction as deeply as possible. If I was going to live with this condition, I believed I needed to learn everything I could about it. I learned about the brain, behavior, withdrawal, cravings, and the many systems involved in motivation, stress, pleasure, and emotional regulation. I also learned that treatment is not one-size-fits-all. The approach that helps one person may not help another. I discovered that twelve-step recovery is meaningful for many people, but it is not the only path. For me, approaches centered on self-efficacy—such as SMART Recovery—offered a language that fit better. I wanted to build skills, examine beliefs, understand triggers, and regain a sense of agency rather than define myself entirely by helplessness. I also became increasingly aware of the limitations of conventional treatment. People can move from one rehabilitation program to another and hear the same information repackaged without receiving new perspectives or practical choices. When a program does not work for someone, the failure is often placed entirely on the person rather than on the possibility that the approach was not a good fit. My own breakthroughs came from learning how different brain systems work together. Dopamine is involved in reward, motivation, movement, attention, and learning, but addiction is not simply a story about “too much dopamine.” Serotonin, GABA, glutamate, endorphins, noradrenaline, and the endocannabinoid system also influence mood, stress, arousal, pain, and recovery. Understanding those systems did not excuse my behavior. It gave me a clearer map of what I was facing. A Different Kind of Recovery I eventually began combining what I had learned with my experience in hypnosis, mindfulness, cognitive behavioral therapy, dialectical behavior therapy, and other practical tools. Recovery became more than avoiding a substance. It became the process of learning how my mind and body worked, recognizing the patterns that kept me trapped, and building new ways to respond. In 2018, I became a certified SMART Recovery facilitator and helped co-run a SMART Recovery group at Recovery at the Crossroads in Blackwood, New Jersey. I began supporting others through peer education and recovery conversations, sharing information I wish I had received much earlier. I do not believe there is one explanation for addiction or one pathway out of it. I believe people need accurate information, dignity, practical tools, and the freedom to find an approach that genuinely helps them. I remain responsible for the harm my addiction caused. Recovery does not require pretending otherwise. But responsibility does not have to mean living forever in shame. I can acknowledge the past without believing that I am nothing more than my worst years. My story did not end when I became addicted. It did not end when my family discovered the truth, when my mother died, or when I entered treatment. Those were painful chapters, but they were not the whole book. The next part of my life began when I stopped asking only, “How do I avoid using?” and started asking, “How do I understand myself well enough to build a life I no longer need to escape from?” That question continues to guide me today.
